name: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
lead: Which resectability box this patient is in, what the next act must not foreclose, and where the neoadjuvant trials disagree badly enough that the sequence has to be decided locally rather than quoted. Revised after reading every paper in the depot in full: the biggest single finding is that almost no trial on this page had a control arm receiving the therapy this page recommends.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 0 · Get a stageable scan before anything else
crit: Pancreas-protocol multiphase CT with a pancreatic parenchymal phase at 40–50 seconds and a portal venous phase at 65–70 seconds
Chest and pelvis CT in the same episode, for complete staging
CA 19-9 and liver function drawn after biliary decompression, not before
Genetic counselling and germline testing offered to every patient, whatever the stage
High-quality imaging no more than 4 weeks old at the time of the operation
gates.ask: Is this scan good enough to decide an operation on, and did anyone put a stent in before it was done?

standard.t: Repeat the scan as a pancreas-protocol CT if the one in front of you is not one — a non-protocol CT is not a staging study.
standard.pref: Every patient referred with an outside scan. NCCN reports that re-imaging patients who arrived with a non-pancreas-protocol CT changed the stage and the management in 56% of cases at a single institution, and that where CT showed a resectable tumour 70% to 85% of patients went on to resection. Both figures are NCCN's citation of single-institution series and are not in the reporting-template paper this item is referenced to.
standard.avoid: Do not accept thick sections, positive oral contrast or a single post-contrast phase. Neutral oral contrast only, because positive contrast degrades the 3D and maximum-intensity-projection reformats that show the vessels. Sections as thin as the scanner allows, under 3 mm and preferably submillimetre, reconstructed at 2–3 mm with multiplanar reformats.
standard.note: Accuracy decays with time because the disease moves: NCCN sets an outer limit of 4 weeks between the staging CT and the operation. Sensitivity for small hepatic and peritoneal deposits is limited however good the protocol is, and protocol quality is not the whole of the problem — in SWOG S1505, 43 of 146 patients centrally reviewed (29%) did not meet the trial's own resectability criteria, 51% of them for arterial interface and 65% for suspicion of distant disease, and adding a mandatory site radiologist checklist moved that only from 33% to 26%. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Report it against the Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association template, in degrees of vessel contact — not in adjectives.
standard.pref: Every staging report. The template covers morphology (appearance in the parenchymal phase, size, location relative to the SMV, duct and biliary cut-off), the arterial evaluation (celiac axis, SMA, common hepatic artery, with vessel contact, soft-tissue contact, hazy attenuation or stranding, focal narrowing and contour irregularity), the venous evaluation (main portal vein and SMV, thrombus, collaterals) and the extrapancreatic evaluation (liver lesions, peritoneal or omental nodules, ascites, suspicious nodes).
standard.avoid: Words like abutment, encasement and involvement are defined in the template by degree — 180 degrees or less of circumferential contact is abutment, more than 180 degrees is encasement — so a report that uses them without the degrees cannot be mapped onto the resectability categories and forces the board to re-read the scan.
standard.note: Downgraded to D on the full-text read. The template is expert consensus from a single meeting at the American Pancreatic Association annual meeting in November 2011, with no Delphi process, no voting, no reported level of agreement, no described literature search and no validation of any kind — the paper does not show that using it changes report completeness, inter-reader agreement, board decisions, resection rates or margins, and reports no inter-reader reproducibility for measuring circumferential contact, which is the measurement the whole template rests on. Variant arterial anatomy — accessory or replaced right hepatic artery, replaced common hepatic artery, and the origin of the replaced or accessory vessel — must still be named whether or not it is in contact, because it changes the operation.

standard.t: Offer genetic counselling and germline testing to every patient with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, regardless of family history.
standard.pref: At diagnosis, in parallel with staging, so a result exists before systemic therapy choices are made. In 3,030 patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma enrolled in the Mayo Clinic pancreas registry between 2000 and 2016, deleterious germline variants in six genes were found in 5.5% overall — CDKN2A (OR 12.33, 95% CI 5.43–25.61), TP53 (6.70, 2.52–14.95), MLH1 (6.66, 1.94–17.53), BRCA2 (6.20, 4.62–8.17), ATM (5.71, 4.38–7.33) and BRCA1 (2.58, 1.54–4.05).
standard.avoid: Do not use family history to select who is tested. In the same cohort the yield was 7.9% with a family history of pancreatic cancer and 5.2% without — a difference far too small to triage on. But do not quote 5.5% as the proportion with an actionable result either: the figure is driven mostly by ATM and BRCA2, and of the six genes only BRCA1/2 has a randomised treatment consequence in this disease, with MLH1 acting through mismatch-repair status rather than through the gene itself.
standard.note: Downgraded to C on the full-text read. This is a clinic-based case series at a tertiary referral centre compared with race and ethnicity matched public sequencing databases (ExAC non-TCGA and gnomAD) rather than with a recruited control group, so it is exposed to differential variant calling and coverage between cases and controls; the CDKN2A and MLH1 intervals rest on a handful of carriers each, and multiplicity across 21 genes and several subgroup strata is not controlled. It is a prevalence and association study: it does not estimate penetrance, carriage was not associated with overall survival (HR 0.86, P=.09), and it does not show that testing changes outcomes. A germline result still drives cascade testing of relatives, which is a separate benefit from the treatment decision.

standard.t: Treat CA 19-9 as a baseline measurement whose value depends on the bilirubin and the patient's Lewis antigen status, not as a diagnostic test.
standard.pref: Draw it once the biliary tree is decompressed and record the bilirubin alongside it, so the number can be compared with later ones. It is most useful as a trajectory under treatment and as one of the three response metrics after neoadjuvant therapy.
standard.avoid: An elevated CA 19-9 does not indicate cancer or advanced disease — it rises with biliary obstruction, cholangitis and benign or malignant inflammation. It is undetectable in Lewis-antigen-negative individuals, in whom NCCN suggests obtaining CEA and CA-125 instead.
standard.note: NCCN grades surveillance CA 19-9 after resection as category 2B, and states there are no data that a rising marker leads to earlier intervention or better outcomes. Treat the two uses — baseline and surveillance — as separate questions. The one place CA 19-9 has randomised-adjacent support is as a response measure: ESMO's 2023 guideline cites a pooled analysis of 17 studies and 2,242 patients in which a fall of more than 50% or normalisation after neoadjuvant treatment was associated with better overall survival (P<0.0001).

alt.t: Pancreas-protocol MRI with contrast as an adjunct to CT, not a replacement for it.
alt.pref: Three situations: a CT-indeterminate liver lesion, a suspected tumour not visible on CT (the isoattenuating tumour, which the template asks to be reported as non-measurable), and iodinated contrast allergy. The protocol is axial T2 single-shot fast spin echo, in- and opposed-phase gradient echo, fat-suppressed T2, diffusion-weighted imaging, dynamic post-contrast 3D fat-suppressed gradient echo in pancreatic, portal venous and equilibrium phases at 2–3 mm, and coronal MRCP under 3 mm.
alt.avoid: Do not substitute MRI for the arterial and venous assessment the pancreas-protocol CT provides, and do not read unenhanced MRI as a staging study — NCCN reserves it for renal failure or a gadolinium contraindication when enhanced CT also cannot be obtained.

alt.t: FDG-PET/CT or PET/MRI after the pancreas-protocol CT in patients with high-risk features, to look for extrapancreatic metastases.
alt.pref: NCCN defines high-risk features as equivocal or indeterminate imaging findings, markedly elevated CA 19-9, a large primary tumour, or large regional lymph nodes. PET before and after starting neoadjuvant therapy also gives the metabolic arm of the three-metric response assessment.
alt.avoid: It is not a substitute for high-quality contrast-enhanced CT and does not belong in routine staging. Order it to answer a question, and name the question.
alt.note: Metabolic tumour volume and total lesion glycolysis appear as hard thresholds in the local liver-only transplant protocol, so if that gate is live the baseline PET has to be acquired in a way that lets those be measured.

alt.t: EUS in selected cases where it is complementary to CT — but not as a routine staging tool.
alt.pref: Separating a benign from a malignant stricture, evaluating a periampullary mass, and characterising a cystic lesion. Across 20 studies and 726 cases, EUS had sensitivity 0.72 and specificity 0.90 for T1–2 and 0.90 and 0.72 for T3–4.
alt.avoid: The T-stage figures are not good enough to overturn a protocol CT, and the procedure is operator dependent. Where EUS is being done anyway, combine it with ERCP in one anaesthetic — see the tissue and drainage gate.
alt.note: The sensitivity and specificity figures are carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page, not in any paper read in full for this depot; the primary reports were not retrieved.

avoid.t: Do not let a stent be placed before the staging scan in a patient who is not septic and whose bilirubin is not rising.
avoid.pref: Where urgent decompression is unavoidable, document why, and complete pancreas-protocol imaging promptly afterwards.
avoid.avoid: Drainage is not routinely recommended before planned upfront surgery, so a stent placed for convenience buys a procedure, its complications, and a degraded baseline CA 19-9, for no benefit.

avoid.t: Do not call a scan negative for metastases and treat that as proof.
avoid.pref: Say what the scan can and cannot exclude, and decide at the board whether staging laparoscopy or PET is worth adding in this patient.
avoid.avoid: CT sensitivity for small hepatic and peritoneal metastases is limited, and the resectability criteria are deliberately built to favour specificity over sensitivity so that no resectable patient is denied an operation. That design means occult metastatic disease is expected, not surprising.

gates.name: 1 · Assign the resectability category
crit: Arterial contact stated in degrees against the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery and common hepatic artery
Venous contact stated in degrees against the SMV and portal vein, with contour irregularity and thrombosis recorded separately
Variant arterial anatomy named, with the degree of contact if present
No distant metastasis, including non-regional nodal metastasis
The category agreed by consensus at a multidisciplinary meeting, not assigned by one reader
Someone has asked whether this scan would survive a central review, because roughly a third of patients called resectable by their own centres do not
gates.ask: Which of the four boxes is this patient in, and who agreed it?

standard.t: Place the patient in exactly one of resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced or metastatic, by consensus at a multidisciplinary meeting, using the stated degrees of contact.
standard.pref: Every non-metastatic patient, before any treatment is offered, because every later gate on this page hangs off which box was ticked. The thresholds are in the quick reference. NCCN is explicit that decisions about resectability status should be made in consensus at multidisciplinary meetings, and ESMO's 2023 guideline asks for the anatomical NCCN criteria to be read alongside the biological and conditional features of the International Association of Pancreatology consensus [III, B], with board discussion in an expert centre [III, A].
standard.avoid: Do not treat the thresholds as biologically derived. The 180-degree cut-point was adopted into the Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association consensus reporting statement from the NCCN criteria of the time rather than derived or validated in it, no outcome study derived it, no inter-reader reproducibility data for measuring circumferential contact were presented with it, and the criteria for resectable disease were deliberately written to favour specificity over sensitivity so that a potentially resectable patient is not denied an operation. They are a shared language, not a prognostic model.
standard.note: Downgraded to D: the category is assigned against a consensus threshold nobody derived. It is also assigned less reliably than the page previously implied. In SWOG S1505, which required formal surgical consultation plus a resectability checklist at 20-plus experienced US centres, central radiology review found 43 of 146 patients (29%) did not meet the trial's resectability criteria — 22 (51%) had arterial interface, 15 (35%) venous interface of 180 degrees or more and 28 (65%) suspicion of distant disease — and all of them had already started protocol therapy. After neoadjuvant therapy, solid tumour contact may be replaced by increased hazy density or stranding around the peripancreatic vessels; NCCN asks for this to be reported on both the staging and the follow-up scans so that the two are comparable.

standard.t: A distant metastasis, including a non-regional nodal metastasis, takes upfront resection off the table regardless of how favourable the local anatomy is.
standard.pref: State this at the board before the anatomy is discussed, so the discussion does not drift into an operative plan for a stage IV patient.
standard.avoid: Do not let a technically beautiful local picture pull a metastatic patient toward resection. NCCN's footnote is unambiguous: distant metastasis, regardless of anatomic resectability, implies disease that should not be treated with upfront resection.

standard.t: Positive cytology from washings taken at laparoscopy or laparotomy is equivalent to M1 disease — and if a resection has already been done, the patient is treated for M1 disease.
standard.pref: Send washings whenever the abdomen is entered for staging or resection, and record the result in the operative note so the oncologist does not have to ask for it.
standard.avoid: Do not treat a positive washing as a technical curiosity in an otherwise successful resection. It changes the postoperative pathway from adjuvant to metastatic.

alt.t: Selective staging laparoscopy, with intraoperative ultrasound as an adjunct, where occult metastatic disease is suspected on imaging or clinical grounds.
alt.pref: Body and tail lesions, equivocal peritoneal or hepatic findings, markedly elevated CA 19-9, and before committing a patient to a long neoadjuvant course. Avoiding an unnecessary laparotomy is achievable in an estimated 23% of patients planned for curative-intent surgery. In a prospective review of 838 patients judged resectable on imaging, 14% were unresectable at laparoscopy — 21% when only pancreatic adenocarcinoma was counted. Preoperative CA 19-9 above 100 U/mL, or above 215 U/mL, is associated with a greater likelihood of a positive finding.
alt.avoid: NCCN does not regard staging laparoscopy as a substitute for poor-quality preoperative imaging, and routine use remains controversial. Its yield depends entirely on how good the CT was and how likely metastatic disease is in that patient.
alt.note: The concern that laparoscopy promotes trocar-site recurrence and peritoneal progression rests on clinical observation and on animal and in vitro data; the one retrospective study addressing it (n=235) found no significant association with poor outcomes. That is weak evidence in both directions. Laparoscopy can be repeated after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, before planned chemoradiation or surgery. Note that in PREOPANC staging laparoscopy was mandatory in the neoadjuvant arm (114 of 119) and discretionary in the surgery arm, and 13 of the 28 patients who never started neoadjuvant treatment were found metastatic at that laparoscopy — which is both a demonstration of its yield and the reason that trial's R0 and nodal comparisons are not symmetrical. [EXPERTISE]

alt.t: Use the term locally advanced only at the time of initial diagnosis, and say so when you use it.
alt.pref: NCCN states the term should only be used at diagnosis, that locally advanced does not imply unresectable tumour, and that once any neoadjuvant therapy has been delivered the criteria for resection should be based on the biological response to treatment.
alt.avoid: A label applied at diagnosis and never revisited is the commonest way a patient who could have been operated on is not. Where there is a response, a second opinion at a centre with expertise in vascular resection and reconstruction is recommended even if the tumour is still called technically unresectable.

avoid.t: Do not close the case on one radiologist's word unresectable.
avoid.pref: Send it to the board with the degrees of contact, and record who agreed the category and on what date.
avoid.avoid: This is a sequence and governance error rather than a judgement call: the guideline requires multidisciplinary consensus, and a single-reader determination removes the patient from every curative gate without one.

avoid.t: Do not re-stage off a post-neoadjuvant scan alone and declare the operation off.
avoid.pref: Judge response on at least two of three metrics — radiologic, biochemical, metabolic — and explore if there is no extrapancreatic progression.
avoid.avoid: Retrospective studies show that radiographic response does not correlate with pathologic response or with margin-negative resection in borderline resectable disease, and that imaging characteristics are an unreliable indicator of resectability after neoadjuvant therapy. NCCN's own instruction is that if no apparent tumour shrinkage is seen and there is no extrapancreatic progression, surgery should still be attempted.

gates.name: 2 · Tissue and drainage, in one anaesthetic
crit: Obstructive jaundice with cholangitis, fever, or intense pruritus
Neoadjuvant therapy planned, or the operation delayed for any reason
A tissue diagnosis is required because the next treatment is not an operation
The diagnosis is uncertain and a removable stent would preserve the option of re-biopsy
Metastatic disease, where enough tissue for next-generation sequencing is itself an indication
gates.ask: Does this patient need tissue before I operate, and if they need a stent, which stent and for how long?

standard.t: In a patient going straight to resection with a high clinical suspicion, do not wait for tissue — biopsy proof of malignancy is not required before resection, and a non-diagnostic biopsy should not delay it.
standard.pref: A pancreas-protocol CT showing a resectable mass with no alternative explanation, in a fit patient, where the operative plan would not change whatever the needle showed.
standard.avoid: Do not carry this permission into any other setting. A pathologic diagnosis is necessary before neoadjuvant therapy, and for locally advanced, borderline resectable and metastatic disease — which is to say for almost everybody who is not going directly to theatre.
standard.note: Treated as a licence to skip tissue in a borderline resectable patient, this becomes the error that starts chemotherapy without a diagnosis.

standard.t: EUS-guided needle biopsy with a latest-generation core needle is the preferred route, and the extra passes are taken at the same sitting and banked.
standard.pref: Every patient who needs tissue and has non-metastatic disease. NCCN prefers EUS over CT-guided biopsy for better diagnostic yield, better safety, and potentially lower risk of peritoneal seeding than the percutaneous approach. Two extra needle passes beyond the diagnostic passes should be taken where safe and feasible and stored for future next-generation sequencing.
standard.avoid: Biopsy the lesion that will give the highest stage — a liver deposit, not the primary, if both are there — and use image-guided biopsy rather than EUS for liver lesions suspicious for metastasis. Sampling only the primary in a patient with a liver lesion wastes the procedure.
standard.note: In metastatic disease, obtaining enough tissue for sequencing is part of the indication, not an afterthought. The seeding argument for EUS over the percutaneous route is NCCN's wording — potentially lower risk — and is not a measured rate. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Where the patient is jaundiced and needs tissue, do the EUS needle biopsy and the ERCP for drainage in the same anaesthesia session.
standard.pref: Best practice per NCCN in obstructive jaundice. It saves a procedure, a sedation and usually a week.
standard.avoid: Do not split them between services and dates by default; that is how patients accumulate procedures and lose weeks before any treatment starts.

standard.t: Biliary drainage is not routinely recommended before an operation that is about to happen — drain for cholangitis or fever, for severely symptomatic jaundice, or because surgery is being delayed, including for neoadjuvant therapy.
standard.pref: Where drainage is indicated it is best accomplished with an endoscopically placed stent. For a jaundiced patient going on to neoadjuvant therapy, decompression is necessary before therapy starts; NCCN describes it as well tolerated with minimal increase in perioperative morbidity, and ESMO recommends endoscopic drainage where bilirubin exceeds 250 micromol/L in patients with cholangitis, those planned for neoadjuvant treatment, or those whose surgery will be delayed beyond 2 weeks [I, B].
standard.avoid: Routine drainage before an imminent operation causes harm: in a multicentre randomised trial of 202 patients with obstructive jaundice from pancreatic head cancer, serious complications within 120 days occurred in 75 of 102 (74%) of the stented group versus 37 of 94 (39%) with surgery alone, relative risk for surgery alone 0.54 (95% CI 0.41–0.71), P<0.001. Complications attributable to drainage occurred in 47 of 102 (46%) versus 2 of 94 (2%) — cholangitis in 27 (26%), stent exchange needed in 31 (30%), occlusion in 15 (15%), pancreatitis in 7 (7%).
standard.note: Both halves of that trial matter, and so do its boundaries. Surgical complications did not differ significantly (35 of 94 [37%] versus 48 of 102 [47%], RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11), nor did mortality from a protocol-specified complication (4 [4%] versus 9 [9%], RR 0.48, 0.15–1.51) or resection rate (67% versus 56%, P=0.11) — so the excess was in drainage-related events and readmissions rather than in the operation, and the trial does not show that drainage makes a pancreatoduodenectomy safer or less safe. Three limits decide how far it travels. It used plastic stents left for 4 to 6 weeks, which is where the cholangitis and exchange rates come from; bilirubin was capped at 250 micromol/L, excluding the most deeply jaundiced; and neoadjuvant chemotherapy was an exclusion criterion, so the trial says nothing about bridging a patient through months of preoperative treatment, which is now the commonest reason to stent. Its control arm also required an operation within one week of diagnosis, guaranteed by dedicated theatre capacity at all 13 hospitals — a unit that cannot deliver that has not got the comparator the trial tested, and delay without drainage is not what was studied. Overall mortality in the trial was 7%, at centres required to perform only 10 resections a year, and 15 of 196 patients (8%) did not have adenocarcinoma on final pathology.

standard.t: Choose the stent for the diagnostic state the patient is in, and keep it as short as feasible.
standard.pref: Self-expanding metal stents are preferable to plastic. If the tissue diagnosis is not certain, use a fully covered SEMS, because it can be removed or exchanged — and it can be removed for better EUS visualisation if the biopsy has to be repeated, then replaced. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, a non-removable partially covered or bare SEMS may be used, since migration is less frequent.
standard.avoid: Plastic stents are for palliation in patients with a predicted survival of less than 3 months. A long stent, or an uncovered metal stent placed before the diagnosis is settled, removes options for no gain.
standard.note: Downgraded to D: no comparative trial supports any of this. NCCN notes stents are an evolving technology, that any stent can occlude, that covered stents may give more durable patency because they prevent tumour ingrowth but may migrate, and that there are no obvious differences between covered and uncovered stents. Partially covered stents were introduced for this reason and still migrate in a substantial number of patients. The one randomised trial of preoperative drainage in this depot used plastic stents only, so the preference for metal rests on practice rather than on a comparison.

alt.t: CT-guided biopsy where EUS-guided biopsy is not feasible.
alt.pref: A patient who cannot have EUS, or in whom the target is not reachable endosonographically.
alt.avoid: It is second choice in non-metastatic disease on yield, safety and the seeding question, so do not reach for it first out of scheduling convenience.

alt.t: Percutaneous biliary drainage, or EUS-guided biliary drainage at a high-volume centre, after a failed ERCP.
alt.pref: NCCN's sequence is to reattempt ERCP at a high-volume centre first, then consider a percutaneous drain, with EUS-guided drainage as an alternative at a high-volume centre.
alt.avoid: Do not move straight to a percutaneous drain after one failed attempt at a low-volume unit. [EXPERTISE]

alt.t: A pancreatic duct stent, in the specific circumstance of persistent pancreatitis from pancreatic duct obstruction that is preventing other therapy.
alt.pref: NCCN lists this as indicated in special circumstances only.
alt.avoid: Not part of routine preoperative preparation, and not a treatment for pain.

avoid.t: Do not draw the baseline CA 19-9 in a jaundiced patient and then use it prognostically.
avoid.pref: Draw it after adequate biliary drainage, with liver function tests, and record the bilirubin beside it.
avoid.avoid: Biliary obstruction and cholangitis both raise CA 19-9, so a pre-drainage value cannot be compared with a post-treatment value or used to triage toward staging laparoscopy. This matters more than it used to, because the response assessment that decides on an operation after neoadjuvant therapy uses CA 19-9 as one of its three metrics and is interpretable only against a baseline drawn in a decompressed patient.

avoid.t: Do not keep re-biopsying a resectable mass you intend to resect.
avoid.pref: Decide in advance what a negative result would change. If the answer is nothing, the patient needs a theatre date, not another needle.
avoid.avoid: Each attempt costs a procedure, a delay and the currency of the 4-week staging scan, and NCCN explicitly says a non-diagnostic biopsy should not delay resection when suspicion is high.

gates.name: 3 · Resectable — upfront resection or chemotherapy first
crit: No arterial tumour contact with the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery or common hepatic artery
No SMV or portal vein contact, or contact of ≤180° without vein contour irregularity
No distant metastasis, including non-regional nodes
Fit for pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy at a high-volume centre
High-risk features either absent, or present and named in the note
gates.ask: Does this patient go to theatre first or to chemotherapy first — and can I say honestly what the five trials show?

opts.name: Upfront resection, then adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX
opts.when: NCCN's stated standard approach in resectable disease has been upfront surgery followed by postoperative treatment, and ESMO's 2023 guideline goes further: neoadjuvant therapy is not recommended for resectable PC due to limited phase III evidence, except in the context of clinical trials — graded [II, E], a recommendation against. No randomised trial has shown a neoadjuvant strategy to be superior in anatomically resectable disease.
opts.pref: A fit patient with resectable anatomy and no high-risk features, where adjuvant chemotherapy can realistically be delivered. The meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (1,194 patients) found no overall survival benefit for neoadjuvant treatment in the resectable subgroup, hazard ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.63–1.28), while finding one in the borderline resectable subgroup, 0.60 (0.38–0.96) — but the test for a difference between those subgroups was not significant (p=0.081), so the split this page is organised around is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect. On mature 5-year data the adjuvant arm of this strategy delivers median overall survival 53.5 months (95% CI 43.5–58.4) against 35.5 months (30.1–40.3) for gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.68 (0.54–0.85), P=.001.
opts.avoid: Do not read upfront surgery as surgery alone, and do not overstate the attrition argument. NCCN and PRODIGE-24's own authors put the proportion of resected patients who never receive adjuvant chemotherapy at up to 30%, and that is the strongest argument for the other sequence — but the randomised data do not show that neoadjuvant sequencing fixes it: pooled across the nine trials, the proportion starting adjuvant therapy was no different (57.7% versus 55.6%, RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.76–1.12, p=0.353). Committing to this option still means committing to a named plan for who delivers chemotherapy and when.

opts.name: Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX, then surgery
opts.when: PREOPANC-2 (n=369 modified intention to treat, 19 Dutch centres) compared eight cycles of full-dose neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX followed by surgery and no adjuvant treatment against the PREOPANC chemoradiotherapy regimen followed by four cycles of adjuvant gemcitabine: median overall survival 21.9 months (95% CI 17.7–27.0) versus 21.3 months (16.8–25.5), hazard ratio 0.88 (0.69–1.13), p=0.32. The trial's conclusion, and NCCN's, is that either regimen may be considered in resectable or borderline resectable disease.
opts.pref: A fit patient with high-risk features, or one in whom the board judges that selecting out occult metastatic disease before a major operation is worth the resection-rate cost — occult metastatic disease was found at surgery in 12 of 156 (8%) after FOLFIRINOX versus 25 of 166 (15%) after chemoradiotherapy, a post hoc comparison. PREOPANC-2 is the trial that justifies using FOLFIRINOX rather than chemoradiotherapy if a neoadjuvant route is chosen, and it is a failed superiority trial, not a win and not a demonstration of equivalence: the confidence interval reaches 1.13, so a 12% relative benefit for FOLFIRINOX is not excluded, and the one significant secondary endpoint went the other way (ypN0 58% versus 47%, p=0.0073, with ypN2 in 20% versus 7%).
opts.avoid: NORPACT-1 is the only randomised trial of neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX against upfront surgery restricted to resectable pancreatic head cancer, and its primary endpoint was significant in favour of upfront surgery: 18-month survival 60% (95% CI 49–71) versus 73% (62–84), p=0.032, with median overall survival 25.1 months (17.2–34.9) versus 38.5 months (27.6–not reached), hazard ratio 1.52 (1.00–2.33), log-rank p=0.050 by intention to treat. Grade 3 or worse events occurred in 42 of 73 (58%) versus 19 of 47 (40%). Read it as a failure to show benefit, not as evidence of harm: it is a phase 2 trial designed at a two-sided alpha of 0.15, nothing is significant per protocol (18-month p=0.14; hazard ratio 1.46, 0.99–2.17, p=0.058), and its delivery failed — 16 of 77 (21%) allocated to neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX never received it and all 16 went straight to resection, only 37 of the 61 who started (61%) completed four cycles, and 16 (26%) received one or two.
opts.note: Two further things decide how much weight NORPACT-1 can carry. Its control arm is the only partly modern comparator in the whole neoadjuvant literature, and only partly: 19 of 44 resected control patients (43%) actually received adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX and 25 of 44 a gemcitabine-based regimen, with mFOLFIRINOX permitted only after an August 2018 amendment. And its 38.5-month control-arm median far exceeds every comparable upfront-surgery arm (14.3 months in PREOPANC), so the headline comparison is driven as much by an unusually good control arm in 63 patients with 28 deaths as by a poor experimental one. Eleven patients (8%) had final pathology other than PDAC, including 3 distal cholangiocarcinomas and 2 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours in the upfront arm, and they remain in the intention-to-treat denominator.

opts.name: Neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy, then surgery, then adjuvant gemcitabine
opts.when: The PREOPANC regimen: three cycles of gemcitabine with 36 Gy in 15 fractions during the second cycle, surgery, then four cycles of adjuvant gemcitabine. The long-term analysis of PREOPANC (n=246, median follow-up 59 months, 210 of 246 patients dead) gave an overall survival hazard ratio of 0.73 (95% CI 0.56–0.96), p=0.025, in resectable and borderline resectable disease combined.
opts.pref: Where the board has decided on a neoadjuvant route and wants the regimen with a positive randomised comparison against upfront surgery. PREOPANC-2 found no survival difference between this and FOLFIRINOX, so either is defensible, and this is the regimen to prefer where FOLFIRINOX is not tolerable.
opts.avoid: Read both reports and note what the comparator was. The initial primary analysis was not significant — median overall survival 16.0 versus 14.3 months, hazard ratio 0.78 (0.58–1.05), p=0.096 — and the resection rate was lower, 61% versus 72%, p=0.058. The difference in medians in the long-term analysis is 1.4 months (15.7 versus 14.3); what separates is the tail, with 5-year survival 20.5% (14.2–29.8) versus 6.5% (3.1–13.7). The adjuvant comparator in both arms was gemcitabine monotherapy, and in the upfront-surgery arm only 65 of 127 patients (51%) received any chemotherapy at all — so the trial compares a front-loaded strategy with a control arm half of which was never treated systemically, and it does not answer today's question.
opts.note: Three further qualifications from the full text. The primary endpoint moved from negative to positive at a second look with no prespecified plan for that analysis and no multiplicity adjustment, so the nominal p=0.025 should be read in that light. A 1.4-month median difference alongside a 14-point difference at 5 years means the hazards are far from proportional, yet a single hazard ratio is quoted. And the subgroup the page relies on is not established: in the long-term analysis the resectable subgroup was non-significant (hazard ratio 0.79, 0.54–1.16, P=.23) and the borderline resectable subgroup significant (0.67, 0.45–0.99, P=.045), with no significant interaction across any of seven prespecified subgroups. Twenty-eight of 119 patients (24%) never started the neoadjuvant regimen, staging laparoscopy was mandatory only in that arm, and WHO performance status 0 was recorded in 58% of the neoadjuvant arm against 39% of the surgery arm without adjustment in the primary model.

opts.name: Enrolment in Alliance A021806, or another randomised trial
opts.when: A021806 is the phase 3 trial that asks this exact question in resectable disease — perioperative versus adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX, enrolment 358, primary endpoint overall survival from randomisation. As of 6 October 2026 its registry record (NCT04340141) shows it active and not recruiting, with primary completion scheduled for December 2028 and no results posted.
opts.pref: The honest position in resectable disease is that the sequencing question is open, so offer a trial wherever one is available.
opts.avoid: Do not cite A021806 as evidence for either sequence, in either direction. Nothing has been published; what is known of it comes from a trials-in-progress abstract and the registry entry. A page that lists it among the trials that showed something is wrong.

standard.order: Ordered by what the randomised evidence actually supports in anatomically resectable disease, which is upfront resection with adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX — not by effect size. The full-text read strengthens that ordering and weakens the page's confidence in everything behind it. ESMO's 2023 guideline recommends against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease at [II, E]. The only trial restricted to this population that compared the two sequences directly, NORPACT-1, had a primary endpoint significant in favour of upfront surgery, though at a two-sided alpha of 0.15, non-significant per protocol, and with 21% of the neoadjuvant arm never receiving the drug and going straight to resection. The decisive structural fact is the comparator: no neoadjuvant trial in this depot gave its control arm modern adjuvant therapy except NORPACT-1, and there only 19 of 44 resected control patients (43%) received adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX. PREOPANC's control arm received adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy and only 51% of it received any chemotherapy; PREOPANC-2 has no upfront-surgery arm at all and gave its FOLFIRINOX arm no adjuvant treatment; ESPAC5's adjuvant therapy was gemcitabine-based in 41 of 43 patients; S1505 and A021501 had no randomised control. So PREOPANC's long-term hazard ratio of 0.73 was obtained in a mixed population against a comparator no pathway would now offer, PREOPANC-2 showed two neoadjuvant regimens to be indistinguishable rather than either to beat surgery first, and NORPACT-1 pointed the other way in a phase 2 trial with a 38.5-month control-arm median that no other trial matches. Pooled across nine randomised trials the resectable subgroup shows no benefit (HR 0.90, 0.63–1.28), the borderline resectable subgroup does (HR 0.60, 0.38–0.96), and the test for a difference between them is not significant (p=0.081). Neoadjuvant treatment lowers the resection rate (72.6% versus 80.6%, RR 0.94, 0.89–0.99) while raising the R0 rate (43.8% versus 33.0% of the R0 denominator, RR 1.35, 1.16–1.57) and the N0 rate (30.9% versus 15.0%, RR 2.03, 1.50–2.74), neither of which translated into survival in any individual trial, and roughly doubles serious adverse events (56.1% versus 27.0%). It does not raise the proportion of patients who start adjuvant therapy (57.7% versus 55.6%, p=0.353), which was the mechanism the whole strategy was built on.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item 1, and the live choice on this page. The trials genuinely disagree and the page does not resolve them. PREOPANC is positive on long-term overall survival after a negative primary analysis, in a mixed population, against adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy half of whose arm received no chemotherapy; PREOPANC-2 is a failed superiority trial between two neoadjuvant regimens with no upfront-surgery arm; NORPACT-1's primary endpoint favours upfront surgery in exactly the population at issue but at alpha 0.15, with 21% non-receipt and a control arm that outperforms every comparator in the literature; ESPAC5 favours short-course neoadjuvant chemotherapy on a secondary endpoint after failing both primary endpoints, in 86 analysed patients with 12 months of follow-up; ESMO recommends against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease at [II, E]; and A021806 has not reported. The group must decide whether the local default for an anatomically resectable tumour without high-risk features is upfront resection, and if it is not, which neoadjuvant regimen and on what grounds — knowing that no trial has compared a neoadjuvant strategy with upfront surgery followed by adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX delivered to everyone who can take it. Audit: resectability category at diagnosis, sequence chosen, resection rate, R0 rate with millimetre clearance, time from diagnosis to first treatment, and the proportion of resected patients who never start adjuvant therapy.

standard.t: Whichever sequence is chosen, write down before the operation who delivers the chemotherapy, when it starts, and who restages before it does.
standard.pref: Every resectable patient. The one claim both camps accept is that a substantial minority of resected patients never get timely adjuvant therapy at the intended dose — NCCN and PRODIGE-24's authors put it at up to 30% — which is a system failure rather than a biological one and is fixable by naming an owner. What the trials do not show is that giving chemotherapy first solves it: across the nine randomised trials the proportion starting adjuvant therapy was the same either way (57.7% versus 55.6%, p=0.353).
standard.avoid: An operative note that ends at the skin, with the oncology referral left to be made after discharge.

alt.t: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a resectable tumour that has high-risk features, named in the note.
alt.pref: NCCN allows neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease, especially with high-risk features, which it defines as equivocal or indeterminate imaging findings, markedly elevated CA 19-9, a large primary tumour, or large regional lymph nodes. The rationale is selection: treating micrometastatic disease earlier, and identifying surgical futility before an operation rather than after it.
alt.avoid: Do not present it as evidence based in this group. The pooled resectable subgroup shows no overall survival benefit (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.63–1.28), none of the randomised trials was restricted to high-risk resectable disease, ESMO recommends against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease outside a trial at [II, E], and NCCN itself says there is limited evidence to recommend specific neoadjuvant regimens outside a clinical trial and that panel practice varies.
alt.note: Downgraded to D on the full-text read: this is a guideline permission with no trial behind it in the population named. Two numbers set the price. Pooled across the nine trials, neoadjuvant treatment lowered the resection rate (72.6% versus 80.6%, RR 0.94, 0.89–0.99) and roughly doubled serious adverse events (56.1% versus 27.0%) — though the published risk ratio for that harm, 1.92 with a reported 95% CI of 1.28 to 1.89, does not contain its own point estimate in either the abstract or the table, so the magnitude as published cannot be relied on even though its direction is clear. If this route is taken, tissue is mandatory first, and the response assessment in the borderline resectable gate applies — including the rule that a patient with no shrinkage but no extrapancreatic progression is still explored.

alt.t: Perioperative chemotherapy as studied in SWOG S1505 — mFOLFIRINOX or nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine, given before and after resection — only with its result stated.
alt.pref: A randomised phase 2 pick-the-winner trial in resectable disease, designed to select a regimen for further study, with 147 patients enrolled and 102 eligible and evaluable after central radiology review. Preoperative chemotherapy was started by 96% of each arm and completed by 84% and 85%; 40 of 55 (73%) and 33 of 47 (70%) underwent resection; R0 was achieved in 34 of 40 (85%) and 28 of 33 (85%) of those resected.
alt.avoid: It selected no winner and cleared no bar. Both arms missed the primary endpoint: 2-year overall survival 47% (95% CI 31–61), P=.15 with mFOLFIRINOX and 48% (31–63), P=.14 with nab-paclitaxel and gemcitabine, against a prespecified historical threshold of 40%, so the between-arm comparison was never performed. Median overall survival was 23.2 and 23.6 months. Do not quote the completion figure the way this page previously did: only 31 of 40 (78% of those resected, 56% of eligible patients) and 26 of 33 (79%, 55%) started postoperative chemotherapy, and all treatment was completed by 49% and 40% — 16 of the 73 patients who had surgery (22%) could not start adjuvant chemotherapy at all. Pathologic complete or major response was 10 of 40 (25%) and 14 of 33 (42%), in resected-only denominators.
alt.note: Downgraded from B to C. There is no randomised control arm: both arms were tested against a historical 2-year survival of 40% drawn from adjuvant trials, whose populations were selected after surviving surgery and recovering, so the comparison is biased against a strategy randomised at diagnosis and the failure to beat 40% is not evidence that perioperative chemotherapy is worse. Nobody in the trial received upfront surgery followed by adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX. Forty-five of 147 randomised patients (31%) were removed from the analysed population, 43 of them for failing central radiology review, after they had already received protocol therapy. Age was capped at 75 and performance status at Zubrod 0–1. Its most durable contribution is the misclassification finding in the resectability gate, not a survival result.

alt.t: PAXG — cisplatin, nab-paclitaxel, capecitabine and gemcitabine — as a neoadjuvant option in certain circumstances only.
alt.pref: A randomised phase 3 trial across 17 Italian academic hospitals (n=260) in pathologically confirmed resectable or borderline resectable disease found median event-free survival 16.0 versus 10.2 months against mFOLFIRINOX, hazard ratio 0.63 (0.47–0.84), p=0.0018.
alt.avoid: The endpoint was event-free survival, not overall survival, and NCCN added it as useful in certain circumstances specifically because not all centres have experience with the regimen. Do not adopt a four-drug regimen on an event-free survival result at a centre that has never given it.
alt.note: The citation for this trial is carried only in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page; the primary report was not retrieved for this depot and was not read in full, so neither the event-free survival figure nor the hazard ratio has been checked against the published paper. Read it before the regimen is used.

avoid.t: Do not use chemoradiotherapy as the primary neoadjuvant modality in place of multiagent chemotherapy — but do not overstate what the trials show about it either.
avoid.pref: Multiagent systemic chemotherapy remains the initial choice in the neoadjuvant setting per NCCN. Chemoradiation is sometimes added after chemotherapy, and its role and necessity remain poorly defined.
avoid.avoid: Alliance A021501, in borderline resectable disease, closed its mFOLFIRINOX-plus-hypofractionated-radiotherapy arm early for futility when only 10 of the first 30 evaluable patients (33%) achieved R0 resection against a threshold of 12, versus 17 of 30 (57%) with mFOLFIRINOX alone. The mFOLFIRINOX arm met its primary endpoint against a historical benchmark (18-month survival 66.7%, 95% CI 56.1–79.4, median overall survival 29.8 months, 21.1–36.6) and the radiotherapy arm did not (47.3%, 35.8–62.5; median 17.1 months, 12.8–24.4). Retrospective comparisons suggest radiation may improve local control with no survival difference — that is the most that can be claimed for it.
avoid.note: Downgraded from B to C, because A021501's design forbids the comparison this item rests on. Each arm was tested against a historical 18-month survival rate of 50% assembled by the investigators from series published 2004–2015, at a one-sided alpha of 0.07; the protocol permitted a between-arm comparison only if both arms were promising, and arm 2 was not, so every arm-versus-arm figure is descriptive and the radiotherapy arm was stopped on a surrogate before its survival data matured. The denominators of 65 and 55 are evaluable patients who initiated treatment, not the 70 and 56 randomised; 16 of arm 1's 70 patients were registered sequentially without randomisation after arm 2 closed; and 15 of 55 arm 2 patients (27%) never received the radiotherapy that defines their arm. Pancreatectomy was completed in only 32 of 65 (49%) and 19 of 55 (35%). PREOPANC-2 cuts directly against a strong version of this recommendation: it found neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy and neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX indistinguishable on overall survival (21.3 versus 21.9 months, HR 0.88, p=0.32). Doses studied for neoadjuvant chemoradiation are 36 Gy in 2.4 Gy fractions, 45–56 Gy in 1.8–2.2 Gy fractions, and 33–50 Gy in 5 fractions. SBRT after modern multiagent chemotherapy appears feasible without excess surgical complications in experienced centres, but NCCN states further study is needed before it is recommended in borderline resectable disease.

avoid.t: Do not start neoadjuvant therapy without a tissue diagnosis.
avoid.pref: Tissue first, in the same anaesthetic as the drainage if the patient is jaundiced.
avoid.avoid: The permission to operate without tissue applies only to going directly to resection. Once a patient is given chemotherapy, a wrong diagnosis is treated for months before anyone notices.

avoid.t: Do not deliver a neoadjuvant course that is not coordinated with the centre that will do the operation.
avoid.pref: NCCN's wording is that when feasible, treatment should be performed at or coordinated through a high-volume centre, and that determinations of resectability after neoadjuvant therapy should be made individually in a multidisciplinary setting.
avoid.avoid: A patient who completes chemotherapy locally and is only then referred arrives with a scan that is weeks old, no baseline PET, and a CA 19-9 drawn while jaundiced — which makes the response assessment impossible to do properly. [EXPERTISE]

gates.name: 4 · Borderline resectable — treat, then re-ask the question
crit: Head or uncinate: solid tumour contact with the SMA of ≤180°, or with the common hepatic artery without extension to the celiac axis or hepatic artery bifurcation
Body or tail: solid tumour contact with the celiac axis of ≤180°
SMV or portal vein contact of >180°, or ≤180° with contour irregularity, or vein thrombosis with suitable vessel above and below for reconstruction
Solid tumour contact with the inferior vena cava
Solid tumour contact with variant arterial anatomy, with the degree of contact recorded
gates.ask: Has this patient responded enough to justify the operation their anatomy is going to require?

standard.t: Multiagent neoadjuvant chemotherapy first, then restage and re-ask the resectability question — this is where the randomised evidence for the neoadjuvant route is strongest.
standard.pref: A fit borderline resectable patient with a tissue diagnosis. In the pooled analysis of nine randomised trials, the borderline resectable subgroup showed an overall survival benefit for neoadjuvant treatment, hazard ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.38–0.96), against none in the resectable subgroup, 0.90 (0.63–1.28). In the long-term PREOPANC analysis the borderline resectable subgroup was the only significant one, hazard ratio 0.67 (0.45–0.99), P=.045. In ESPAC5, 1-year overall survival was 39% (95% CI 24–61) with immediate surgery, 78% (60–100) with gemcitabine plus capecitabine, 84% (70–100) with FOLFIRINOX and 60% (37–97) with capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy, p=0.0028, with pooled neoadjuvant versus surgery hazard ratio 0.29 (0.14–0.60), p=0.0052.
standard.avoid: State the limits in the same breath, because they are large. ESPAC5 randomised 90 patients against a target of 100 and analysed 86; its primary endpoints were recruitment rate and resection rate and both were negative — recruitment ran at 2.16 patients per month across 16 sites, and resection occurred in 21 of 31 (68%) after immediate surgery versus 30 of 55 (55%) after neoadjuvant therapy, p=0.33, numerically favouring immediate surgery, with R0 resection in 3 of 21 (14%) versus 7 of 30 (23%), p=0.49. Follow-up was capped at 12 months and there were 31 deaths in the whole trial. The control arm's median CA 19-9 was 802 kU/L against 322 to 623 kU/L in the neoadjuvant arms, an unadjusted and strongly prognostic imbalance in a trial with 16 to 31 patients per arm. Of the 43 patients who received adjuvant therapy anywhere in the trial, 41 (95%) got gemcitabine or gemcitabine plus capecitabine and only 2 (5%) got modified FOLFIRINOX.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C on the full-text read. The resectable-versus-borderline split that this gate depends on is not statistically established: the between-subgroup test in the pooled analysis was not significant (p=0.081), PREOPANC's interaction test was not significant in either report, and PREOPANC-2 found no treatment-effect heterogeneity in any subgroup (all interaction p at or above 0.23). The pooled estimate is also unstable — it depends on post hoc removal of NORPACT-1 and the pooled ESPAC5 chemotherapy comparison as outliers, which drops the only trial whose control arm partly resembles current practice and collapses heterogeneity from I² 55.8% to 0% by construction. ESPAC5's own internals cut against its mechanism: the chemoradiotherapy arm had the best pathology (37% R0, 25% node positive) and the worst neoadjuvant survival, and the authors note the survival benefit was unrelated to the resection rate. Disease-free survival from surgery was 33% (19–58) after immediate surgery and 59% (46–74) after the combined neoadjuvant arms, hazard ratio 0.53 (0.28–0.98), reported as p=0.016 in the abstract and p=0.043 in the results text. Grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 2 of 28 (7%) after immediate surgery and 17 of 50 (34%) after neoadjuvant therapy.

standard.t: Restage with pancreas-protocol CT or MRI of the abdomen plus chest and pelvis CT after neoadjuvant therapy, and judge response on two of three metrics.
standard.pref: Every patient at the end of neoadjuvant therapy. The three metrics are radiologic (RECIST change on high-quality triple-phase CT or contrast-enhanced MRI), biochemical (CA 19-9 or CEA, interpretable only if the baseline was elevated and liver function has normalised) and metabolic (FDG-PET SUV or metabolic tumour volume against a baseline treatment-naive avid scan). Where the metrics conflict — tumour smaller on CT but CA 19-9 rising — NCCN asks for a third metric and a board discussion, deciding on two of three. The biochemical metric is the one with the most supporting data: ESMO cites a pooled analysis of 17 studies and 2,242 patients in which a CA 19-9 fall of more than 50% or normalisation after neoadjuvant treatment was associated with better overall survival (P<0.0001).
standard.avoid: Do not read mild increases in perivascular soft tissue as progression; NCCN states this alone does not represent progression, ESMO states that persistent perivascular soft tissue is not synonymous with residual tumour, and after neoadjuvant therapy solid contact is often replaced by hazy density or stranding.
standard.note: Examples of an optimal response given by NCCN are CA 19-9 normalisation, or near-normalisation, or at least a 50% decrease, and a complete or near-complete metabolic response on PET. The degree of significance is explicitly left to the local treatment team, which makes it a ratification item. ESMO adds the relevant caveat about the radiologic metric: imaging performance for restaging after chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy is lower than in treatment-naive settings. The trials bear that out — pathologic and nodal response in PREOPANC-2 and NORPACT-1 moved substantially without survival moving at all.

standard.t: Operate 4 to 8 weeks after completing neoadjuvant therapy, and only where there is a high likelihood of achieving R0 while avoiding R2.
standard.pref: The surgical principles NCCN sets for an anatomically advanced tumour that has responded are en bloc resection of the tumour and at-risk tissue to a negative margin, re-establishment of end-organ arterial inflow and venous outflow, restoration of gastrointestinal continuity, and biliary drainage. Much of this is assessed intraoperatively, because cross-sectional imaging distinguishes viable tumour from scar poorly.
standard.avoid: Do not attempt a resection whose likely outcome is R2. And do not abandon one because the vessel contact looks unchanged — if there is no apparent shrinkage and no extrapancreatic progression, NCCN's instruction is that surgery should still be attempted.

opts.name: Venous (portal vein / SMV) resection and reconstruction
opts.when: NCCN states venous resection of the portal/SMV axis is supported by evidence if complete tumour excision to R0 is technically feasible with reasonably limited risks.
opts.pref: A responder whose only barrier to R0 is a reconstructable venous segment, at a centre that does these routinely, with suitable vessel proximal and distal to the involved site.
opts.avoid: It is associated with higher complexity, greater potential blood loss, increased postoperative morbidity and mortality, and a higher likelihood of a positive margin. A vein resection done to convert an R2 into an R1 is not a gain.

opts.name: Consolidative chemoradiation before surgery
opts.when: NCCN says consolidative chemoradiation may be considered after chemotherapy and before surgical resection where the response is significant, and may be considered where the response is minimal as an alternative to switching regimens.
opts.pref: Where the board wants to improve the chance of a clear margin in a tumour whose anatomy makes R0 marginal.
opts.avoid: Its role and necessity remain poorly defined. A021501 closed its radiotherapy arm early for futility on R0 rate in the first 30 evaluable patients (10 of 30 versus 17 of 30) and its arms are by design not comparable, so the descriptive difference in median overall survival (17.1 versus 29.8 months) cannot be read as harm from radiotherapy — but nothing in the trial supports adding it, and 15 of 55 patients allocated to it never received it.

opts.name: Arterial resection (hepatic artery, celiac axis, SMA)
opts.when: NCCN restricts it to centres with proven experience in pancreatectomy with vascular resection and reconstruction, and to highly selected patients after extensive neoadjuvant therapy with objective responses.
opts.pref: Almost nobody. Where it is contemplated, NCCN requires that the patient be counselled about the operative morbidity and mortality risk, the potential effect on quality of life, and that the long-term benefit — the chance of cure — is currently unknown.
opts.avoid: It is often part of a multivisceral resection with significantly greater morbidity and mortality. Do not offer it for a minimal response: NCCN's governing rule is that the more complex and risky the resection, the greater the objective response needed to justify it.

alt.order: Ordered by how well the guideline supports each, not by survival data — there is no randomised comparison of any of these three in borderline resectable disease, and the one randomised trial that tested adding radiotherapy to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in this population stopped that arm for futility. Venous resection is the only one NCCN says is supported by evidence; consolidative chemoradiation is a may be considered whose necessity the guideline calls poorly defined; arterial resection is a highly selected salvage at specialist centres with an explicitly unknown long-term benefit.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item 2: does this programme offer arterial resection or arterial divestment for PDAC at all, and if so under what minimum volume, which surgeons, and with what consent document? NCCN leaves the decision to centres with proven experience and requires explicit counselling that the chance of cure is unknown — that is a governance decision, not a case-by-case one. Ratification item 3: what counts locally as a significant response, since NCCN hands the definition to the local treatment team. Audit: response category recorded, resection attempted, R0 rate and 90-day mortality, by vascular resection type.

alt.t: Switch to a different regimen and reassess, rather than operating, where the response is minimal or there has been local progression without metastases.
alt.pref: NCCN's response table: with a minimal response, resection is considered in selected tumours without or with limited vascular involvement and no significant increase in surgical risk, and otherwise a different neoadjuvant therapy is considered with reassessment after second-line chemotherapy. With local progression and no metastatic progression, switching regimen is recommended, and resection may then be considered if there is no further progression and R0 is technically feasible — for a tumour with vascular involvement, only after a significant response to the second regimen.
alt.avoid: Do not interpret switch and reassess as indefinite therapy. Set the reassessment date when the switch is made.

alt.t: Where the response warrants resection but the operation is not technically feasible locally, get a second opinion at a centre with expertise in vascular resection.
alt.pref: NCCN recommends this explicitly at every response category in its table. It is the step most often skipped.
alt.avoid: Do not record not resectable here as not resectable. [EXPERTISE]

avoid.t: Do not abandon the operation because the degree of vessel contact has not changed.
avoid.pref: Judge the response on the three metrics and the clinical picture — performance status, pain, satiety, weight and nutrition, diabetes control are all listed by NCCN as possible metrics of response.
avoid.avoid: NCCN's significant-response row states that resection is recommended in the majority of cases independent of the degree of vascular involvement if R0 is technically feasible. Radiographic vascular contact after chemotherapy frequently represents fibrosis, imaging cannot tell the two apart, and ESMO states that imaging performance after chemotherapy is lower than in treatment-naive settings. Note also that less vascular work was needed after neoadjuvant therapy in the trials that counted it — concomitant venous resection in 14% versus 29% in NORPACT-1 (p=0.0034) and vascular resection in 16.5% versus 21.4% in the pooled analysis — so unchanged contact on the scan is a poor guide to what the operation will require.

avoid.t: Do not operate for a minimal response when the operation required is an arterial resection.
avoid.pref: Switch regimen, reassess, and only reconsider an arterial resection after a significant response.
avoid.avoid: This inverts NCCN's rule that the risk of the operation sets the threshold for the response needed to justify it, and it is the combination with the worst morbidity and mortality on the page.

avoid.t: Do not use the word unresectable for a patient who has not yet had systemic therapy.
avoid.pref: Borderline resectable is a treatment category, not a verdict. Say what the barrier to R0 is and what would have to change.
avoid.avoid: A patient told at diagnosis that they are inoperable rarely gets re-asked the question, which is how a responder is lost.

gates.name: 5 · The operation, and what R0 actually means
crit: Pancreatoduodenectomy for head and uncinate tumours; distal pancreatectomy for body and tail
Standard, not extended, lymphadenectomy
Peritoneal washings sent, and the result recorded in the operative note
Specimen inked and sliced to a protocol that allows millimetre reporting of every margin
Done at a high-volume centre, by a surgeon who does them
gates.ask: Did I take the right nodes, and will the pathologist be able to tell me the margin in millimetres?

standard.t: Standard lymphadenectomy, to the stations the International Study Group on Pancreatic Surgery names — extended lymphadenectomy gives no survival benefit.
standard.pref: For pancreatoduodenectomy the ISGPS consensus is to resect stations 5, 6, 8a, 12b1, 12b2, 12c, 13a, 13b, 14a, 14b, 17a and 17b, using Japanese Pancreas Society nomenclature. For cancers of the body and tail, removal of stations 10, 11 and 18 is standard. Lymphadenectomy also matters for adequate nodal staging, which drives the adjuvant discussion.
standard.avoid: Extended lymphadenectomy — nodes along the left side of the SMA and around the celiac trunk, splenic artery or left gastric artery — showed no survival benefit over standard lymphadenectomy in the trials the consensus summarises and cannot be recommended. There was no level I evidence on the prognostic impact of positive para-aortic nodes.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C, and flagged for provenance: this consensus statement is cited from its abstract only. No new papers were obtained for this depot and the full text was not retrieved, so the station list and the no-benefit claim have not been checked against the published trials the consensus relies on, and neither has the strength of agreement behind either. ISGPS reached consensus on selectively removing suspected nodes outside the resection area for frozen section, but no consensus on whether to continue or terminate the resection when those nodes are positive — so that is a local decision made in advance, not in the room. Both pancreatic resection in a relatively fit patient and non-resectional palliative treatment were accepted as reasonable in that situation. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: R0 in this disease means more than 1 mm of clearance — report the distance in millimetres for every margin within 1.0 cm of tumour.
standard.pref: Every specimen. Per the current College of American Pathologists protocol, tumour at or within 1 mm of a resection margin constitutes a positive margin, and ESMO's 2023 guideline uses the same definition. NCCN asks for clearance reported with millimetre accuracy for all margins where tumour is within 1.0 cm, and with centimetre accuracy beyond that, so that the data accumulate for future analysis.
standard.avoid: Do not present the 1 mm rule as established in pancreatic cancer. NCCN states that the recommendation is based primarily on extrapolation from data on rectal adenocarcinoma and that there is currently a lack of definitive evidence for what constitutes an adequate margin in pancreatic resection specimens. A standardised definition does not yet exist.
standard.note: Downgraded from C to D on the full-text read: this is a threshold nobody derived. The single study that supplied the clinical argument for it, 163 consecutive pancreatoduodenectomies at one centre, answered its own question in the null — median survival 15.4 months (95% CI 11.3–18.2) for equivocal R1, tumour within 1 mm but not reaching the margin, against 12.6 months (9.2–14.3) for unequivocal R1, log-rank P=0.102 — and concluded the two should be treated as one category on the strength of a non-significant test. Equivocal R1 versus R0 was also non-significant (P=0.114), so the study cannot separate the intermediate group from either neighbour. R0 (n=35) gave median survival 25.4 months with a 95% CI of 10.5 to 40.8 months, and margin status did not survive multivariable adjustment (univariate HR 1.747, 1.117–2.734, P=0.015; adjusted HR 1.443, 0.896–2.324, P=0.132), where lymph node ratio, tumour size and adjuvant chemotherapy did. Only 27% of that cohort received adjuvant chemotherapy, in 1997–2007. The practical consequence matters more than the prognostic one: applying the rule moved the R1 rate at that centre from 44% to 79%, which means R0 rates are substantially a function of local pathology protocol and the R0 figures quoted across the trials on this page — PREOPANC 71% of resected, ESPAC5 14% to 23%, NORPACT-1 56% versus 39%, APACT 76% with no central pathology review — are not comparable with one another. The 16-versus-14-month and 35-month margin-clearance figures carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page come from a different review, appear in a sentence that inverts them, and were not retrieved for this depot; confirm the direction against the published discussion before quoting them.

standard.t: Dissect the specimen to a stated protocol — axial or bivalve — and accept that there is no single correct method.
standard.pref: Axial slicing, perpendicular to the long axis at regular intervals, preserves spatial relationships and is useful for radiologic-pathologic correlation. The bivalve method, bisecting along probes in the bile and pancreatic ducts, is better for localising small lesions near the ampulla or ducts and for assessing ductal involvement and margins. Knowing the clinically suspected lesion is what should pick the method.
standard.avoid: What is not optional is clear and accurate assessment of the margins, tumour size, and the relationship to pancreatic surfaces, margins, bile duct, main pancreatic duct and duodenum. Organs resected en bloc need serial sectioning to assess both direct extension and separate metastatic deposits, with at least one section demonstrating each.
standard.note: In distal pancreatectomy, assess the peripancreatic soft-tissue surfaces and the pancreatic neck, document splenic vessel involvement and splenic invasion, and consider shaving and submitting the splenic artery and vein margins. Frozen section of the pancreatic neck is a recommended option. Direct tumour invasion of the spleen is pT3.

standard.t: Send peritoneal washings whenever the abdomen is open, and act on a positive result.
standard.pref: At staging laparoscopy and at resection. Intraoperative ultrasound can be used as an adjunct to further evaluate the liver, the tumour and vascular involvement. The yield is real: in PREOPANC, 13 of the 28 patients allocated to neoadjuvant therapy who never started it were found metastatic at the mandatory staging laparoscopy.
standard.avoid: Positive cytology is equivalent to M1 disease. If a resection has already been performed in such a patient, they are treated for M1 disease — so the result has to reach the oncologist, not sit in the chart.

alt.t: A written minimum annual volume for pancreatoduodenectomy at this centre, with a textbook-outcome audit behind it.
alt.pref: NCCN's opening line in this guideline is that decisions about diagnosis, resectability and management should involve multidisciplinary consultation at a high-volume centre, and it repeats high-volume centre at the drainage, vascular resection, recurrence and gastric outlet gates. A threshold that is written down makes the referral decision auditable.
alt.avoid: The guideline never states a number, and no number here is evidence based. Volume-outcome relationships in pancreatic surgery are observational and consistent; the threshold itself is a governance choice. [EXPERTISE]
alt.note: NCCN never states a number, and no number here is evidence based. Volume-outcome relationships in pancreatic surgery are observational and consistent; the threshold itself is a governance choice. The one randomised dataset in this depot that looked at it found centre volume associated with survival in a post hoc multivariable model (10 or more patients enrolled, HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.98, P=.03, in PRODIGE-24's 77 hospitals) — a finding confounded with case mix, surgical quality, access to relapse therapy and country, and selected by a stepwise procedure with no multiplicity correction. Do not cite it as a derived threshold. [EXPERTISE]

alt.t: Resection of a local recurrence, in a carefully restaged patient, as part of a multimodal plan rather than as an isolated operation.
alt.pref: In a pooled analysis of 55 patients from 19 studies who underwent pancreatectomy for recurrent pancreatic cancer, 1-, 3- and 5-year survival were 82.2%, 49.2% and 40.6%. NCCN asks for careful evaluation in a multidisciplinary clinic with detailed restaging, and a plan that may include neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy and then resection.
alt.avoid: Fifty-five patients across nineteen studies is a selected series of selected series. Chemoradiation can be considered for local recurrence if radiation was not given before, but NCCN notes limited data to support specific radiotherapy recommendations in this setting. Where there is metastatic disease with or without local recurrence, this is a systemic problem — see the metastatic gate.

alt.t: Resection of limited pulmonary-only metastases after resection, in a selected patient.
alt.pref: The lung is a common site of recurrence after pancreatic resection, and NCCN states resection may be considered for those with limited pulmonary-only metastases.
alt.avoid: NCCN also states that more data are needed before recommendations can be made about managing pulmonary metastases, so this is a case-by-case board decision and not a pathway.

avoid.t: Extended lymphadenectomy.
avoid.pref: Standard lymphadenectomy to the ISGPS stations.
avoid.avoid: Extending the dissection to the left side of the SMA and around the celiac trunk, splenic artery or left gastric artery showed no survival benefit in the trials the ISGPS consensus summarises, and the consensus is that extended lymphadenectomy cannot be recommended. The consensus statement is cited from its abstract only; the full text was not retrieved for this depot.

avoid.t: A pathology report that says margins negative without millimetres.
avoid.pref: Agree the reporting format with pathology once, in writing, including which margins are inked, which are shaved and which are taken perpendicular.
avoid.avoid: Without millimetre clearance the adjuvant radiation discussion cannot be had, and the data NCCN asks the field to accumulate are not accumulated. The guideline's own argument is that if under 1 mm clearance proves to carry an unacceptably high local recurrence rate, then postoperative radiotherapy would deserve strong consideration in exactly those patients — which is unanswerable without the number.

avoid.t: Attempting a resection whose likely outcome is R2.
avoid.pref: NCCN's instruction is that resection should only be attempted if there is a high likelihood of achieving R0 while avoiding an R2 resection.
avoid.avoid: An R2 resection in this disease delivers the morbidity of a major pancreatectomy with none of the oncologic benefit, and it delays systemic therapy.

gates.name: 6 · Adjuvant therapy, and what surveillance is actually for
crit: A macroscopically complete resection has been performed
Restaging before adjuvant therapy shows no recurrence
Performance status and recovery allow a multiagent regimen, or do not
No neoadjuvant therapy was given — or it was, and the response is known
Germline and somatic results are back, or have been chased
gates.ask: Which regimen, when does it start, and does this patient still have resected-stage disease at all?

opts.name: mFOLFIRINOX for 24 weeks
opts.when: PRODIGE 24 / CCTG PA.6 (n=493) is the strongest adjuvant result in this disease and NCCN lists mFOLFIRINOX as a preferred adjuvant option for patients who had no neoadjuvant therapy. ESMO's 2023 guideline takes the same position for fit patients at [I, A], and recommends completing 6 months of adjuvant chemotherapy at [I, A].
opts.pref: A recovered patient with good performance status. On the mature 5-year analysis, median disease-free survival 21.4 months (95% CI 17.5–26.7) versus 12.8 months (11.6–15.2) against gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.66 (0.54–0.82), P<.001; median overall survival 53.5 months (43.5–58.4) versus 35.5 months (30.1–40.3), hazard ratio 0.68 (0.54–0.85), P=.001; 5-year overall survival 43.2% (36.5–49.7) versus 31.4% (25.5–37.5); metastasis-free survival 29.4 versus 17.7 months.
opts.avoid: The toxicity is the whole of the trade-off and must be said out loud: grade 3 or 4 adverse events in 180 of 237 (75.9%) versus 128 of 242 (52.9%), with the one treatment-related death in the gemcitabine arm. Delivery was poor — 67.2% completed all 12 cycles, only 33.6% achieved a relative dose intensity of 0.80 or more, and 55% discontinued oxaliplatin at least once — so adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX in practice means a dose-attenuated, incompletely delivered regimen. Eligibility was restricted to age 18 to 79, no coronary disease, WHO performance status 0 or 1, full recovery from surgery, a clear postoperative scan and a postoperative CA 19-9 below 180 U/mL, so these figures do not transfer to a patient who has not recovered from a pancreatoduodenectomy, and they are not the expectation for resected PDAC in general.
opts.note: Three things the 3-year report did not show. The effect attenuated with mature data, as early stopping for benefit at 91.8% of expected events predicts: the disease-free survival hazard ratio moved from 0.58 to 0.66, overall survival from 0.64 to 0.68, and the much-quoted 54.4-month median to 53.5 months. Most patients in both arms still relapse — 5-year disease-free survival differs by only 7.1 points (26.1% versus 19.0%) against 11.8 points at 5-year overall survival, so part of the survival gain accrues after relapse. And post-relapse survival was numerically worse in the mFOLFIRINOX arm (13.1 versus 15.0 months), with chemotherapy at relapse reaching 66.9% against 83.0% of relapsing control patients, 74.2% of whom received FOLFIRINOX — so the trial partly measures the benefit of giving the regimen early rather than at relapse. In the 101 patients aged 70 or older (20.5% of the trial) the disease-free survival benefit did not reach significance (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.53–1.39). Quality of life was never collected.

opts.name: Gemcitabine with capecitabine
opts.when: NCCN's other preferred adjuvant option for patients who had no neoadjuvant therapy, and ESMO's alternative for patients over 75, ECOG performance status 2 or a contraindication to mFOLFIRINOX at [I, B]. ESPAC-4 (n=730 analysed) gave median overall survival 28.0 months (95% CI 23.5–31.5) versus 25.5 months (22.7–27.9) against gemcitabine monotherapy, hazard ratio 0.82 (0.68–0.98), stratified log-rank p=0.032.
opts.pref: A patient who wants adjuvant treatment but cannot take a triplet — poorer performance status, neuropathy, a slow recovery, or a preference against irinotecan and oxaliplatin. Its population is the least selected in the adjuvant literature: WHO performance status up to 2, R1 margins allowed and no ceiling on postoperative CA 19-9, which is why its medians sit below PRODIGE-24's and CONKO-001's.
opts.avoid: Do not offer it as equivalent to mFOLFIRINOX, and state both halves. The comparator was gemcitabine alone, the two combinations have never been compared directly, and the difference in medians bought over gemcitabine was 2.5 months. The relapse-free survival endpoint was negative (13.9 versus 13.1 months, hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.73–1.02, p=0.082), the trial was stopped and published early at 458 of 480 target deaths on a signal of efficacy, and the widely quoted 5-year figures (28.8% versus 16.3%) are estimates extrapolated well past the bulk of the data at 43.2 months median follow-up. Grade 3–4 events occurred in 226 of 359 (63%) versus 196 of 366 (54%), with neutropenia 38% versus 24% and hand-foot syndrome 7% versus 0%, and 169 of 364 combination patients (46%) did not complete all six cycles.
opts.note: The benefit sits almost entirely in the R0 subgroup — median overall survival 39.5 months (32.0–58.0) versus 27.9 months (23.8–34.6) in R0, against 23.7 months (20.7–27.1) versus 23.0 months (21.6–26.2) in R1 — reported as a trend test across four groups with no treatment-by-margin interaction test, and 60% of the trial was R1.
