Reading ESPAC-4 as support for adjuvant gemcitabine with capecitabine specifically in a margin-positive patient is reading something the data do not show. The trial is also the source of the prognostic weight of postoperative CA 19-9: 113 of 662 patients (17%) had a value above 92.5 kU/L with median survival 13.1 months (10.8–16.2) against 29.6 months (26.6–32.1) below it, which is the selection step CONKO-001 and PRODIGE-24 applied and ESPAC-4 did not.

opts.name: Gemcitabine alone
opts.when: An other recommended option in NCCN. CONKO-001 (n=354 analysed) established that adjuvant therapy beats observation: median disease-free survival 13.4 months (95% CI 11.6–15.3) versus 6.7 months (6.0–7.5), HR 0.55 (0.44–0.69), P<.001, and final median overall survival 22.8 versus 20.2 months, hazard ratio 0.76 (0.61–0.95), P=.01, with 5-year survival 20.7% (14.7–26.6) versus 10.4% (5.9–15.0) and 10-year 12.2% versus 7.7% at a median follow-up of 136 months.
opts.pref: A frail patient in whom the choice is between single-agent treatment and none.
opts.avoid: The median overall survival gain over observation was 2.6 months; the durable difference is in the 5- and 10-year rates. Eligibility required postoperative CEA and CA 19-9 both below 2.5 times the upper limit of normal — about 92.5 kU/L for CA 19-9 — which ESPAC-4 later showed silently removes the 17% of resected patients whose median survival is 13.1 months, so the curves describe a favourably selected population.
opts.note: Downgraded from A to B on the full-text read. Overall survival was a secondary endpoint that became significant only on the final of several analyses, nine years after the primary report, with no multiplicity adjustment reported for the repeated testing. The authors themselves note that because relapse was common in the first year and gemcitabine was standard therapy at relapse, the design is better read as immediate versus delayed gemcitabine than as chemotherapy versus none. The primary disease-free survival endpoint was assessed in part by abdominal ultrasound every 8 weeks with no central radiology review and recurrence dated from the first subjective symptom, in an open-label trial — which is why a 2.4-fold disease-free survival difference sits beside a 2.6-month median survival difference. Eighteen of 186 patients (10%) never started gemcitabine, mainly for postoperative complications, and only 62% completed all six cycles. Enrolment ran 1998 to 2004 across 88 centres with no central pathology review and no uniform margin definition, so neither its R1 rate nor its 20.2-month observation arm is a usable benchmark today.

opts.name: A fluoropyrimidine alone
opts.when: NCCN lists fluorouracil with leucovorin and continuous-infusion fluorouracil as other recommended adjuvant options, and capecitabine monotherapy as a treatment option.
opts.pref: Where gemcitabine is contraindicated or the patient will not tolerate it.
opts.avoid: No trial establishes a fluoropyrimidine alone as equivalent to the combinations above. The arms that support it sit inside ESPAC-1 and ESPAC-3, neither of which was retrieved or read in full for this depot; their medians (20.1 and 23.0 months) are in the same range as every other single-agent arm from that era, and NCCN notes scepticism about the efficacy of the fluorouracil and folinic acid regimens used in those trials.

standard.order: Ordered by the size and quality of the randomised comparison each regimen won, which is a real ranking here — unusually for this page — but a narrower one than the medians suggest. PRODIGE 24 is the only adjuvant trial to put an 18-month difference in median overall survival on the table, and it did so against the then-standard, in a population restricted to age under 80, no cardiac disease, WHO performance status 0 or 1, full surgical recovery and postoperative CA 19-9 below 180 U/mL; nothing in it describes what to do for a patient who has not recovered from a pancreatoduodenectomy, and its 5-year disease-free survival advantage is 7.1 percentage points. Every comparator in this list is adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy or observation, so the ordering is a chain of comparisons against regimens no pathway would now offer a fit patient, and the two preferred options have never been compared with each other. NCCN also notes how similar the single-agent arms of the older trials were to one another — 22.8 months in the gemcitabine arm of CONKO-001, 20.5 in the gemcitabine-containing arm of RTOG 9704, 20.1 in the bolus fluorouracil arm of ESPAC-1, and 23.6 and 23.0 in the two arms of ESPAC-3 — which is a useful reminder of how small the single-agent era's differences were, and a reminder that those arms were selected very differently on CA 19-9 and age.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item 4: is mFOLFIRINOX the local default for every recovered good-performance-status patient who had no neoadjuvant therapy, given 75.9% grade 3–4 toxicity, a relative dose intensity of 0.80 or more in only 33.6% of patients, no significant benefit in the 101 patients aged 70 or older (HR 0.86, 0.53–1.39) and post-relapse survival numerically worse than in the gemcitabine arm — and what performance-status or recovery threshold moves a patient to gemcitabine with capecitabine? Ratification item 5: what is the local rule for adjuvant therapy after neoadjuvant therapy? NCCN says only that the options depend on the response to neoadjuvant therapy and other clinical factors, and ESMO states plainly that the benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy following neoadjuvant therapy and pancreatectomy remains to be established with randomised data lacking. No trial defines total duration, whether to continue the same regimen or switch, or what to do after a complete pathologic response — and PREOPANC-2's FOLFIRINOX arm gave no adjuvant treatment at all. Audit: regimen, cycles completed, dose intensity, time from surgery to first cycle, and grade 3–4 toxicity.

standard.t: Restage before the first cycle — a proportion of patients have already relapsed.
standard.pref: Every patient. NCCN states it is important to evaluate for disease recurrence before initiating adjuvant therapy because of the risk of early relapse. A patient who has relapsed is on the metastatic gate, not this one.
standard.avoid: Do not start a 24-week adjuvant course on the assumption that the postoperative scan will be clean.

standard.t: Prioritise completing the course over starting it quickly.
standard.pref: A retrospective analysis of ESPAC-3 found that completion of the six-course chemotherapy, but not the time to initiate it, was an independent prognostic factor for survival. NCCN's inference is that delaying until the patient has fully recovered from surgery may allow completion of the full course and improve outcomes.
standard.avoid: This is a retrospective analysis of a randomised trial, not a randomised comparison of timing, and it is vulnerable to the obvious confounder — patients who complete treatment are patients who were well enough to complete it. Do not use it to justify an open-ended delay. The same confounding appears in PRODIGE-24's own mature report, where completing all cycles predicted survival (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49–0.84, P=.002; 5-year overall survival 41.9% versus 27.4%) in a landmark analysis while achieving a relative dose intensity of 0.80 or more did not (HR 1.01, 0.80–1.28, P=.93) — which is the clue that completion marks patient fitness rather than drug effect, and that pushing a patient through all 12 cycles is not what the finding supports.
standard.note: Downgraded from C to D. The primary report for the ESPAC-3 analysis is carried only in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page; it was not retrieved or read in full for this depot, so none of its figures has been checked. The PRODIGE-24 landmark analysis quoted above is post hoc, with variables selected by stepwise procedures and no multiplicity correction.

alt.t: Adjuvant nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine — only if both halves of APACT are stated.
alt.pref: A patient who cannot take mFOLFIRINOX and in whom a taxane doublet is preferred to gemcitabine with capecitabine. At the 5-year cutoff, with 88% data maturity, median overall survival was 41.8 versus 37.7 months against gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.678–0.947), P=.0091, with 5-year overall survival 38% versus 31%.
alt.avoid: APACT (n=866) missed its primary endpoint: independently assessed disease-free survival 19.4 months (95% CI 16.62–21.91) versus 18.8 months (13.83–20.30), hazard ratio 0.88 (0.729–1.063), P=.18. The trial's own statement is that because the primary endpoint was not met, all other comparisons are descriptive, and the journal's relevance note calls it a negative phase 3 study that fails to change the standard of care. The overall survival figure comes from the third of three successive cutoffs, with the P value improving from .045 to .0232 to .0091 across December 2018, April 2020 and April 2021 with no prespecified plan for repeated testing and no multiplicity adjustment anywhere. Grade 3 or worse treatment-emergent events occurred in 371 of 429 (86%) versus 286 of 423 (68%), serious events in 41% versus 23%, and two treatment-emergent deaths occurred in each arm.
alt.note: Downgraded from B to C. The unpriced cost is neurological: grade 3 or worse peripheral neuropathy in 15% of the combination arm and 0% of the gemcitabine arm, with 84% of those affected not improved to grade 1 or less at the primary cutoff and a median 195 days to improve by one grade — in a trial that collected no quality-of-life data at all. Only 287 of 432 patients completed six cycles against 310 of 434 on gemcitabine, 64% needed a dose reduction, and the population is the most selected in the adjuvant literature: CA 19-9 below 100 U/mL with a median of 13.6 U/mL, a clear screening scan, ECOG 0–1, and 1,226 patients screened to randomise 866, which is why the gemcitabine arm reached 37.7 months. The trial's most durable contribution has nothing to do with the regimen: in the same gemcitabine arm, blinded independent review gave a median disease-free survival of 18.8 months and the unblinded investigators gave 13.7 months, with 77% concordance and 48% to 51% of patients censored. Every other adjuvant trial on this page used unblinded investigator-assessed disease-free survival and reported 12.8 to 13.4 months, so disease-free survival differences in open-label adjuvant trials are partly a detection artefact.

alt.t: Adjuvant chemoradiation after chemotherapy, in a node-negative patient, as a discussion rather than a recommendation.
alt.pref: RTOG 0848 randomised the addition of fluoropyrimidine-based chemoradiation after adjuvant gemcitabine-based chemotherapy in resected pancreatic head cancer. Patients with node-negative disease had longer overall and disease-free survival with the addition; patients with node-positive disease did not.
alt.avoid: Do not extend this to node-positive disease — in RTOG 0848 chemoradiation did not improve overall or disease-free survival in that group, which is the opposite of the intuition. The benefit was seen in patients who received single-agent gemcitabine as their systemic therapy, so it does not transfer to a patient who had mFOLFIRINOX, and no study has shown superiority of chemoradiation before versus after chemotherapy in the adjuvant setting.
alt.note: Downgraded from C to D: the RTOG 0848 primary publication was not retrieved or read in full for this depot, and the result is carried only in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page. Adjuvant chemoradiation remains a controversial topic in resected pancreatic cancer, and NCCN warns that RTOG 9704 cannot be compared directly with CONKO-001, ESPAC-1 or ESPAC-3 because of differences in design, imaging timing and patient characteristics. The margin-status subset analyses are retrospective and carried in the same extraction: pooled analyses report benefit in both R0 and R1 subsets, with a relative risk of 0.52 (95% CI 0.36–0.74, P<.001) in one R1 analysis and a non-significant hazard ratio of 0.72 (0.47–1.10) in a four-study meta-analysis. None of these figures has been checked against a primary report.

alt.t: Surveillance after resection — history and examination, CA 19-9 and contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis — offered with an explicit statement of what it is for.
alt.pref: NCCN's stated rationale is consensus-based: earlier identification of recurrence may allow enrolment in investigational studies or other treatment. CA 19-9 is listed as category 2B.
alt.avoid: Say what is known. A SEER-Medicare analysis showed no significant survival benefit for patients who received regular surveillance CT scans. There are no data that a rising tumour marker leads to earlier intervention and better outcomes, and no evidence that serial ctDNA monitoring improves outcomes.
alt.note: Downgraded from C to D: the rationale is consensus and the only outcome data quoted are negative. The surveillance interval is a local decision on this page. The guideline footnote that defines it did not survive the machine extraction supplied to the programme, so no interval is quoted here; confirm it against the current published guideline before publication and record which version was used. [PAYER]

avoid.t: Do not start adjuvant therapy without restaging.
avoid.pref: Scan, then start.
avoid.avoid: This is a sequence error rather than a judgement call: a patient with radiologic recurrence is on a different pathway and a different conversation.

avoid.t: Do not give adjuvant chemoradiation to a node-positive patient on the strength of RTOG 0848.
avoid.pref: Where the discussion is being had at all, have it in node-negative disease, after chemotherapy, with radiation oncology review.
avoid.avoid: The trial's node-positive subgroup showed no improvement in overall or disease-free survival. Extending a subgroup result to the subgroup it excluded is the specific error here — and the subgroup result itself is carried only in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page, with no primary report read for this depot.

avoid.t: Do not present adjuvant nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine as established.
avoid.pref: Where a doublet is needed, gemcitabine with capecitabine has a positive primary endpoint and NCCN's preferred label; nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine does not.
avoid.avoid: APACT's blinded independently assessed primary endpoint was negative, hazard ratio 0.88 (0.729–1.063), P=.18, and the trial states that all other comparisons are therefore descriptive. The overall survival signal that followed came from the third of three successive data cutoffs with no prespecified repeated-testing plan, at the cost of 86% grade 3 or worse treatment-emergent events and 15% grade 3 or worse peripheral neuropathy against 0%, 84% of it unresolved at the primary cutoff, with no quality-of-life data.

gates.name: 7 · Locally advanced — induction therapy and the conversion question
crit: Head or uncinate: solid tumour contact of >180° with the SMA or celiac axis
Body or tail: solid tumour contact of >180° with the SMA or celiac axis, or contact with the celiac axis and aortic involvement
Complete occlusion of the SMV or portal vein not amenable to resection and primary reconstruction
No distant metastasis
Performance status and biliary drainage adequate for multiagent therapy, or not
gates.ask: Can induction therapy turn this into an operation, and does adding radiation help me get there?

standard.t: Multiagent induction chemotherapy for a patient with adequate performance status, good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake — with the reassessment date set when it starts.
standard.pref: ECOG 0–1, or ECOG 2 with intermediate performance status, treated per the metastatic first-line options. In the patient-level meta-analysis of FOLFIRINOX in locally advanced disease (13 studies, 689 patients; 11 studies and 315 locally advanced patients with survival data), pooled median overall survival from the start of FOLFIRINOX was 24.2 months (95% CI 21.7–26.8) and median progression-free survival 15.0 months (13.8–16.3), with 1-year survival 79.5% and 2-year survival 50.1%. Resection followed in a pooled 25.9% (20.2–31.9), and 60 of the 81 resected patients with margin data were R0, pooled 78.4% (60.2–92.2).
standard.avoid: Every one of those figures comes from single-arm cohorts with no randomised comparator, eleven of thirteen retrospective, and the pooled population is selected — median overall survival across the individual studies ranged from 10.0 to 32.7 months. Survival was measured from the start of FOLFIRINOX, so every patient had to survive diagnosis, staging, biliary drainage and the decision to treat before entering the analysis; LAP07's 7.7-month median for patients who progressed during induction shows how large the invisible group is. A pooled 63.5% of patients also received radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy (I² 90%, per-study range 31% to 100%), so the resection rate cannot be attributed to chemotherapy alone. The 78.4% R0 figure has a resected-only denominator — 81 of 325 patients, so it describes 19% of the cohort. Grade 3 or 4 events ran at 60.4 per 100 patients, and the report of no deaths attributed to FOLFIRINOX toxicity across 490 patients is a retrospective-records artefact rather than a safety finding.
standard.note: Downgraded from C to D on the full-text read. Because patient-level data were pooled into a single Kaplan-Meier curve rather than meta-analysed, no I² or prediction interval is reported for overall survival at all, so the narrow 95% CI of 21.7 to 26.8 months reflects the number of patients and not the three-fold disagreement between studies. The pooled population is not one population: only three of thirteen studies enrolled exclusively locally advanced patients, seven had no formal resectability criteria, and none used staging laparoscopy. Across studies there was no correlation between overall survival and radiotherapy use (p=0.12), resection rate (p=0.39) or number of FOLFIRINOX cycles (p=0.95), so none of the obvious explanations for the 24.2-month figure can be shown to drive it. The comparator the authors offer, 6 to 13 months with gemcitabine, is a narrative historical range and not a synthesis. Their own conclusion is that these results need testing in a randomised controlled trial and that it remains unestablished which patients benefit from radiotherapy or resection afterwards. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Re-ask the resectability question on biological response, not on the label the patient arrived with.
standard.pref: NCCN states the term locally advanced should only be used at initial diagnosis, that locally advanced does not imply unresectable tumour, and that once neoadjuvant therapy has been delivered the criteria for resection should be based on the biological response. Where there is a response, a second opinion at a centre with expertise in vascular resection and reconstruction is recommended even if the patient is considered technically unresectable locally.
standard.avoid: Do not let the second opinion be the step that is skipped because the first assessment was done by the person who would have to do the operation.
standard.note: The response assessment and the resection criteria are those in the borderline resectable gate — two of three metrics, and the rule that a riskier operation needs a bigger response to justify it.

standard.t: Offer conversion surgery only where R0 is achievable, and only after an objective response.
standard.pref: A responder in whom en bloc resection to a negative margin, re-established arterial inflow and venous outflow, gastrointestinal continuity and biliary drainage are all achievable — assessed partly intraoperatively, because imaging distinguishes viable tumour from scar poorly.
standard.avoid: Arterial resection in this group is the highest-risk operation on the page and NCCN restricts it to specialist centres, highly selected patients, extensive neoadjuvant therapy and objective response, with explicit counselling that the chance of cure is unknown.
standard.note: CONKO-007 gives the one randomised figure on how often conversion actually happens from this starting point, and the one randomised figure on what it costs. Of 336 patients randomised after 3 months of induction chemotherapy without progression, 62 of 169 in the chemoradiotherapy arm and 60 of 167 in the chemotherapy arm underwent surgery — 36% to 37%, with no difference between arms (P=.91) — and R0 was achieved in 43 of 169 (25%) and 30 of 167 (18%). Thirty-day postoperative mortality was 5 of 60 and 5 of 62, 8% in both arms. One operative death in twelve is the number to put in the consent conversation, and the trial's conclusion that conversion surgery did not increase postsurgical mortality means only that it did not differ between the randomised arms. Those 336 patients are also the 64% of enrolled patients who survived and did not progress through 3 months of chemotherapy: the 159 of 495 (32.1%) who progressed during induction had a median survival of 9 months with no 5-year survivors.

opts.name: Continue chemotherapy alone after induction
opts.when: LAP07 (449 enrolled, 442 eligible, 269 randomised after 4 months of gemcitabine-based induction without progression) found no overall survival difference between continuing chemotherapy and adding chemoradiotherapy: median overall survival from first randomisation 16.5 months (95% CI 14.5–18.5) with chemotherapy versus 15.2 months (13.9–17.3) with chemoradiotherapy, hazard ratio 1.03 (0.79–1.34), P=.83. The independent data monitoring committee stopped accrual when the interim analysis crossed the futility boundary at 221 deaths.
opts.pref: The default after induction for a patient in whom the objective is survival rather than local control or conversion to resection.
opts.avoid: LAP07's chemotherapy backbone was gemcitabine with or without erlotinib, not FOLFIRINOX, so it does not test chemoradiotherapy after a modern triplet; CONKO-007 later did and was also null. Read the null carefully: the trial was stopped at its interim analysis for futility and that analysis was declared final, so it never reached its planned 392 deaths, and a confidence interval of 0.79 to 1.34 cannot exclude a clinically meaningful 20% benefit or harm — this is underpowered, not equivalent. Survival was measured from the first randomisation while the intervention was allocated at the second, so four months are common to both arms by construction and any true effect is diluted toward the null.
opts.note: Two further qualifications. Despite a formal radiotherapy quality assurance programme, only 37 of 117 assessable plans (32%) were per protocol, 59 (50%) had minor and 21 (18%) major deviations, with survival 17.0 versus 13.4 months for per-protocol or minor versus major deviations (HR 1.43, 0.86–2.36, P=.17) — underpowered, but pointing in the harmful direction, so the trial cannot cleanly separate radiotherapy does not work from this radiotherapy was not delivered well enough. And curative-intent resection was achieved in only 18 of 442 patients (4%), 11 of them R0, with median overall survival 30.9 months in those 18 — gemcitabine-based induction almost never converts locally advanced disease. Erlotinib added to gemcitabine was useless and possibly harmful (11.9 versus 13.6 months, HR 1.19, 0.97–1.45, P=.09).

opts.name: Chemoradiotherapy after induction, for local control or to raise the chance of R0
opts.when: CONKO-007 (525 enrolled, 495 received induction — 402 FOLFIRINOX, 93 gemcitabine — and 336 randomised without progression at 3 months to continuing chemotherapy or to 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions with concurrent gemcitabine) missed its primary endpoint: overall R0 resection rate 43 of 169 (25%) with chemoradiotherapy versus 30 of 167 (18%) with chemotherapy, P=.113. Among the patients who actually underwent surgery, R0 was 43 of 62 (69.4%) versus 30 of 60 (50.0%), P=.04, and the overall distribution of R0, R1, R2 and no resection also favoured it, P=.02. Median follow-up was 76 months.
opts.pref: Where the board's objective is specifically local control, or a clear margin in a patient who has responded and in whom surgery is planned. The local-control effect is the most solid finding in either trial: in CONKO-007, locoregional recurrence as a first event at 5 years was 29.9% versus 40.9%, hazard ratio 0.41 (95% CI 0.227–0.746), P=.004, and all locoregional recurrence 46.9% versus 63.2%, hazard ratio 0.33 (0.206–0.530), P<.001, with distant metastasis identical (82.7% versus 84.7%, P=.52). LAP07 found the same direction (locoregional progression 32% versus 46%, P=.03) and a longer delay to reintroduction of any treatment (6.1 versus 3.7 months, P=.02).
opts.avoid: Neither trial shows a survival benefit. CONKO-007 found no overall survival difference, hazard ratio 0.937 (95% CI 0.747–1.174), P=.57, with 151 deaths in each arm, and surgery was performed equally often in the two arms (P=.91). Its 5-year survival claim (10.1% versus 3.8%) is a tail comparison inside a null trial, reported without a p value and with standard errors of 2.5% and 1.8% on 8 and 4 patients at risk. The R0 advantage that did reach significance is conditional on reaching theatre, which was not randomised, and the authors state that physicians' knowledge of the R0 endpoint changed their behaviour — which is exactly the mechanism that produces an R0 difference in the operated subgroup and none in the randomised population. Surgery itself was strongly associated with longer survival (hazard ratio 0.525, 0.408–0.676, P<.001, median 19 versus 13 months), which in a non-randomised comparison of operated against non-operated patients is selection, not treatment effect.
opts.note: Downgraded from B to C. The primary endpoint was changed mid-trial from overall survival to R0 resection rate, and the effect size for the new endpoint was calculated from unblinded interim data on 180 already-enrolled patients in which one arm's R0 rate was already nearly twice the other's — the sample size and the hypothesis were set using the result, and the trial still failed even that favourably chosen endpoint. Radiotherapy was never centrally reviewed, for stated financial reasons, in a trial whose whole question is whether radiotherapy helps; LAP07, which did review it, found 18% major deviations. Gemcitabine was the radiosensitiser, which the authors concede SCALOP suggests is inferior to capecitabine. Pathologic response did favour chemoradiotherapy (complete response 11 of 169 versus 1 of 167, P=.01; circumferential-margin-negative 28 of 33 versus 15 of 26, P=.04; ypN0 35 of 47 versus 23 of 45, P=.03). Thirty-day postoperative mortality was 8% in both arms.

opts.name: Upfront chemoradiation or SBRT, without induction chemotherapy
opts.when: NCCN permits upfront chemoradiation or SBRT in select patients with locally advanced disease. If disease progresses, the options are a clinical trial (preferred), systemic therapy, or chemoradiation or SBRT if radiation was not previously given and the primary site is the sole site of progression.
opts.pref: A narrow group — a patient who cannot have multiagent chemotherapy, or in whom a local problem dominates. SBRT should be delivered at an experienced high-volume centre with image-guided radiotherapy, or in a trial.
opts.avoid: Do not use it as the default first treatment for a fit locally advanced patient. Systemic therapy addresses the occult metastatic disease that is the usual cause of death in this group, and NCCN states further studies are needed before SBRT is recommended even in borderline resectable disease.

alt.order: Ordered by what each option is for, not by survival, because no option here improves survival over another: both randomised trials of adding radiation after induction therapy were null for overall survival, and one of them was stopped early for futility while the other failed a primary endpoint it had rewritten mid-trial from its own unblinded interim data. Continuing chemotherapy is first because it is what the negative trials support; chemoradiotherapy is second because its demonstrated gains are local control (CONKO-007 locoregional recurrence HR 0.33, P<.001; LAP07 32% versus 46%, P=.03) and margin quality in the operated subgroup (69.4% versus 50.0%, P=.04), both legitimate objectives and neither of which is survival; upfront radiotherapy without induction is last because it treats the organ and not the disease.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item 6: does this programme offer consolidative chemoradiotherapy after induction in locally advanced disease routinely, only where conversion to resection is the explicit objective, or not at all? The two randomised trials are both null for overall survival; CONKO-007's R0 benefit is confined to patients who reached theatre, its primary endpoint was changed mid-trial and powered from its own unblinded interim data, and its radiotherapy was never centrally reviewed; LAP07 was stopped at interim for futility with 18% major radiotherapy protocol deviations. Neither trial tested radiotherapy after a FOLFIRINOX backbone followed by modern surgery with modern adjuvant therapy. Ratification item 14 covers the operation itself: CONKO-007's 30-day postoperative mortality after conversion surgery was 8% in both arms. Audit: induction regimen, proportion reaching exploration, resection rate, R0 rate with millimetre clearance, 30- and 90-day postoperative mortality, local progression, and overall survival from the start of induction.

alt.t: Palliative and best supportive care, single-agent chemotherapy, or palliative radiotherapy, for a patient with poor performance status.
alt.pref: NCCN's options for ECOG 3 in locally advanced disease. Select patients with poor performance status may still benefit from single-agent chemotherapy or from targeted therapy based on molecular profiling.
alt.avoid: Do not put a patient with ECOG 3 through a triplet to avoid the conversation. Survival benefit from systemic therapy in this disease is largely confined to patients with adequate performance status, good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake.

avoid.t: Do not promise an operation at the start of induction therapy.
avoid.pref: Say what the numbers are: about a quarter of locally advanced patients treated with FOLFIRINOX in the pooled single-arm data went on to resection, and in the one randomised trial starting from unresectable disease, 122 of 336 patients randomised after 3 months without progression reached theatre (36% to 37%) and 73 of 336 (22%) achieved R0 — with 30-day postoperative mortality of 8% in both arms. Of the 495 patients who started induction, 159 (32.1%) progressed before randomisation and had a median survival of 9 months.
avoid.avoid: A patient who was told the chemotherapy was to shrink it so we can operate and who then does not reach an operation has been given the wrong frame for most of their remaining time.

avoid.t: Do not treat an unresectable label applied at diagnosis as final.
avoid.pref: Re-ask on biological response, and send responders for a second opinion at a vascular-resection centre as NCCN recommends.
avoid.avoid: This is the commonest way a potentially convertible patient is lost, and NCCN addresses it twice — in the instruction that the term should only be used at diagnosis, and in the explicit second-opinion recommendation.

avoid.t: Do not offer radiotherapy as a survival-prolonging treatment in locally advanced disease.
avoid.pref: Offer it, where it is offered, for local control or for margin quality in a patient heading to theatre, and say which. The local-control effect is real and randomised: locoregional recurrence hazard ratio 0.33 (95% CI 0.206–0.530), P<.001, in CONKO-007 and 32% versus 46% locoregional progression in LAP07.
avoid.avoid: LAP07: hazard ratio 1.03 (0.79–1.34), P=.83, stopped early for futility at its interim analysis, which then became the final one. CONKO-007: hazard ratio 0.937 (0.747–1.174), P=.57, primary endpoint not met. Two randomised trials, both null for overall survival, and neither powered to exclude a clinically meaningful difference.

gates.name: 8 · Metastatic disease — the line, and what the molecular report changes
crit: Distant metastasis on imaging, or positive peritoneal cytology
A tissue diagnosis with enough material banked for next-generation sequencing
Performance status graded: ECOG 0–1 with good biliary drainage and nutrition, ECOG 2, or poor
Germline testing and comprehensive genomic profiling ordered, with HER2 immunohistochemistry
Biliary and gastric outlet patency, pain, nutrition and thrombosis addressed as treatment, not afterthoughts
gates.ask: What is the right first-line regimen for this performance status, and what will the molecular report actually change?

opts.name: FOLFIRINOX or mFOLFIRINOX
opts.when: PRODIGE 4 / ACCORD 11 (n=342, ECOG 0–1) established the triplet: median overall survival 11.1 months (95% CI 9.0–13.1) versus 6.8 months (5.5–7.6) against gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.57 (0.45–0.73), P<0.001, with median progression-free survival 6.4 months (5.5–7.2) versus 3.3 months (2.2–3.6), hazard ratio 0.47 (0.37–0.59), and an objective response rate of 31.6% versus 9.4%.
opts.pref: A patient with ECOG 0–1, good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake. It is the regimen with the largest relative survival effect in this disease and the one whose population is best defined, and it is the only first-line triplet with quality-of-life data: definitive deterioration of global health status at 6 months in 31% versus 66%, hazard ratio 0.47 (0.30–0.70), P<0.001 — a time-to-event measure that a regimen delaying progression by 3.1 months will improve almost mechanically, so read it as consistent with the survival result rather than as independent evidence.
opts.avoid: The toxicity excluded ECOG 2 patients for a reason: grade 3–4 neutropenia 45.7% versus 21.0% with filgrastim given to 42.5% versus 5.3%, febrile neutropenia 5.4%, diarrhoea 12.7% versus 1.8%, sensory neuropathy 9.0% versus 0%, with one treatment-related death in each arm. Do not give it to a jaundiced, undrained or malnourished patient — eligibility required bilirubin at or below 1.5 times the upper limit, age under 76, no cardiac disease and measurable disease, and NCCN's definition of good performance status for this disease includes biliary drainage and nutritional intake, not just the ECOG number.
opts.note: Two things the trial does not establish. The regimen as delivered was already dose-attenuated (relative dose intensity 78% to 82%), which is part of why modified FOLFIRINOX performs similarly, so the trial does not show full-dose FOLFIRINOX is necessary. And 82.5% of FOLFIRINOX patients received gemcitabine afterwards while about half the gemcitabine patients received an oxaliplatin-based regimen, with post-second-line survival identical at 4.4 months in both arms — so the 4.3-month difference reflects first-line sequencing rather than anything unique to the four-drug combination. The phase 2 and phase 3 patients were pooled, with the trial continued only because the phase 2 response gate was met. Nothing in the trial addresses adjuvant or neoadjuvant use, and PREOPANC-2 and NORPACT-1 show that extrapolation does not hold.

opts.name: NALIRIFOX
opts.when: NAPOLI 3 (n=770, 187 sites, 18 countries) gave median overall survival 11.1 months (95% CI 10.0–12.1) versus 9.2 months (8.3–10.6) with nab-paclitaxel and gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.83 (0.70–0.99), p=0.036, with median progression-free survival 7.4 versus 5.6 months, hazard ratio 0.69 (0.58–0.83), p<0.0001. NCCN recognises high-level evidence supporting NALIRIFOX over nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine.
opts.pref: The same population as FOLFIRINOX, where the liposomal-irinotecan schedule is preferred on toxicity or logistics. Eligibility was deliberately broad, with no upper age limit and no exclusion for clinical ascites, which is the one axis on which it is less selected than PRODIGE 4.
opts.avoid: NCCN states plainly that this regimen does not appear to have clear advantages compared with FOLFIRINOX or mFOLFIRINOX, and there is no randomised comparison between them — NALIRIFOX is FOLFIRINOX with liposomal irinotecan substituted and lower oxaliplatin, and PRODIGE 4's median was also 11.1 months. Grade 3 or worse treatment-emergent events occurred in 322 of 370 (87%) versus 326 of 379 (86%), with treatment-related deaths in 2% of each arm — this is not a gentler triplet, though grade 3–4 peripheral neuropathy was lower (3.2% versus 5.8%). The margin is narrow: the design required a hazard ratio below 0.844 at a final-analysis alpha of 0.048, and the point estimate sits just inside it.
opts.note: The hierarchical testing sequence broke at step three — objective response rate 41.8% versus 36.2%, odds ratio 1.26 (0.95–1.69), p=0.11 — so the formal evidence chain stops after progression-free survival and every later p value, including the sensitivity analyses, is nominal. Follow-up was 16.1 months with asymmetric censoring in the winning arm (12% versus 2% still on treatment at cutoff), which is the configuration in which an early positive signal attenuates. Progression was assessed by investigators with no blinded central review, in an open-label trial. The sensitivity analysis censoring at subsequent therapy gives 15.1 versus 9.2 months, three times the primary result, and is informative censoring that should not be read as the true effect. Quality of life and cost were not reported, in a trial whose practical question is whether a proprietary liposomal formulation justifies its price; the sponsor participated in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation and manuscript approval.

opts.name: Nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine
opts.when: MPACT (n=861) gave median overall survival 8.5 months (95% CI 7.89–9.53) versus 6.7 months (6.01–7.23) against gemcitabine alone, hazard ratio 0.72 (0.62–0.83), P<0.001, with 1-year survival 35% versus 22% and 2-year 9% versus 4%.
opts.pref: A patient who cannot take a triplet — ECOG 2 equivalent, significant neuropathy, or a preference against a 46-hour infusion — but who is fit for a doublet. Its floor was a Karnofsky score of 70, so it admits frailer patients than PRODIGE 4, and the largest reductions in risk of death were in patients with worse disease.
opts.avoid: It was the comparator NALIRIFOX beat in NAPOLI 3, so do not choose it for a triplet-eligible patient on the grounds of equivalence. State both halves of its own result: a 1.8-month median gain, grade 3 or worse peripheral neuropathy in 17% versus 1% and fatigue in 17% versus 7%, and no quality-of-life data collected at all — PRODIGE 4, run in the same era, did collect it. The combination arm also received a higher median cumulative gemcitabine dose than the monotherapy arm (11,400 versus 9,000 mg/m²) because patients stayed on treatment longer, so part of the benefit is more gemcitabine and the trial cannot separate the two.
opts.note: Its bilirubin ceiling was the upper limit of normal, stricter than PRODIGE 4's 1.5 times, which excludes many jaundiced patients with pancreatic head cancer — so the two landmark first-line trials selected differently in opposite directions on two different axes and their medians (8.5 and 11.1 months) are not comparable. The neuropathy recovery data are reported among patients who improved, with no cumulative incidence of unresolved neuropathy at a fixed time; APACT, the adjuvant trial of the same regimen, later found 84% of grade 3 or worse neuropathy had not improved to grade 1 or less at its primary cutoff. The preceding four-centre phase 1–2 result of 12.2 months did not replicate, falling by more than 3 months in the phase 3 trial — a caution that applies to every single-arm or few-centre figure quoted on this page.

opts.name: Gemcitabine alone, or palliative and best supportive care
opts.when: NCCN recommends systemic therapy for patients with good or intermediate performance status, and makes palliative and best supportive care including palliative radiotherapy the preferred option for poor performance status; patients with ECOG 4 should be supported exclusively by palliative and best supportive care.
opts.pref: A frail patient in whom single-agent treatment is the ceiling, or one for whom the honest offer is symptom control. Select patients with poor performance status may still benefit from single-agent chemotherapy or from a targeted agent identified on molecular profiling.
opts.avoid: Do not treat a declining patient with a doublet to avoid the conversation. NCCN notes that patients with advanced disease can deteriorate abruptly — bleeding, thromboembolism, escalating pain, stent occlusion, cholangitis — and that new symptoms are often wrongly attributed to chemotherapy when the cause is gastric outlet obstruction or carcinomatosis.

standard.order: Ordered by performance-status fit and by the comparator each trial beat, not by head-to-head data. There is no randomised comparison of NALIRIFOX with FOLFIRINOX, and NCCN says so; the two triplets sit at the same median (11.1 months) against different comparators in different eras. The sequence down the list tracks declining fitness, which is the variable that actually decides.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item 7: which triplet is the local first-line standard — (m)FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX — and on what grounds, given no comparative trial, identical medians (11.1 months) against different comparators in different eras, and a cost difference? The full-text read adds that the cross-trial comparison is not like for like either: PRODIGE 4 capped age at 76 and allowed bilirubin up to 1.5 times normal, MPACT had no age cap but required bilirubin within normal limits, and NAPOLI 3 had neither cap and allowed ascites, so the three populations are selected differently on opposite axes. NAPOLI 3's margin is narrow (HR 0.83, upper bound 0.99, against a design threshold of 0.844) and its hierarchical testing broke at the response-rate step. The group should also decide what counts locally as good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake, since that phrase, not the ECOG score alone, is NCCN's eligibility definition. Audit: first-line regimen, performance status at start, drainage and nutritional status, dose intensity, cycles delivered, and reason for discontinuation.

standard.t: Order comprehensive genomic profiling and germline testing at the first visit, and bank enough tissue for it.
standard.pref: Every patient with metastatic disease. NCCN asks for testing for fusions (ALK, NRG1, NTRK, ROS1, FGFR2, RET), mutations (BRAF, BRCA1/2, KRAS, PALB2), amplifications (HER2), microsatellite instability, mismatch repair deficiency and tumour mutational burden, using an FDA-approved or validated NGS assay, plus HER2 by immunohistochemistry with or without FISH. In metastatic disease, enough tissue for sequencing should be obtained at biopsy, with two extra needle passes banked.
standard.avoid: Do not wait for the result before starting treatment. NCCN is explicit that if BRCA1/2 status is unknown, the patient is treated with systemic therapy as clinically indicated. The sequencing changes the maintenance and later-line decisions, not usually the first-line one. And do not quote the 5.5% germline figure as the proportion with an actionable result: it is driven mostly by ATM and BRCA2, and of the six genes it covers only BRCA1/2 has a randomised treatment consequence in this disease.
standard.note: Downgraded from A to B. The recommendation is NCCN's; the evidence under it is mixed. The germline prevalence estimate comes from a clinic-based case series compared with public sequencing databases rather than a recruited control group, and carriage was not associated with survival (HR 0.86, P=.09). What is randomised is narrower: a phase 3 progression-free survival result in germline BRCA1/2 after platinum, and a phase 3 survival result in RAS G12 disease after prior therapy. Everything else on the molecular list is single-arm, in alterations reaching 1% to 2% of the disease or less, with pancreatic subsets of 10 to 40 patients and no screening denominators reported — so the testing is justified by the small number of large effects, not by the length of the panel. Screen for clinical-trial eligibility at the same visit; NCCN strongly encourages enrolment at every stage. [PAYER]

standard.t: Treat biliary and gastric outlet patency, pain, nutrition and thrombosis as part of the treatment plan, with named owners.
standard.pref: For biliary obstruction NCCN prefers an endoscopic biliary metal stent, with percutaneous biliary drainage and subsequent internalisation as the alternative. For gastric outlet obstruction, EUS-guided gastrojejunostomy at a high-volume centre is an option. Exocrine insufficiency, pain and nutrition need active management because NCCN's own definition of a treatable performance status depends on them.
standard.avoid: Do not attribute intractable nausea and vomiting to chemotherapy without excluding gastric outlet obstruction, or abdominal bloating and reduced intake without considering peritoneal carcinomatosis — NCCN names both as recognised misattributions.
standard.note: A short course of radiotherapy may be given to painful metastatic sites such as bone. Plastic biliary stents may be considered for palliation where predicted survival is under 3 months. [EXPERTISE]

opts.name: Daraxonrasib, for RAS-mutated disease after prior therapy
opts.when: RASolute 302 (phase 3, n=500 randomised, 248 daraxonrasib and 252 investigator's-choice chemotherapy, more than 90% with RAS G12 mutations) had dual primary endpoints in the RAS G12 population and met both: median overall survival 13.2 versus 6.6 months, hazard ratio 0.40, P<0.001, and median progression-free survival by blinded independent central review 7.3 versus 3.5 months, hazard ratio 0.45.
opts.pref: A previously treated patient with a documented RAS G12 mutation, which is the population in which benefit is established. Grade 3 or higher adverse events were less frequent than with chemotherapy, 61.8% versus 69.6%, treatment-related discontinuation far less, 1.2% versus 11.2%, and time to deterioration in quality of life and in pain favoured daraxonrasib.
opts.avoid: Check availability, regulatory status and coverage before raising it with a patient, and state three limits. The benefit is established only for RAS G12 disease: in patients without a G12 mutation the hazard ratio was 1.38 (95% CI 0.60–3.17), a point estimate favouring chemotherapy. The effect size is inseparable from the comparator's delivery — 38 of 252 patients (15.1%) assigned to chemotherapy never received it against 7 of 248 (2.8%) assigned daraxonrasib, 29 of them withdrawing, and some no longer met eligibility because ECOG had risen above 1 by the time treatment was due, which an oral agent started the same day does not face. And the result is in the previously treated setting only — it says nothing about first line, about the adjuvant setting, or about use around an operation.
opts.note: The comparator was unconstrained investigator's choice from gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel, modified FOLFIRINOX, FOLFOX or liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil, given per local prescribing practice, and its 6.6-month median sits at the low end of published second-line outcomes, so its quality is not auditable from the report. The trial was open label with no crossover; overall survival in an open-label trial remains exposed to differential post-progression therapy, which is not detailed by arm. The sponsor supported the trial and performed and validated the statistical analyses, with five author employees. An overall survival hazard ratio of 0.40 in second-line PDAC is extraordinarily large and should be read with the comparator's 15.1% non-receipt and 11.2% toxicity discontinuation in view.

opts.name: Olaparib maintenance, for germline BRCA1/2 after platinum
opts.when: The POLO trial (n=154 randomised 3:2 from 3,315 screened) randomised patients with metastatic disease and a germline BRCA1/2 mutation who had not progressed after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum-based therapy to olaparib or placebo. Median progression-free survival by blinded independent central review was 7.4 versus 3.8 months, hazard ratio 0.53 (95% CI 0.35–0.82), P=0.004.
opts.pref: Exactly that population: germline BRCA1/2, platinum-exposed, no progression at 16 weeks. This is the clearest reason to have the germline result early.
opts.avoid: Say the other half. At the interim analysis, at 46% data maturity against a final analysis planned at 69%, there was no overall survival difference — 18.9 versus 18.1 months, hazard ratio 0.91 (0.56–1.46), P=0.68 — there was no difference in health-related quality of life (between-group difference in global health status −2.47, 95% CI −7.27 to 2.33), and grade 3 or worse adverse events were more frequent with olaparib, 40% versus 23%. Objective response was 23% versus 12%, and time to second progression was also non-significant (HR 0.76, 0.46–1.23).
opts.note: Downgraded from A to B. The comparator was placebo, not maintenance chemotherapy or a de-escalated fluoropyrimidine, so the trial establishes that olaparib beats stopping treatment, not that it beats continuing anything — which is the comparison the 16-week decision actually faces. Only 154 of 3,315 screened patients (4.6%) were randomised, and the conditioning step (germline testing plus four months of platinum without progression) is itself the strongest prognostic selection in the trial: a placebo-arm median of 18.1 months in metastatic pancreatic cancer is far above the 6 to 11 months typical of the disease, so these numbers are not comparable with those from unselected trials. Nine placebo patients (15%) received a PARP inhibitor after progression, cited as biasing overall survival toward the null without a sensitivity analysis. The sponsor funded the trial and supplied the companion diagnostic. The page previously quoted the placebo-arm median as 16.1 months; the published figure is 18.1.

opts.name: Pembrolizumab or dostarlimab, for MSI-high or dMMR disease
opts.when: NCCN lists pembrolizumab for MSI-high, dMMR or TMB-high (≥10 mutations/Mb) disease across lines, and dostarlimab for MSI-high or dMMR as subsequent therapy.
opts.pref: The small minority of pancreatic tumours that are MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient. It is the one alteration on this list that can produce a durable response.
opts.avoid: Do not test for it late. A patient who has exhausted chemotherapy before anyone checked mismatch repair status has lost the opportunity, and the frequency in PDAC is low enough that nobody finds it by clinical suspicion. Graded D because no trial in pancreatic cancer supports either agent: both are tumour-agnostic approvals carried here through the NCCN listing, and no primary report was retrieved or read in full for this depot.

opts.name: Sotorasib or adagrasib, for KRAS G12C
opts.when: NCCN lists both as subsequent therapy options at any performance status. KRAS p.G12C occurs in approximately 1 to 2% of pancreatic cancers.
opts.pref: A previously treated patient with a G12C mutation where daraxonrasib is unavailable. Sotorasib in the pooled phase 1–2 CodeBreaK 100 pancreatic cohort (n=38, all previously treated, about 79% with two or more prior lines): centrally confirmed objective response in 8 of 38 (21%, 95% CI 10–37) with no complete responses, median progression-free survival 4.0 months (2.8–5.6), median overall survival 6.9 months (5.0–9.1). Adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 phase 2 non-lung, non-colorectal cohort: objective response in 7 of 21 pancreatic patients (33.3%) by blinded central review, median progression-free survival 5.4 months, median overall survival 8.0 months.
opts.avoid: Downgraded to D, and correct the denominators: these are single-arm results in 38 and 21 pancreatic patients, not in the larger numbers this page previously implied. The sotorasib cohort had no prespecified response benchmark and no hypothesis test at all, so there is no threshold it could have failed, and its 10% to 37% confidence interval is compatible with the under-10% historical second-line benchmark the authors invoke. Adagrasib's prespecified 10% null applies to the pooled tumour-agnostic cohort, not to the pancreatic subgroup, and six patients counted as evaluable by investigators were excluded by central review for having no measurable disease at baseline, moving the denominator in the favourable direction. Median overall survival of 6.9 and 8.0 months in third-line-or-later populations with ECOG 0–1 and a life expectancy requirement is indistinguishable from the natural history of those populations. The allele covers 1% to 2% of the disease, and neither report gives a screening denominator. Do not present them as comparable to the RASolute 302 result.

opts.name: Zenocutuzumab, for NRG1 fusions
opts.when: NCCN lists zenocutuzumab-zbco as a subsequent therapy option for NRG1 fusion-positive disease at performance status 0–2. In the eNRGy basket trial, 36 of 158 patients in the primary efficacy population had pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and all 36 were KRAS wild-type: 15 of 36 (42%, 95% CI 25–59) responded by investigator assessment and 16 of 36 (44%, 28–62) by blinded independent central review, with median duration of response 7.4 months (4.0–11.2) investigator-assessed and 9.1 months centrally. Twenty-four of 31 pancreatic patients with baseline data (77%) had a CA 19-9 fall of at least 50%.
opts.pref: A patient with KRAS wild-type disease, where NRG1 fusions are enriched — in a single-institution series the median age of 10 patients with a detectable NRG1 fusion was 48.5 years, and KRAS wild-type status is the practical trigger to look.
opts.avoid: Downgraded to D. Single-arm, 36 pancreatic patients inside a basket trial sized only for the pooled estimate, with a 95% CI of 25% to 59% that cannot distinguish a major advance from a modest one. No progression-free or overall survival is reported for the pancreatic subgroup, so no survival claim can be derived from it. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed response in an open-label trial with blinded central review only as a secondary endpoint, and the primary efficacy population is a post-enrolment construct — 204 treated patients become 158 evaluable, with exclusions for short follow-up falling disproportionately on early progressors. Only 9 of 47 responses across the whole trial were ongoing at a median follow-up of 7.1 months. Adverse events were mostly grade 1 or 2 with treatment-related grade 3–4 in 7%, so the risk is low — but NRG1 fusions occur in well under 1% of PDAC, no screening denominator is given, and the sponsor designed the trial, analysed the data and drafted the manuscript.

opts.name: An NTRK, RET, BRAF or FGFR-directed agent, by alteration
opts.when: NCCN lists entrectinib, larotrectinib or repotrectinib for NTRK fusion-positive disease; selpercatinib for RET fusions (11 pancreatic patients, at least half with an objective response); dabrafenib with trametinib for BRAF V600E, with ORR 38–47% across the NCI-MATCH subprotocol and the ROAR basket trial; and erdafitinib for FGFR alterations, with response in 10 of 18 pancreatic patients (56%) in RAGNAR.
opts.pref: Rare alterations where the alternative is further cytotoxic chemotherapy in a previously treated patient. Each is a basket-trial or subgroup result in single-digit to low-double-digit pancreatic numbers.
opts.avoid: Downgraded to D: none of these reports was retrieved or read in full for this depot, and all the figures are carried in the NCCN listing supplied to this page. Do not treat the gene as the target. The pancreatic subsets in these trials are tiny — one patient with pancreatic cancer in the larotrectinib analysis, two of three responders among pancreatic patients in the entrectinib trials — and response rates from mixed-tumour baskets do not transfer cleanly to this disease.

alt.order: Ordered by the strength of the evidence in pancreatic cancer specifically and by how many patients the alteration reaches, not by response rate. Daraxonrasib is first because it is the only randomised phase 3 result here, and the only one with a survival endpoint — but its benefit is established in the RAS G12 population that was its primary analysis set, and the non-G12 subgroup points the other way (HR 1.38, 0.60–3.17). Olaparib is second because POLO is randomised and double-blind but in 154 patients found from 3,315 screened, against placebo rather than continued chemotherapy, and positive only for progression-free survival with no overall survival or quality-of-life difference at interim. Everything below is single-arm, in rare alterations, with pancreatic subsets of 21 to 38 patients, no control groups, and in two cases no prespecified efficacy threshold at all.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item 8: what is the local sequence after first-line failure, and where does daraxonrasib sit in it given its availability, cost, the absence of any first-line or perioperative data, and the fact that 15.1% of its comparator arm never received the chemotherapy it was allocated? The group should also agree who owns chasing the molecular report, because the commonest failure in this disease is a result that arrives after the patient is too unwell to act on it. Audit: proportion of metastatic patients with a completed germline result and a completed genomic profile before second line, time from biopsy to report, and proportion of actionable results acted on. [PAYER]

alt.t: A chemotherapy holiday or maintenance therapy for a patient doing well on first-line treatment.
alt.pref: NCCN offers either for patients who do well on initial therapy. Set the reassessment interval and the trigger for restarting when the holiday begins.
alt.avoid: Do not drift into a holiday without a date for the next scan.

alt.t: Rucaparib maintenance for germline or somatic BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 variants, as a second option after platinum.
alt.pref: A phase 2 trial of maintenance rucaparib after at least 16 weeks of platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced disease with germline or somatic pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 reported median progression-free survival of 13.1 months and median duration of response 17.3 months, with no new safety signal.
alt.avoid: Downgraded to D: single-arm phase 2 with no control, and the primary report was not retrieved or read in full for this depot — the figures are carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page. The 13.1-month progression-free survival figure cannot be compared with POLO's 7.4 months. Its one advantage over the POLO population is that it included somatic as well as germline variants and PALB2.

avoid.t: Do not treat metastatic pancreatic cancer without a tissue diagnosis.
avoid.pref: Biopsy the lesion that gives the highest stage, with image guidance for liver lesions, and bank material for sequencing at the same sitting.
avoid.avoid: NCCN requires a pathologic diagnosis before systemic therapy in metastatic disease. Treating on imaging alone commits a patient to months of cytotoxic therapy on an assumption.

avoid.t: Do not offer prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin routinely.
avoid.pref: Treat established venous thromboembolism, and keep a low threshold for investigating it — the risk in pancreatic cancer is substantially raised.
avoid.avoid: CONKO-004 showed that prophylactic enoxaparin lowered symptomatic venous thromboembolism (hazard ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.19–0.83, P=0.01, n=160 versus 152) but progression-free and overall survival did not differ. NCCN does not recommend prophylactic LMWH at this time, citing the absence of a survival effect. Graded D because the trial was not retrieved or read in full for this depot; the figures are carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page.

avoid.t: Do not resect the primary tumour, or a metastasis, for metastatic disease outside a prospective protocol.
avoid.pref: NCCN's wording is the ceiling of what can be said: in select rare cases, surgery can be considered in patients with a sustained and deep response to systemic therapy, ideally at high-volume centres, and patients with indolent or oligometastatic disease should be referred to a high-volume centre for evaluation.
avoid.avoid: Everything beyond that sentence is retrospective and selected. The liver-only question has its own gate on this page and is protocol-only.

avoid.t: Do not let the molecular report arrive after it can be used.
avoid.pref: Order profiling at the first visit, bank the extra passes at the index biopsy, and name the person who chases the result.
avoid.avoid: This is an operational failure, not a clinical judgement, and it is the one that most often costs a patient a targeted option in this disease — including the two options on this page with randomised support.

gates.name: 9 · Liver-only metastases — the experimental transplant gate
crit: Liver-only metastatic PDAC, no extrahepatic disease on PET-CT, negative staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings
A sustained response through at least 6 months of first-line systemic therapy, with CA 19-9 fall of 85% or more or normalisation, and at least 12 months from diagnosis without progression
Primary tumour resectable or borderline resectable, so pancreatectomy can be done at the same operation
Age 18–65, ECOG 0–1, otherwise transplantable on standard AASLD/AST criteria
An open IRB-approved protocol with DSMB oversight, institutional transplant-selection and allocation-ethics approval, and consent that benefit is unproven and graft access may be unavailable
gates.ask: Is this patient on a protocol, and does anyone in the room believe the operation adds anything to the chemotherapy that got them here?

standard.t: This is investigational for the whole of its length, and the local protocol says so on its first page: liver transplantation for PDAC with liver metastases is not a standardized OPTN exception diagnosis and is not among the recommended diagnoses in the December 2025 transplant-oncology guidance, and no MELD exception score is recommended or guaranteed.
standard.pref: Where the question is raised at all, route it to the transplant surgeon and to research governance at the same time, not to one and then the other. The programme's own V2 document states that the protocol must not be activated without prospective IRB approval, DSMB oversight, institutional transplant-selection and allocation-ethics approval, independent living-donor advocacy where applicable, and explicit consent that benefit is unproven and graft access may be unavailable.
standard.avoid: Do not raise transplantation with a patient or family as an available option before an open protocol exists. The controlling allocation sources are OPTN Policies 9.4 and 9.5 as currently posted and the December 2025 National Liver Review Board transplant-oncology guidance, and the guidance is not OPTN policy and does not define a clinical standard of care.
standard.note: Policy review date on the local document is 16 July 2026, and V2 is dated 23 July 2026. The V2 revision note records what was wrong with V1: it conflated phase 3 daraxonrasib survival results with phase 1–2 response and ctDNA findings, proposed unapproved post-transplant drug combinations without IND controls, omitted inequality operators from its stopping rules, and included a non-retrievable personal citation. Read V2.

standard.t: Off protocol, the treatment for liver-only metastatic PDAC is systemic therapy — this is the metastatic gate on this page, and nothing else.
standard.pref: Every patient with liver-only metastatic disease, including every patient who is later considered for a protocol, since 6 to 12 months of systemic therapy with a documented sustained response is itself the entry condition.
standard.avoid: Do not let the existence of a protocol change the first-line conversation. NCCN's position on surgery in metastatic disease is confined to select rare cases with a sustained and deep response, ideally at high-volume centres.
standard.note: Both first-line trials cited here enrolled narrower populations than the patients this gate will see: PRODIGE 4 capped age at 76 with bilirubin at or below 1.5 times normal, and NAPOLI 3 required ECOG 0–1 while allowing any age and clinical ascites. Neither says anything about surgery or transplantation.

standard.t: Know the survival benchmark this operation would have to beat — and it is not the all-comer figure for stage IV disease.
standard.pref: Quote this at the board before any protocol discussion. In a single-centre registry cohort of 241 patients with clinical stage IV PDAC and synchronous metastases, median overall survival was 7 months (95% CI 5–9), the same in the 144 patients with liver-only metastases. Among the 54 patients who received chemotherapy and survived to a 12-month landmark, median overall survival was 26 months (19–33) with 1-, 3- and 5-year survival of 91%, 34% and 25%; for the 27 with liver-only disease who met the same two conditions it was 26 months (17–39) with 96%, 33% and 24%. The 9 patients (4% of the cohort) who had a resectable or borderline resectable primary and resectable liver-only metastases and met both conditions had median overall survival of 39 months (13–not reached), with 2-, 3- and 5-year survival of 67%, 56% and 0% — there were no 5-year survivors.
standard.avoid: The benchmark for a protocol operation in this population is therefore roughly 26 to 39 months, not the 7 to 12 months usually quoted for metastatic disease, and all of it was achieved with no operation at all. The authors' own conclusion is that outcomes of resection in metastatic pancreatic cancer should be assessed against the expected survival of patients potentially eligible for surgery, not against all-comers with stage IV disease. Note also how far from oligometastatic this population is: of the 80 patients whose imaging was reviewed, 5 (6%) had a single liver lesion, 17 (20%) had 2 to 4 and 58 (74%) had 5 or more, and only 35 of 80 (44%) had resectable liver disease.
standard.note: That 39-month figure rests on nine patients, five of whom had died, with a confidence interval from 13 months to not reached, and the 12-month landmark was imposed specifically to mitigate immortal-time bias. Two features make it a conservative comparator rather than a flattering one: imaging was available for review in only 80 of 183 patients with liver metastases (44%), and CA 19-9 was deliberately excluded from the selection criteria, so median CA 19-9 in the benchmark cohort was 3,101 U/mL and 64% of those with a trend available were rising — patients no surgeon would operate on. The durable finding is methodological: a landmark analysis is mandatory and resected-only denominators are uninterpretable. It is still the right comparator, and it is the number the local protocol's own consent section alludes to when it says median overall survival may approach 40 months without surgery in patients with favourable biology who survive beyond 12 months on chemotherapy.

opts.name: Protocol A — investigational lower-risk cohort
opts.when: Prospective single-arm phase 2, primary endpoint 3-year overall survival after transplant. Entry: five or fewer liver metastases confirmed on PET-CT and cross-sectional imaging; at least 6 months of first-line FOLFIRINOX, mFOLFIRINOX, NALIRIFOX or gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel; RECIST 1.1 partial response or stable disease sustained for at least 6 months; CA 19-9 fall of 85% or more or normalisation; declining or undetectable RAS-mutant ctDNA; at least 12 months from diagnosis without progression; primary resectable or borderline resectable; no extrahepatic disease on PET-CT within 4 weeks of listing; negative staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings and portal nodal sampling. The operation is simultaneous pancreatectomy and orthotopic liver transplantation, aborted if peritoneal cytology or distant nodes are positive on frozen section.
opts.pref: A patient whose biology has already declared itself over a year of treatment, who is young and fit, and who understands that this has no established precedent.
opts.avoid: The exclusions do as much work as the inclusions and should be read as part of the definition: any extrahepatic disease including bone, lung or peritoneum; poorly differentiated or undifferentiated histology; signet-ring cell features; disease progression at any point during neoadjuvant therapy; PET metabolic tumour volume above 70 cm³ or total lesion glycolysis above 260 g; CA 19-9 rising or above 500 U/mL at listing; prior liver radiation; uncontrolled biliary obstruction or active cholangitis; medical contraindication to transplantation or immunosuppression; another malignancy within 5 years. The protocol's own stopping rules are perioperative mortality above 10% in the first 10 patients, 1-year overall survival below 50%, and a 1-year recurrence rate above 60%, each triggering an enrolment pause and DSMB review.

opts.name: Protocol B — high-risk experimental cohort
opts.when: Prospective single-arm phase 1/2; phase 1 endpoints are 30- and 90-day perioperative morbidity and mortality, phase 2 endpoint is 2-year overall survival. Entry: ten or fewer liver metastases with bilobar disease permitted; at least one prior line with progression or intolerance; an eligible RAS mutation as defined by the current daraxonrasib investigational protocol, with drug exposure requiring an FDA-authorized IND and sponsor confirmation; no extrahepatic disease on PET-CT; willingness to be evaluated for living donor liver transplantation. Conversion is assessed at 6 months and requires all of: RECIST partial or complete response; CA 19-9 fall of 85% or more or normalisation; ctDNA fall of 50% or more; PET metabolic tumour volume of 70 cm³ or less; no new disease sites; negative staging laparoscopy with washings; resectable primary.
opts.pref: Nobody, until the phase 1 safety lead-in has been run under an IND with an independent DSMB. The conversion-rate stopping rule — a pause and DSMB review if conversion to transplant is below 20% at the interim analysis after 20 enrolled patients — is the honest statement of how uncertain the premise is.
opts.avoid: V2 removed most of what V1 permitted at investigator discretion, and the differences matter: investigational daraxonrasib only at the IND-authorized dose and schedule within a formal phase 1 safety lead-in, because 300 mg daily is not a transplant-validated dose; no discretionary daraxonrasib-plus-chemotherapy combinations, each of which requires its own prespecified IND dose-escalation cohort and stopping rules; no routine post-transplant daraxonrasib maintenance and no mandatory 12-month course; daraxonrasib plus afatinib must not be administered under the protocol at all. Deceased-donor transplantation is not a fallback entitlement and may proceed only through lawful allocation at calculated MELD or a separately approved non-standard exception with institutional allocation-ethics approval. Living donation does not remove the need for independent donor-risk review.

alt.order: Ordered by how much of each is unproven, and the order is not a ranking of benefit — there is no outcome data for either cohort, in this programme or anywhere. Protocol A is first only because its entry conditions select patients whose disease has already behaved indolently for a year, so the selection is doing work that the operation has not been shown to do. Protocol B's premise — that a RAS inhibitor response can convert higher-burden liver-only disease into transplantable disease — rests on a drug result in previously treated metastatic disease and on preclinical work, and nothing more.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item 9: does this programme open either cohort at all, and under whose governance? This is a graft-stewardship and research-ethics decision before it is a clinical one, and the page records only what the local protocol says — it takes no institutional position of its own, because none has been ratified. Ratification item 10: if a cohort opens, what is the consent standard, given that the honest comparator (26–39 months on systemic therapy in a responder) is close to anything the operation could plausibly deliver? Registry entry for every patient enrolled is required by the protocol.

alt.t: Pancreatectomy with liver metastasectomy, rather than transplantation, within a prospective protocol — the nearer-term version of the same question.
alt.pref: A sustained and deep response on systemic therapy, low-volume liver-only disease, a resectable primary, and a prospective protocol with registry entry. Two 2025 meta-analyses report a pooled overall survival hazard ratio of 0.41 for resection against non-surgical therapy — 0.41 (95% CI 0.31–0.53) across 7 studies pooled from a review of 16 studies and 999 resected patients in one, and 0.41 (0.32–0.52) across 6 studies and 1,348 patients in the other.
alt.avoid: Treat that as one estimate, not two. The two reviews draw on substantially overlapping studies (Shao, Shi, Pausch and Hank appear in both), so citing both double-counts a single evidence base, and both are built entirely from retrospective series with complete selection asymmetry. One pooled only univariate hazard ratios by explicit design and never mentions immortal-time bias, reporting I² of 12% from seven retrospective studies with different definitions of oligometastasis; the other found I² of 64.5% in the same literature. The meta-regression in the second is the finding that matters: the relative rate of chemotherapy between arms explained 87.1% of the between-study heterogeneity, roughly half the non-surgical patients received gemcitabine monotherapy against multi-agent regimens in the surgical arm, and the adjusted effect reached HR 0.18 (0.08–0.40) only where both pre- and postoperative systemic chemotherapy were given, with no difference in any other scenario — an estimate fitted to 7 comparisons with 11 candidate covariates that the authors themselves describe as mathematical rather than empirical. The first review's own data point the same way: three studies that mandated a RECIST response plus a CA 19-9 fall reported an average median overall survival of 32.5 months in 114 resected patients against 9.2 months in 148 who did not meet the response criteria, a 23-month gap generated by a response criterion rather than an operation, and the best outcomes in the whole review came from 52 patients whose liver metastases had completely regressed and who had only the primary resected (median 23 months). Three of its included studies found synchronous-resection patients did worse than patients resected for non-metastatic disease at the same centres (14.9 versus 22.5 months).
alt.note: Downgraded from C to D. The National Cancer Database picture shows what the national experience actually is: of 47,785 patients with liver-only stage IV disease, 891 (1.9%) underwent pancreatic resection and only 137 (0.29%) had simultaneous liver metastasectomy; only 120 of the 891 (13.5%) received any preoperative chemotherapy, and 85% had the primary removed without touching the liver metastases, a practice with no supporting evidence. Median overall survival in the whole surgical cohort was 10.74 months against 3.4 months unmatched — essentially what PRODIGE 4 and MPACT achieved with chemotherapy alone in unselected metastatic disease — and the quoted 15.6 versus 8.1 months comes from matching 137 surgical patients to 137 of 25,268 chemotherapy patients on six demographic variables, with none of the variables that decide the operation (metastasis number or size, response to chemotherapy, CA 19-9 trajectory, performance status) matched at all. Its adjusted Cox model reports well-to-moderately differentiated tumours at HR 4.09 (2.32–7.23) for death, the opposite of the known direction and of the paper's own logistic model, which suggests a coding problem in the analysis that produced the headline HR 0.5. Operative cost is real: in the meta-analysis that reported it, overall morbidity was 53%, major morbidity 4% and 30-day mortality 2%, with 99% of liver resections being wedge excisions. The NCDB authors' own conclusion is the one to quote: attempts at an aggressive surgical approach for liver-only stage IV pancreatic adenocarcinoma should only be performed under a well-designed prospective clinical trial. And the matched comparator figure of 8.1 months is far below the 26 to 39 months seen in patients selected for 12-month survival, which is why the benchmark question above matters more than any of these hazard ratios. [REGISTRY]

alt.t: mTOR-inhibitor-based immunosuppression if a transplant is performed under protocol — borrowed reasoning, and labelled as such.
alt.pref: The local protocol's regimen is basiliximab induction, low-dose tacrolimus with mycophenolate for weeks 1–4, then conversion to everolimus (trough 5–8 ng/mL) with tacrolimus tapered to 3–5 ng/mL, with everolimus preferred over sirolimus for a lower risk of hepatic artery thrombosis, adapted from the IHPBA consensus guidelines for transplantation in non-resectable colorectal liver metastases and from AASLD/AST candidate-evaluation guidance.
alt.avoid: The antitumour rationale is entirely extrapolated, and the two papers behind it are not pancreatic cancer papers. The hepatocellular carcinoma meta-analysis found, in its three randomised trials, overall survival relative risks for mTOR-inhibitor-based immunosuppression of 1.04 (95% CI 1.00–1.08) at 1 year, 1.09 (1.02–1.16) at 2 years, 1.13 (1.04–1.24) at 3 years and 1.13 (1.02–1.26) at 5 years, with recurrence-free survival 1.08 (1.02–1.15) at 1 year, 0.98 (0.75–1.28) at 2 years and 1.14 (1.03–1.25) at 3 years — the 1-year overall survival estimate touches the null and the 2-year recurrence-free estimate is non-significant. Its 14 cohort studies gave consistently larger estimates (1.13 to 1.24), which is the signature of confounding by indication, since an mTOR inhibitor is preferentially given to patients judged fit for it. Renal toxicity was lower (RR 0.75, 0.60–0.93). There is no equivalent evidence in PDAC, and no reason to assume a different tumour responds the same way to the same manoeuvre.
alt.note: Downgraded from C to D, and flagged for provenance. The page previously quoted a recurrence relative risk of 0.69 (0.53–0.88) and a 5-year overall survival relative risk of 1.16 (1.07–1.26) for this meta-analysis; neither figure appears in the paper as read in full, and the figures above replace them. Both supporting papers are used only in this gate and neither can support any claim about pancreatic cancer: one concerns immunosuppression after liver transplantation for hepatocellular carcinoma, the other is the AASLD and American Society of Transplantation practice guideline on evaluating adult liver transplant candidates, whose only mentions of the pancreas concern neuroendocrine tumour liver metastases. The IHPBA consensus on transplantation for non-resectable colorectal liver metastases is cited from its abstract only; its full text was not retrieved for this depot.

avoid.t: Do not transplant for PDAC outside an approved protocol.
avoid.pref: Systemic therapy, as in the metastatic gate, with trial screening.
avoid.avoid: There is no standardized OPTN exception for this diagnosis, it is not among the recommended diagnoses in the December 2025 transplant-oncology guidance, and no MELD exception is recommended or guaranteed. A one-off compassionate case is not a protocol.
