avoid.t: Do not use the TransMet result to justify transplantation for PDAC.
avoid.pref: Cite it for what it is — the trial that validated liver transplantation in a different disease. TransMet randomised 94 patients with permanently unresectable colorectal liver metastases from a resected BRAF-non-mutated primary, responsive to at least 3 months and no more than 3 lines of chemotherapy, with no extrahepatic disease: 5-year overall survival 56.6% (95% CI 43.2–74.1) versus 12.6% (5.2–30.1) by intention to treat, hazard ratio 0.37 (0.21–0.65), P=0.0003, and 73.3% versus 9.3% per protocol.
avoid.avoid: It is a colorectal trial in a disease with a different metastatic biology and a vastly better natural history after liver-only metastasectomy, it required organ allocation priority that PDAC does not have, serious adverse events occurred in 32 of 40 transplanted patients (80%), three needed retransplantation and one of those died of multi-organ failure. There is no equivalent trial in PDAC and no result to extrapolate from.
avoid.note: Downgraded from B to C and flagged for provenance: TransMet is cited from its abstract only. No new papers were obtained for this depot and the full text was not retrieved, so none of its figures has been checked against the published report, and its limitations have not been read.

avoid.t: Do not use the daraxonrasib result as a transplant-enabling result.
avoid.pref: Cite RASolute 302 in the metastatic gate, where it belongs: previously treated metastatic disease, overall survival and progression-free survival endpoints, 13.2 versus 6.6 months, hazard ratio 0.40.
avoid.avoid: These data do not establish transplant benefit or peri-transplant safety, and V2 of the local protocol says so in those words. Nothing in the trial addresses immunosuppression interaction, wound healing, graft function, infection risk or the CYP3A4 interaction with tacrolimus and everolimus. The response and ctDNA figures come from the earlier phase 1–2 cohorts, not from the phase 3 report — V1 of the protocol conflated the two and V2 corrected it — and the phase 1–2 figures themselves do not match what the local protocol quotes.
avoid.note: The phase 1–2 report, read in full for this depot, gives the following for the subgroup it describes: among patients with a RAS G12 mutation receiving 300 mg as second-line therapy (n=26 of 38 with any RAS mutation), objective response 35% (95% CI 17–56), disease control 92% (75–99), median duration of response 8.2 months, median progression-free survival 8.5 months (6.7–10.5) and median overall survival 13.1 months (10.9 to not evaluable); across all any-RAS patients at 300 mg in the second line, 11 of 38 responded (29%, 15–46). Two figures the local protocol and an earlier version of this page carried are not supported by that report: median overall survival of 14.5 months (the published figure is 13.1 months), and 47% complete ctDNA clearance, which does not appear in the paper as read and must be re-sourced before it is quoted anywhere. The subgroup itself is defined by three simultaneous filters applied after the data were seen — allele, dose and line — out of 168 treated patients, and its reported 6-month overall survival of 100% (95% CI 100–100) is a marker of that selection rather than of drug effect. The study's stated primary objective was safety, with no hypothesis tested and no threshold it could have failed: treatment-related adverse events occurred in 96% of 168 patients, treatment-related grade 3 or higher in 30%, any-cause grade 3 or higher in 65%, and 48% of the 300-mg group needed a dose interruption or reduction. Three exploratory 300-mg cohorts, including the untreated-PDAC and RAS wild-type cohorts, were removed from the report.

avoid.t: Do not place a deceased-donor organ against a calculated MELD without a separately approved non-standard exception and institutional allocation-ethics approval.
avoid.pref: The local protocol prefers living donation specifically to avoid competing with established indications, with independent living-donor advocacy — and states that living donation does not remove the need for independent donor-risk review.
avoid.avoid: Deceased-donor use requires lawful allocation at calculated MELD or a separately approved non-standard request plus institutional allocation-ethics approval. It is not a fallback entitlement if a living donor is not found.

quickref.title: Resectability criteria at diagnosis
quickref.intro: The arterial and venous thresholds, in degrees, that decide which gate this patient is on.
rows: Resectable — arterial
No tumour contact with the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery or common hepatic artery
Resectable — venous
No contact with the SMV or portal vein, or ≤180° contact without vein contour irregularity
Borderline — head/uncinate arterial

Contact with the common hepatic artery without extension to the celiac axis or hepatic artery bifurcation, allowing safe complete resection and reconstruction; or SMA contact ≤180°; or contact with variant arterial anatomy (accessory or replaced right hepatic artery, replaced common hepatic artery, and the origin of the replaced or accessory vessel), with the degree recorded
Borderline — body/tail arterial
Celiac axis contact ≤180°
Borderline — venous

SMV or portal vein contact >180°; or ≤180° with vein contour irregularity; or vein thrombosis with suitable vessel proximal and distal allowing safe complete resection and vein reconstruction; or contact with the inferior vena cava
Locally advanced — head/uncinate arterial
SMA or celiac axis contact >180°
Locally advanced — body/tail arterial
SMA or celiac axis contact >180°; or celiac axis contact with aortic involvement
Locally advanced — venous
Complete SMV or portal vein occlusion, not amenable to resection and primary reconstruction
Metastatic
Any distant metastasis, including non-regional nodal metastasis, or positive peritoneal cytology
quickref.foot: Decisions about resectability status should be made in consensus at a multidisciplinary meeting, not by a single reader. Three caveats sit on this table. First, nobody derived these thresholds: the 180-degree cut-point was adopted into the Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association consensus statement from the NCCN criteria of the time, at a single meeting in November 2011 with no Delphi process, no voting and no described literature search, and that statement reports no inter-reader reproducibility data for measuring circumferential contact and no validation that using it changes report completeness, board decisions, resection rates or margins. Second, the category is assigned less reliably than the degrees imply: in SWOG S1505, at experienced US trial centres with a protocol scan and formal surgical consultation, central radiology review found 29% of patients called resectable did not meet the criteria — 51% with arterial interface, 35% with venous interface of 180 degrees or more and 65% with suspicion of distant disease — and a site radiologist checklist moved that only from 33% to 26%. Third, the criteria for resectable disease deliberately favour specificity over sensitivity so that no potentially resectable patient is denied an operation — occult metastatic disease is therefore expected rather than surprising, and CT sensitivity for small hepatic and peritoneal deposits is limited. After neoadjuvant therapy solid tumour contact may be replaced by increased hazy density or stranding around the peripancreatic vessels, and NCCN asks for this to be reported on both the staging and follow-up scans; mild increases in perivascular soft tissue do not alone represent progression, and ESMO states that imaging performance after chemotherapy is lower than in treatment-naive settings. Distant metastasis, regardless of anatomic resectability, implies disease that should not be treated with upfront resection. Locally advanced is a term for the time of diagnosis only and does not imply unresectable tumour. Imaging protocol: pancreatic parenchymal phase at 40–50 seconds and portal venous phase at 65–70 seconds, sections under 3 mm and preferably submillimetre, neutral oral contrast, with multiplanar reformats and a maximum-intensity-projection or 3D volumetric reconstruction for the vessels; high-quality CT no more than 4 weeks before surgery.
quickref.src: NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma, extracted text supplied to the programme (dated 22 April 2026), Criteria Defining Resectability Status at Diagnosis and Principles of Diagnosis, Imaging and Staging; thresholds reported against Al-Hawary 2014, PMID 24354378, which adopted rather than derived them; misclassification rate from Sohal 2021 SWOG S1505, PMID 33475684; restaging caveat from Conroy 2023 ESMO guideline, PMID 37678671

quickref.title: The neoadjuvant trials, side by side — and what each one's control arm got
quickref.intro: What each trial actually compared, in which population, what it showed and what its comparator was — because they do not agree, and because only one of them gave its control arm modern adjuvant chemotherapy.
rows: PREOPANC (n=246, resectable + borderline)

Neoadjuvant gemcitabine chemoradiotherapy vs upfront surgery, both arms adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy — and only 65 of 127 (51%) of the surgery arm received any chemotherapy. First report negative: median OS 16.0 vs 14.3 months, HR 0.78 (0.58–1.05), P=.096; resection 61% vs 72% (P=.058). Long-term positive at a second, unplanned look: HR 0.73 (0.56–0.96), P=.025, medians 15.7 vs 14.3, 5-year OS 20.5% vs 6.5%. Resectable subgroup HR 0.79 (0.54–1.16), P=.23; borderline 0.67 (0.45–0.99), P=.045; no significant interaction. 24% of the neoadjuvant arm never started it; staging laparoscopy mandatory in that arm only
PREOPANC-2 (n=369, resectable + borderline)

Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX with no adjuvant treatment vs the PREOPANC chemoradiotherapy regimen with adjuvant gemcitabine. No upfront-surgery arm at all. Failed superiority: median OS 21.9 vs 21.3 months, HR 0.88 (0.69–1.13), p=0.32 — the interval reaches 1.13, so this is not a demonstration of equivalence. Only 114 of 185 (62%) completed eight FOLFIRINOX cycles, 82% needed dose reductions. One significant secondary endpoint, favouring chemoradiotherapy: ypN0 58% vs 47%, p=0.0073
NORPACT-1 (n=140, resectable head only)

Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX vs upfront surgery. The only trial whose control arm partly received modern adjuvant therapy — 19 of 44 resected control patients (43%) got adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX. Primary endpoint significant in favour of upfront surgery: 18-month survival 60% vs 73% (p=0.032); median OS 25.1 vs 38.5 months, HR 1.52 (1.00–2.33), log-rank p=0.050 by ITT. Phase 2, designed at two-sided alpha 0.15; nothing significant per protocol (p=0.14; HR 1.46, 0.99–2.17, p=0.058). 16 of 77 (21%) never received FOLFIRINOX and all 16 went straight to resection; only 37 of 61 who started (61%) completed four cycles. The 38.5-month control-arm median exceeds every comparable upfront-surgery arm
ESPAC5 (n=90 randomised, 86 analysed, borderline only)

Four arms: immediate surgery vs gemcitabine+capecitabine vs FOLFIRINOX vs capecitabine chemoradiotherapy. Adjuvant therapy anywhere in the trial was gemcitabine-based in 41 of 43 patients (95%). Both primary endpoints negative — recruitment 90 of a 100 target at 2.16/month, resection 68% vs 55% (P=0.33, favouring immediate surgery), R0 14% vs 23% (P=0.49). 1-year OS 39% vs 78% vs 84% vs 60% (P=0.0028), pooled HR 0.29 (0.14–0.60): a secondary endpoint, 31 deaths, follow-up capped at 12 months, control-arm CA 19-9 802 vs 322–623 kU/L unadjusted. The chemoradiotherapy arm had the best pathology and the worst survival
SWOG S1505 (n=147 enrolled, 102 analysed, resectable)

Perioperative mFOLFIRINOX vs perioperative gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel. No randomised control — each arm tested against a historical 2-year survival of 40% from adjuvant trials, and both arms missed it: 47% (P=.15) and 48% (P=.14). Median OS 23.2 and 23.6 months. No winner picked. 45 of 147 (31%) removed from the analysed population after treatment, 43 of them on central radiology review. Its durable finding is that 29% of patients called resectable by their own centres did not meet the criteria
Alliance A021501 (n=126 registered, borderline only)

Neoadjuvant mFOLFIRINOX vs mFOLFIRINOX plus hypofractionated radiotherapy, each against a historical 18-month survival of 50% at one-sided alpha 0.07; postoperative therapy was FOLFOX6, reaching 34% and 24%. No randomised control, and the design forbids comparing the arms. Arm 1 met its benchmark (18-month OS 66.7%, 56.1–79.4; median 29.8 months); arm 2 closed early for futility on R0 rate in the first 30 patients (10 of 30 vs 17 of 30) with 18-month OS 47.3% and median 17.1 months. 16 of arm 1's 70 patients were registered without randomisation after arm 2 closed; 27% of arm 2 never received radiotherapy
Alliance A021806 (n=358, resectable)

Perioperative vs adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX, primary endpoint overall survival — the only trial that asks the question this gate faces. No results. Active, not recruiting; primary completion scheduled December 2028
Pooled, 9 randomised trials (n=1,194)

Overall HR 0.73 (0.55–0.98), I² 55.8%; by subgroup borderline resectable 0.60 (0.38–0.96) and resectable 0.90 (0.63–1.28) — but the between-subgroup test was not significant (p=0.081). Resection rate lower (72.6% vs 80.6%, RR 0.94); R0 higher (43.8% vs 33.0%, RR 1.35); N0 higher (30.9% vs 15.0%, RR 2.03); serious adverse events roughly doubled (56.1% vs 27.0%, RR reported as 1.92 with a 95% CI of 1.28–1.89 that does not contain its own point estimate). Adjuvant therapy initiation did not differ (57.7% vs 55.6%, p=0.353), which undercuts the mechanism the strategy rests on. The pooled comparator is overwhelmingly adjuvant gemcitabine or S-1; the headline estimate depends on post hoc removal of NORPACT-1, the only trial with a partly modern comparator and the only one favouring upfront surgery
ESMO 2023 guideline

Neoadjuvant therapy is not recommended for resectable pancreatic cancer due to limited phase III evidence, except in the context of clinical trials — [II, E], a recommendation against. Induction is favoured over upfront surgery in borderline resectable disease on weaker language (impact on OS seems promising). The guideline predates PREOPANC-2, NORPACT-1 and the 2025 meta-analyses, and describes no literature search strategy
quickref.foot: Reading the table by resectability category is the most coherent way to hold it together — in borderline resectable disease the randomised evidence leans toward neoadjuvant chemotherapy (pooled HR 0.60, and ESPAC5's survival signal), while in anatomically resectable disease it does not (pooled HR 0.90, NORPACT-1 pointing the other way, and ESMO recommending against at [II, E]). But the full-text read says that reading is a hypothesis, not a result: the between-subgroup test in the pooled analysis was not significant (p=0.081), PREOPANC's interaction test was not significant in either report, and PREOPANC-2 found no treatment-effect heterogeneity in any subgroup. Five traps. The comparator. Only NORPACT-1 gave its control arm modern adjuvant therapy, and there only 43% of resected control patients received adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX — so the question a board actually faces, neoadjuvant chemotherapy against upfront surgery with adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX, has never been tested; A021806 will test it and has published nothing. PREOPANC. Its positive result came from a second, unplanned look at a trial whose primary analysis was negative, in a mixed population, against adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy half of whose arm received no chemotherapy at all; the median difference is 1.4 months and the separation is in the 5-year tail. NORPACT-1. Phase 2, designed at a two-sided alpha of 0.15, non-significant per protocol, with 21% of allocated patients never receiving the regimen and all of them going straight to resection, and a control-arm median of 38.5 months that exceeds every comparable arm in the literature. ESPAC5. It failed both primary endpoints and its resection rate numerically favoured immediate surgery, so its survival figures are a secondary endpoint at 12 months of follow-up with 31 deaths and an unadjusted three-fold CA 19-9 imbalance against the control arm. The pooled analysis. Its headline estimate depends on post hoc removal of NORPACT-1 — the only trial with a partly modern comparator and the only one favouring upfront surgery — and its serious-adverse-event risk ratio of 1.92 is published with a 95% CI of 1.28 to 1.89 that does not contain its own point estimate. The surrogates do not help: R0 and N0 rates improved with neoadjuvant therapy in the pooled data and in NORPACT-1, nodal status improved with chemoradiotherapy in PREOPANC-2, and ESPAC5's chemoradiotherapy arm had the best pathology and the worst survival — in none of these did the pathology move survival.

quickref.title: What the molecular result changes
quickref.intro: Which alteration leads to which agent, with the figure that justifies it and the population it was measured in.
rows: Germline, any patient

Test everyone, regardless of family history: deleterious variants in CDKN2A, TP53, MLH1, BRCA2, ATM or BRCA1 in 5.5% of 3,030 registry patients — 7.9% with a family history, 5.2% without. A clinic-based case series against public sequencing databases, not a recruited control group; carriage was not associated with survival (HR 0.86, P=.09); and of the six genes only BRCA1/2 has a randomised treatment consequence in this disease, so 5.5% is not the actionable fraction
RAS G12 mutation, previously treated

Daraxonrasib: median OS 13.2 vs 6.6 months in the RAS G12 population, HR 0.40, P<0.001; PFS by blinded central review 7.3 vs 3.5 months, HR 0.45. Phase 3, n=500, open label, unconstrained investigator's-choice comparator. Non-G12 patients: HR 1.38 (0.60–3.17), favouring chemotherapy. 38 of 252 (15.1%) of the chemotherapy arm never received it, against 7 of 248 (2.8%) on daraxonrasib
Germline BRCA1/2, platinum-exposed

Olaparib maintenance after ≥16 weeks platinum without progression: PFS 7.4 vs 3.8 months, HR 0.53 (0.35–0.82), P=.004; no OS difference at interim (46% maturity), 18.9 vs 18.1 months, HR 0.91 (0.56–1.46), P=.68; no quality-of-life difference; grade ≥3 AEs 40% vs 23%. Comparator was placebo, not continued chemotherapy; 154 randomised from 3,315 screened (4.6%)
BRCA1/2 or PALB2, germline or somatic
Rucaparib maintenance after ≥16 weeks platinum: median PFS 13.1 months, median duration of response 17.3 months — single-arm phase 2, no control, primary report not read for this depot
MSI-high or dMMR
Pembrolizumab, or dostarlimab as subsequent therapy. Pembrolizumab also for TMB-high (≥10 mut/Mb). Tumour-agnostic approvals; no pancreatic trial read for this depot
KRAS G12C (1–2% of PDAC)

Sotorasib: 8 of 38 responded (21%, 10–37), PFS 4.0 months, OS 6.9 months — no prespecified benchmark and no hypothesis test. Adagrasib: 7 of 21 pancreatic patients responded (33.3%) on central review, PFS 5.4 months, OS 8.0 months, against a 10% null that applies to the pooled basket and not to this subgroup. Both single-arm, no screening denominator
NRG1 fusion

Zenocutuzumab: 15 of 36 pancreatic patients responded by investigator assessment (42%, 25–59) and 16 of 36 centrally (44%); median duration of response 7.4 months (4.0–11.2) investigator-assessed, 9.1 months centrally. All 36 were KRAS wild-type, and no PFS or OS is reported for this subgroup. Enriched in younger KRAS wild-type patients — median age 48.5 years in a 10-patient series
NTRK fusion
Entrectinib, larotrectinib or repotrectinib — basket-trial results with 1 to 3 pancreatic patients each; no primary report read for this depot
RET fusion
Selpercatinib — 11 pancreatic patients, at least half with an objective response; no primary report read for this depot
BRAF V600E
Dabrafenib with trametinib — ORR 38–47% across the NCI-MATCH subprotocol and the ROAR basket trial, in mixed tumour types; no primary report read for this depot
FGFR alteration
Erdafitinib — 10 of 18 pancreatic patients responded (56%) in RAGNAR; no primary report read for this depot
HER2

Test by IHC ± FISH as well as on the NGS panel; fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan was studied in 25 pancreatic patients in DESTINY-PanTumor2, under 20% of whom were IHC 3+; no primary report read for this depot
quickref.foot: Two operational points matter more than any single row. Order profiling and germline testing at the first visit and bank two extra needle passes at the index biopsy, because the commonest failure in this disease is a report that arrives after the patient is too unwell to act on it — and do not wait for the result to start treatment, since NCCN states that if BRCA1/2 status is unknown the patient is treated as clinically indicated. Then read the denominators. Apart from daraxonrasib and olaparib, every row here is a single-arm result in a pancreatic subset of between one and thirty-eight patients, usually drawn from a mixed-tumour basket trial, with no screening denominator reported, and response rates from baskets do not transfer cleanly to this disease; two of the rows — sotorasib's pancreatic cohort and the subgroup reads from the adagrasib basket — had no prespecified efficacy threshold applying to pancreatic patients at all, so there was nothing they could have failed. Read the germline row the same way: 5.5% is a prevalence estimate from a clinic-based case series compared with public sequencing databases rather than a recruited control group, carriage was not associated with survival, and of the six genes only BRCA1/2 carries a randomised treatment consequence in this disease — so 5.5% is not the actionable fraction. Do not treat the gene as the target; different alterations in the same gene do not predict the same response, which is the point the non-G12 subgroup of RASolute 302 makes (HR 1.38, 0.60–3.17).

quickref.title: The experimental liver-only transplant protocol — and its comparator
quickref.intro: What the local protocol requires, and the survival figure it would have to beat. Protocol-only, investigational throughout.
rows: Policy status
Not a standardized OPTN exception diagnosis; not among the recommended diagnoses in the December 2025 transplant-oncology guidance; no MELD exception score recommended or guaranteed
Required before activation

Prospective IRB approval, DSMB oversight, institutional transplant-selection and allocation-ethics approval, independent living-donor advocacy where applicable, consent that benefit is unproven and graft access may be unavailable
Protocol A — disease burden
Liver-only, ≤5 metastases on PET-CT and cross-sectional imaging; no extrahepatic disease on PET-CT within 4 weeks of listing
Protocol A — therapy and response

≥6 months first-line FOLFIRINOX, mFOLFIRINOX, NALIRIFOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel; RECIST partial response or stable disease sustained ≥6 months; CA 19-9 fall ≥85% or normalisation; declining or undetectable RAS-mutant ctDNA; ≥12 months from diagnosis without progression
Protocol A — patient and primary

Age 18–65, ECOG 0–1, biopsy-proven PDAC, primary resectable or borderline resectable, negative staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings and portal nodal sampling, standard transplant evaluation complete
Protocol A — exclusions

Any extrahepatic disease; poorly differentiated or undifferentiated histology; signet-ring features; progression at any point on neoadjuvant therapy; PET metabolic tumour volume >70 cm³ or total lesion glycolysis >260 g; CA 19-9 rising or >500 U/mL at listing; prior liver radiation; uncontrolled biliary obstruction or cholangitis; another malignancy within 5 years
Protocol A — stopping rules
Perioperative mortality >10% in the first 10 patients; 1-year OS <50%; 1-year recurrence >60% — each triggers enrolment pause and DSMB review
Protocol B — who

Liver-only, ≤10 metastases, bilobar permitted; ≥1 prior line with progression or intolerance; eligible RAS mutation per the current daraxonrasib investigational protocol, with an FDA-authorized IND and sponsor confirmation; willing to be evaluated for living donation
Protocol B — conversion gate at 6 months
All of: RECIST partial or complete response; CA 19-9 fall ≥85% or normalisation; ctDNA fall ≥50%; PET metabolic tumour volume ≤70 cm³; no new sites; negative staging laparoscopy; resectable primary
Protocol B — stopping rules
Perioperative mortality >15% in the first 5 patients; conversion <20% at interim after 20 enrolled; 1-year OS <40%
Operation and immunosuppression

Simultaneous pancreatectomy and orthotopic liver transplantation; abort on positive peritoneal cytology or distant nodal involvement on frozen section. Basiliximab induction, low-dose tacrolimus with mycophenolate weeks 1–4, conversion to everolimus (trough 5–8 ng/mL) with tacrolimus tapered to 3–5 ng/mL
The comparator to beat

In 241 patients with stage IV PDAC and synchronous liver metastases, median OS was 7 months (5–9) overall and the same in the 144 with liver-only disease. Among the 54 who received chemotherapy and survived to a 12-month landmark, median OS was 26 months (19–33); for the 27 of those with liver-only disease, 26 months (17–39). The 9 patients (4%) who also had a resectable or borderline resectable primary and resectable liver-only metastases reached 39 months (13–not reached) — with 5-year survival of 0%, and with no operation. The 39-month figure rests on 9 patients, 5 of them dead, and the benchmark cohort's median CA 19-9 was 3,101 U/mL with 64% rising
quickref.foot: The benchmark row is the most important one on this page's transplant gate. A protocol that selects for a sustained response over 12 months is selecting the patients whose expected survival on chemotherapy alone is 26 to 39 months, not the 7 to 12 months usually quoted for metastatic disease — so the margin any operation has to generate is much narrower than it looks; the 39-month figure rests on nine patients, five of them dead, and that cohort had no 5-year survivors. Version control matters here: V2 of the protocol (revised 23 July 2026, policy review 16 July 2026) removed what V1 permitted at investigator discretion — daraxonrasib only at an IND-authorized dose within a formal phase 1 safety lead-in rather than 300 mg daily, no discretionary chemotherapy combinations, no routine post-transplant maintenance or mandatory 12-month course, and no daraxonrasib plus afatinib under the protocol at all. Two of the protocol's own daraxonrasib figures do not survive the full-text read and should be corrected before activation: the phase 1–2 median overall survival it quotes as 14.5 months is 13.1 months (95% CI 10.9 to not evaluable) in the published report, in a 26-patient subgroup defined by allele, dose and line after the data were seen, and the 47% complete ctDNA clearance figure does not appear in that report as read. The second is not cosmetic — declining or undetectable RAS-mutant ctDNA is an entry criterion in Protocol A and a ctDNA fall of 50% or more is a conversion criterion in Protocol B, so both gates are calibrated against an unverified number. Deceased-donor transplantation is not a fallback entitlement and requires lawful allocation at calculated MELD or a separately approved non-standard exception with institutional allocation-ethics approval; living donation does not remove the need for independent donor-risk review. Verify the current OPTN policy text and the review-board guidance before any listing decision.
