honest.t: The single most important thing the full-text read changed: almost no trial on this page compared its intervention with the therapy this page recommends. Every adjuvant comparator is gemcitabine monotherapy or observation, and every neoadjuvant comparator is upfront surgery followed by adjuvant gemcitabine — except one.
honest.why: In the nine randomised neoadjuvant trials pooled in the 2025 meta-analysis, the upfront-surgery arms received adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy, S-1, gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel or PEXG, and only NORPACT-1 used mFOLFIRINOX — where in turn only 19 of 44 resected control patients (43%) actually received it and 25 of 44 received a gemcitabine-based regimen. PREOPANC gave adjuvant gemcitabine in both arms and only 65 of 127 patients (51%) in the surgery arm received any chemotherapy at all. ESPAC5's adjuvant therapy was gemcitabine or gemcitabine with capecitabine in 41 of 43 patients. PREOPANC-2 has no upfront-surgery arm and gave its FOLFIRINOX arm no adjuvant treatment. S1505 and A021501 had no randomised control at all. On the adjuvant side, PRODIGE-24, ESPAC-4 and APACT all ran against gemcitabine monotherapy, and CONKO-001 against observation. So the sequencing question — neoadjuvant chemotherapy against upfront surgery with adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX delivered to everyone who can take it — has never been tested. A021806 is the trial that will test it, and it has reported nothing.

honest.t: NORPACT-1's primary endpoint was statistically significant in favour of upfront surgery, and that is still not evidence that neoadjuvant chemotherapy is harmful.
honest.why: 18-month survival was 60% (95% CI 49–71) with neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX against 73% (62–84) with upfront surgery, p=0.032, with median overall survival 25.1 against 38.5 months, hazard ratio 1.52 (1.00–2.33), log-rank p=0.050 by intention to treat. Four things bound that result. The trial was designed as an exploratory phase 2 study at a two-sided alpha of 0.15. Nothing is significant per protocol (18-month p=0.14; hazard ratio 1.46, 0.99–2.17, p=0.058). Sixteen of 77 patients (21%) allocated to neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX never received it and all 16 went straight to resection, so the intention-to-treat comparison is not a comparison of two delivered strategies; of the 61 who did start, only 37 (61%) completed four cycles and 16 (26%) received one or two. And the control arm's 38.5-month median exceeds every comparable upfront-surgery arm in the literature (14.3 months in PREOPANC), in 63 patients with 28 deaths, with 3 cholangiocarcinomas and 2 neuroendocrine tumours among the 11 non-PDAC diagnoses left in its denominator. Read it as a failure to show benefit in a trial that failed to deliver its intervention, which is what the authors say.

honest.t: The meta-analysis most likely to be cited as settling the sequencing question excludes, post hoc, the one trial whose control arm resembles current practice — and reports a harm estimate whose confidence interval does not contain its own point estimate.
honest.why: The 2025 pooled analysis of nine trials and 1,194 patients gives an overall hazard ratio of 0.73 (0.55–0.98) with I² 55.8%, borderline resectable 0.60 (0.38–0.96) and resectable 0.90 (0.63–1.28). It then removes NORPACT-1 and the pooled ESPAC5 chemotherapy comparison as influence outliers, which collapses heterogeneity to I² 0% by construction and tightens the overall estimate to 0.74 (0.64–0.85) — while removing the only included trial that gave its control arm adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX and the only one favouring upfront surgery. The honest reading is that the pooled estimate is unstable and depends on whether the modern comparator is included. Separately, its serious-adverse-event estimate is reported in both the abstract and the table as a risk ratio of 1.92 with a 95% CI of 1.28 to 1.89 — an interval that does not contain 1.92 — so the magnitude of that harm as published cannot be relied on, although its direction (56.1% versus 27.0%) is clear and clinically important. ESPAC5's four arms are also entered in multiple ways and PREOPANC three times, and survival for several trials was reconstructed from Kaplan-Meier curves.

honest.t: The resectable-versus-borderline split that this entire page is organised around is not statistically established.
honest.why: Every test of it has failed. In the pooled analysis the between-subgroup test was p=0.081, and the paper nonetheless concludes that neoadjuvant therapy should be regarded as standard of care in borderline resectable disease. In PREOPANC's initial report the interaction test was P=.14, and in the long-term report no interaction test was significant across any of seven prespecified subgroups. In PREOPANC-2 no subgroup showed treatment-effect heterogeneity at all (every interaction p at or above 0.23). The split is a coherent and probably correct clinical hypothesis — it matches the biology and the pathology data — but it is a hypothesis, and the page uses it to route patients to different gates.

honest.t: ESMO's 2023 guideline recommends against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease, at grade II, E — and this page had not said so.
honest.why: The wording is neoadjuvant therapy is not recommended for resectable PC due to limited phase III evidence, except in the context of clinical trials, graded [II, E]. That is the most authoritative European statement on the question and it is a recommendation against, not a permission. Two qualifications belong with it: the guideline is a September 2023 snapshot that predates PREOPANC-2, NORPACT-1 and the 2025 meta-analyses, and its literature was selected by the authors with no described search strategy, no date limits and no screening flow, with statements the panel considered justified standard practice published ungraded. Its support for induction in borderline resectable disease rests on a five-study meta-analysis (OS HR 0.61, 0.44–0.85) and on PREOPANC's 113-patient borderline subgroup, and is worded as impact on OS seems promising rather than graded like its [I, A] adjuvant recommendations.

honest.t: The attrition argument — that a third of resected patients never get adjuvant therapy, so chemotherapy should come first — is the main mechanistic case for neoadjuvant sequencing, and the randomised data do not support it.
honest.why: Pooled across the nine randomised trials, the proportion of patients who started adjuvant therapy was no different between the two strategies: 57.7% after neoadjuvant treatment against 55.6% after upfront surgery, RR 0.92 (95% CI 0.76–1.12), p=0.353. NORPACT-1 shows the same pattern in detail: any chemotherapy was more often received with the neoadjuvant strategy (95% versus 75%, p=0.0006) but adjuvant initiation (66% versus 75%, p=0.21) and completion (53% versus 49%, p=0.40) did not differ. PREOPANC's neoadjuvant arm had more total chemotherapy exposure, but that is a design artefact: the comparator arm was allowed only postoperative chemotherapy, which half of it never received. The up-to-30% attrition figure is real and is a system failure worth fixing with a named owner — it is just not an argument that these trials settle.

honest.t: Roughly a third of patients called resectable are not, and that misclassification sits under every gate on this page.
honest.why: SWOG S1505 required a pancreas-protocol scan within 28 days, formal surgical consultation confirming resectability within 21 days, and enrolment at experienced US trial centres. Central radiology review then found that 43 of 146 patients reviewed (29%) did not meet the trial's own resectability criteria: 22 (51%) had arterial interface, 15 (35%) venous interface of 180 degrees or more, and 28 (65%) suspicion of distant disease. All of them had already started protocol therapy, because the review was retrospective. Adding a mandatory site radiologist checklist after the interim analysis moved the rate only from 33% to 26%. Nothing on this page assumes a misclassification rate at all, and the resectability category is what decides which gate a patient enters.

honest.t: The resectability thresholds are a shared language, not a biological boundary, and nobody derived them. A tumour with 181 degrees of SMA contact is not categorically different from one with 179.
honest.why: The degrees come from the Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association consensus reporting statement, which was produced at a single meeting in November 2011 with no Delphi process, no voting, no reported level of agreement and no described literature search; the 180-degree cut-point was adopted from the NCCN criteria of the time rather than derived or validated in it. The statement reports no inter-reader reproducibility data for measuring circumferential contact, which is the measurement everything else rests on, and no validation that using the template changes report completeness, inter-reader agreement, board decisions, resection rates or margins. NCCN states the criteria for resectable disease were written to favour specificity over sensitivity so that no potentially resectable patient is denied an operation. Their value is that they make boards and trials comparable, which is real but different from prognostic validity — and the S1505 finding above shows how imperfectly even that works.

honest.t: R0 is defined on this page as more than 1 mm of clearance, that number is borrowed, and the study behind it answered its own question in the null.
honest.why: NCCN states the CAP protocol's 1 mm rule is based primarily on extrapolation from rectal adenocarcinoma data and that there is currently a lack of definitive evidence for what constitutes an adequate margin in pancreatic resection specimens; ESMO uses the same definition. The single study that supplied the clinical argument, 163 consecutive pancreatoduodenectomies at one centre, found median survival 15.4 months for equivocal R1 (within 1 mm, not reaching the margin) against 12.6 months for unequivocal R1 at P=0.102, and concluded the two should be treated as one category on the strength of that non-significant test; equivocal R1 versus R0 was also non-significant (P=0.114), so the study cannot separate the intermediate group from either neighbour. Its R0 group was 35 patients with a median of 25.4 months and a 95% CI from 10.5 to 40.8 months, margin status did not survive multivariable adjustment (adjusted HR 1.443, 0.896–2.324, P=0.132) while lymph node ratio, tumour size and adjuvant chemotherapy did, and only 27% of the cohort received adjuvant chemotherapy. The practical consequence is larger than the prognostic one: applying the rule moved the R1 rate at that centre from 44% to 79%, so R0 rates are substantially a function of local pathology protocol and the R0 figures quoted across the trials on this page are not comparable with one another. Reporting in millimetres is still how the field will eventually get a derived threshold.

honest.t: Disease-free survival in the open-label adjuvant trials this page relies on is partly a detection artefact, and the trial that showed it is the one this page treats as the weakest.
honest.why: APACT is the only adjuvant pancreatic trial to use blinded independently assessed disease-free survival as its primary endpoint, and in the same gemcitabine arm, central review gave a median of 18.8 months while the unblinded investigators gave 13.7 months, with 77% concordance and 48% to 51% of patients censored. The investigator figure matches the gemcitabine arms of ESPAC-4 (13.4 months) and PRODIGE-24 (12.8 months), both of which used unblinded investigator assessment, as did CONKO-001 — where recurrence was dated from the first subjective symptom and assessed in part by abdominal ultrasound with no central review. That is why CONKO-001 can show a 2.4-fold disease-free survival difference beside a 2.6-month median survival difference. Every adjuvant disease-free survival hazard ratio on this page should be read with a five-month detection allowance.

honest.t: PRODIGE-24's 54.4-month median was an artefact of an immature database, and the mature data are a smaller result than the headline.
honest.why: The trial was stopped early for efficacy at 91.8% of expected disease-free survival events, and with mature 5-year data the disease-free survival hazard ratio moved from 0.58 to 0.66, overall survival from 0.64 to 0.68, and the median from 54.4 to 53.5 months. Five-year disease-free survival differs by only 7.1 percentage points (26.1% versus 19.0%) against 11.8 points at 5-year overall survival, so part of the survival gain accrues after relapse — and post-relapse survival was numerically worse in the mFOLFIRINOX arm (13.1 versus 15.0 months), with chemotherapy at relapse reaching 66.9% of its relapsing patients against 83.0% of the control arm's, 74.2% of whom received FOLFIRINOX. Delivery was poor: 67.2% completed all 12 cycles and only 33.6% achieved a relative dose intensity of 0.80 or more. The population was age 18 to 79, no coronary disease, WHO 0–1, fully recovered, with a clear postoperative scan and postoperative CA 19-9 below 180 U/mL; in the 101 patients aged 70 or older the benefit did not reach significance (HR 0.86, 0.53–1.39), and the median age of this disease is around 70. Quality of life was never collected.

honest.t: APACT was a negative trial. Its overall survival result is a descriptive secondary endpoint read at the third of three successive data cutoffs.
honest.why: The blinded independently assessed primary endpoint failed — disease-free survival 19.4 versus 18.8 months, hazard ratio 0.88 (0.729–1.063), P=.18 — and the paper itself states that because the primary endpoint was not met, all other comparisons are descriptive. The overall survival P value improved from .045 to .0232 to .0091 across cutoffs in December 2018, April 2020 and April 2021, with no prespecified plan for repeated testing and no multiplicity adjustment anywhere in the trial. The price was 86% grade 3 or worse treatment-emergent events against 68%, and grade 3 or worse peripheral neuropathy in 15% against 0%, of which 84% had not improved to grade 1 or less at the primary cutoff — in a trial that collected no quality-of-life data. The population was the most selected in the adjuvant literature: CA 19-9 below 100 U/mL with a median of 13.6 U/mL, 1,226 screened to randomise 866, which is why its gemcitabine arm reached 37.7 months.

honest.t: The randomised trials of consolidative radiotherapy are null for survival, and the one that produced a positive margin result rewrote its primary endpoint mid-trial using its own unblinded interim data.
honest.why: LAP07 gave a hazard ratio of 1.03 (0.79–1.34), P=.83, was stopped at its interim analysis for futility with that analysis declared final, never reached its planned 392 deaths, and measured survival from the first randomisation while allocating the intervention at the second — so it is underpowered rather than equivalent, and half its radiotherapy plans had minor and 18% major protocol deviations. CONKO-007 gave a hazard ratio of 0.937 (0.747–1.174), P=.57, and missed its primary endpoint (R0 25% versus 18%, P=.113) — an endpoint changed mid-trial from overall survival to R0 rate, with the new effect size calculated from unblinded interim data on 180 already-enrolled patients in which one arm's R0 rate was already nearly double the other's, and with no central radiotherapy review at all for stated financial reasons. Its significant R0 advantage (69.4% versus 50.0%, P=.04) is confined to the patients who reached theatre, which was not randomised, and the authors state that physicians' knowledge of the R0 endpoint changed their behaviour. What both trials do show, consistently, is better local control: locoregional recurrence hazard ratio 0.33 (0.206–0.530), P<.001, in CONKO-007 and 32% versus 46% locoregional progression in LAP07. Offer radiotherapy for that, and say so.

honest.t: Conversion surgery after induction therapy for locally advanced disease carries an 8% 30-day mortality in the only randomised trial that reports it, and this page had not said so.
honest.why: In CONKO-007, 30-day postoperative mortality was 5 of 60 and 5 of 62 — 8% in both arms. The trial's conclusion that chemoradiotherapy did not increase postsurgical mortality means only that it did not differ between the randomised arms. One operative death in twelve belongs in the consent conversation for an operation whose benefit, within that trial, rests on a non-randomised comparison of operated with non-operated patients (HR 0.525, 0.408–0.676). The denominator also matters: those 336 randomised patients are the 64% of enrolled patients who survived and did not progress through three months of chemotherapy, and the 159 of 495 (32.1%) who did progress had a median survival of 9 months with no 5-year survivors. LAP07, from gemcitabine-based induction, achieved curative-intent resection in 18 of 442 patients (4%).

honest.t: The 24.2-month median survival quoted for FOLFIRINOX in locally advanced disease, and the 25.9% resection rate that goes with it, come from single-arm cohorts with no control group — and none of the obvious explanations for the figure can be shown to drive it.
honest.why: The patient-level meta-analysis pooled 11 studies and 315 locally advanced patients, eleven of the thirteen included studies retrospective, none using staging laparoscopy, and only three enrolling exclusively locally advanced patients while seven had no formal resectability criteria. Individual-study medians ranged from 10.0 to 32.7 months, and because patient-level data were pooled into a single Kaplan-Meier curve rather than meta-analysed, no I² or prediction interval is reported for survival — the narrow 95% CI of 21.7 to 26.8 months reflects patient numbers, not the disagreement between studies. A pooled 63.5% also received radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy (I² 90%, range 31% to 100%), yet across studies there was no correlation between survival and radiotherapy use (p=0.12), resection rate (p=0.39) or number of cycles (p=0.95). Survival was measured from the start of FOLFIRINOX, so everyone who deteriorated or was found metastatic before chemotherapy could start is invisible; LAP07's 7.7-month median for patients who progressed during induction indicates the size of that group. The 78.4% R0 rate has a resected-only denominator of 81 of 325 patients, so it describes 19% of the cohort. The comparator offered for 24.2 months — 6 to 13 months with gemcitabine — is a narrative historical range. The authors' own conclusion is that the result needs a randomised trial and that it remains unestablished who benefits from radiotherapy or resection afterwards.

honest.t: The DROP trial does not say what this page used it to say about drainage before neoadjuvant therapy, and it did not show that drainage makes the operation less safe.
honest.why: It randomised 202 patients to a plastic stent for 4 to 6 weeks or to surgery within one week, excluded patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy by protocol, and capped bilirubin at 250 micromol/L. Serious complications within 120 days were 74% versus 39% (RR 0.54, 0.41–0.71, P<0.001), but that total bundles drainage complications with surgical complications, which guarantees the direction: complications attributable to drainage occurred in 46% versus 2%, while surgical complications did not differ significantly (37% versus 47%, RR 0.79, 0.57–1.11), nor did mortality (4% versus 9%, RR 0.48, 0.15–1.51) or resection rate (67% versus 56%, P=0.11). Its 26% cholangitis and 30% stent-exchange rates are largely properties of plastic endoprostheses; every neoadjuvant protocol in this depot specifies or prefers self-expanding metal stents, which were not tested. And its control strategy required dedicated theatre capacity at all 13 hospitals to operate within seven days — a unit that cannot deliver that has not got the comparator the trial tested, because delay without drainage is not what was studied. Fifteen of 196 patients (8%) did not have adenocarcinoma on final pathology, and overall mortality was 7%.

honest.t: Whether to offer arterial resection or arterial divestment for PDAC at this centre has not been decided, and no number for minimum annual volume has been set.
honest.why: NCCN restricts arterial resection to centres with proven experience in pancreatectomy with vascular resection and reconstruction, in highly selected patients after extensive neoadjuvant therapy with objective response, and requires that patients be told the long-term benefit — the chance of cure — is currently unknown. It names no volume threshold, and nor does this page. The one randomised dataset here that touched volume found it in a post hoc multivariable model of PRODIGE-24's 77 hospitals (10 or more patients enrolled, HR 0.77, 0.61–0.98, P=.03), selected by a stepwise procedure with no multiplicity correction and confounded with case mix, surgical quality, access to relapse therapy and country. Volume-outcome relationships in pancreatic surgery are observational and consistent; the threshold is a governance choice, not a measurable one. [EXPERTISE]

honest.t: What counts as a significant response after neoadjuvant therapy is a local definition, and until it is written down it is being applied inconsistently — and the metrics it rests on are poor surrogates.
honest.why: NCCN hands the definition to the local treatment team in the footnote to its own response table, offering only examples: CA 19-9 normalisation, near-normalisation or at least a 50% decrease, and a complete or near-complete metabolic response on PET. Since the response category determines whether a vascular resection is offered, an unwritten definition means the same patient gets different answers from different surgeons on different weeks. The full-text read adds that the surrogates themselves do not track survival. NORPACT-1 improved R0 (56% versus 39%, p=0.018) and N0 (29% versus 14%, p<0.0001) and survival went the other way. PREOPANC-2's one significant secondary endpoint was nodal (ypN0 58% versus 47%) and survival did not move. ESPAC5's chemoradiotherapy arm had the best R0 and nodal results and the worst survival. The one metric with supporting data is biochemical: ESMO cites a pooled analysis of 17 studies and 2,242 patients in which a CA 19-9 fall of more than 50% or normalisation was associated with better overall survival (P<0.0001), and ESMO also states that imaging performance after chemotherapy is lower than in treatment-naive settings.

honest.t: The surveillance schedule after resection is not stated on this page, because the guideline footnote that defines the interval did not survive the machine extraction supplied to the programme.
honest.why: Rather than quote an interval from memory, this page quotes what the guideline says about the value of surveillance: a SEER-Medicare analysis showed no significant survival benefit from regular surveillance CT, there are no data that a rising tumour marker leads to earlier intervention or better outcomes, CA 19-9 is graded category 2B, and there is no evidence that serial ctDNA monitoring improves outcomes. The stated rationale is consensus — that earlier identification may allow enrolment in trials or other treatment. Confirm the interval against the current published guideline and record the version used.

honest.t: Adjuvant therapy after neoadjuvant therapy is improvised, everywhere, including here — and the guidelines now say so in as many words.
honest.why: NCCN says only that the options depend on the response to neoadjuvant therapy and other clinical factors. ESMO states that the benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy following neoadjuvant therapy and pancreatectomy remains to be established and that randomised data are lacking. No trial defines total perioperative duration, whether to continue the same regimen or switch, or what to do after a complete pathologic response — and the trials do not even agree on the shape of the sequence: PREOPANC-2's FOLFIRINOX arm gave no adjuvant treatment at all while its chemoradiotherapy arm gave four cycles of gemcitabine, S1505 continued the same regimen and reached only 55% to 56% of eligible patients, and A021501 gave four cycles of FOLFOX6 to 24% to 34%. There is no defensible default, which is why this is an approvals item rather than a recommendation.

honest.t: The targeted agents below daraxonrasib and olaparib rest on pancreatic subsets of 21 to 38 patients, and two of them had no efficacy threshold they could have failed.
honest.why: The sotorasib pancreatic cohort pooled 38 patients across phase 1 dose exploration, phase 1 expansion and phase 2, with no prespecified response benchmark and no hypothesis test, and its response interval (10% to 37%) is compatible with the under-10% historical benchmark the authors invoke. Adagrasib's prespecified 10% null applies to the pooled tumour-agnostic cohort of 57 evaluable patients, not to its 21 pancreatic patients, and six patients counted as evaluable by investigators were removed by central review for having no measurable disease, moving the denominator favourably. Zenocutuzumab's 36 pancreatic patients were all KRAS wild-type, its primary endpoint was investigator-assessed response with blinded central review only secondary, its primary efficacy population is a post-enrolment construct (204 treated to 158 evaluable, with short-follow-up exclusions falling on early progressors), and no progression-free or overall survival is reported for the pancreatic subgroup at all. None of the three reports a screening denominator, so the testing burden implied by any of them is invisible. The NTRK, RET, BRAF and FGFR entries were not retrieved for this depot.

honest.t: RASolute 302's hazard ratio of 0.40 is the largest effect on this page, it is established only in RAS G12 disease, and it is inseparable from how badly its comparator arm was delivered.
honest.why: The dual primary endpoints were met in the RAS G12 population: median overall survival 13.2 versus 6.6 months, hazard ratio 0.40, P<0.001, and progression-free survival by blinded central review 7.3 versus 3.5 months, hazard ratio 0.45. In patients without a G12 mutation the hazard ratio was 1.38 (95% CI 0.60–3.17), a point estimate favouring chemotherapy. And 38 of 252 patients (15.1%) allocated to chemotherapy never received it, against 7 of 248 (2.8%) allocated daraxonrasib — 29 of them withdrawing, and some no longer eligible because ECOG had risen above 1 by the time treatment was due, which an oral agent started the same day does not face. Those patients remain in the comparator's intention-to-treat survival curve. The comparator itself was unconstrained investigator's choice given per local prescribing practice, with a 6.6-month median at the low end of published second-line outcomes, and its quality is not auditable from the report. The sponsor supported the trial and performed and validated the analyses. The direction of the result is not in doubt; the magnitude should be read with the comparator in view.

honest.t: The daraxonrasib figures the local transplant protocol relies on do not match the published phase 1–2 report, and one of them could not be found in it at all.
honest.why: The phase 1–2 study, read in full for this depot, reports for its RAS G12 second-line 300 mg subgroup (n=26 of 168 treated patients) an objective response of 35% (95% CI 17–56), median progression-free survival 8.5 months (6.7–10.5) and median overall survival 13.1 months (10.9 to not evaluable); across all any-RAS second-line 300 mg patients, 11 of 38 responded (29%, 15–46). The local protocol and an earlier version of this page carried a median overall survival of 14.5 months and a 47% complete ctDNA clearance figure. The 14.5-month figure is wrong against the published report, and the ctDNA figure does not appear in it as read — it must be re-sourced before it is quoted, in the protocol or anywhere else, since ctDNA decline is an entry and conversion criterion in both local cohorts. The subgroup is also defined by three filters applied after the data were seen (allele, dose, line), its reported 6-month overall survival of 100% (95% CI 100–100) is a marker of that selection, the study's stated primary objective was safety with no hypothesis tested, and three exploratory 300 mg cohorts including the untreated-PDAC and RAS wild-type cohorts were removed from the report.

honest.t: Liver transplantation for PDAC with liver-only metastases has no outcome data, in this programme or anywhere, and this page takes no institutional position on whether either cohort should open.
honest.why: Where the page speaks in an institutional voice about this gate it is quoting the local V2 protocol, which states its own investigational status, its allocation position and its governance requirements. There is no ratified roadmap behind any of it. The supporting arguments are an analogy to a colorectal trial (TransMet: 94 patients, different disease, allocation priority PDAC does not have, serious adverse events in 32 of 40 transplanted patients — and cited here from its abstract only), retrospective resection series with complete selection asymmetry, a systemic-therapy trial in previously treated metastatic disease that says nothing about transplantation, and immunosuppression reasoning extrapolated from hepatocellular carcinoma. That is four kinds of borrowed evidence and no direct evidence.

honest.t: Two of the papers in this page's depot are not pancreatic cancer papers at all, and nothing on this page about pancreatic cancer rests on them.
honest.why: The hepatocellular carcinoma meta-analysis of mTOR-inhibitor immunosuppression and the AASLD and American Society of Transplantation guideline on evaluating adult liver transplant candidates are both legitimately cited by the liver-only-metastasis gate — the first for the borrowed antitumour rationale behind the protocol's everolimus conversion, the second for the standard transplant candidacy criteria the protocol requires — and they are used only there. Neither can support any claim about pancreatic cancer: the guideline's only mentions of the pancreas concern neuroendocrine tumour liver metastases. The figures this page previously attributed to the hepatocellular meta-analysis (recurrence RR 0.69, 0.53–0.88, and 5-year overall survival RR 1.16, 1.07–1.26) do not appear in it as read; what it reports is, in its three randomised trials, overall survival relative risks of 1.04 (1.00–1.08) at 1 year rising to 1.13 (1.02–1.26) at 5 years, with recurrence-free survival non-significant at 2 years (0.98, 0.75–1.28), and consistently larger estimates from its 14 cohort studies, which is the signature of confounding by indication.

honest.t: The pooled hazard ratio of 0.41 for resecting liver-only metastatic PDAC appears twice in the 2025 literature from largely the same patients, and the better of the two analyses shows it tracks chemotherapy rather than surgery.
honest.why: Two 2025 meta-analyses report 0.41 (0.31–0.53) and 0.41 (0.32–0.52) from substantially overlapping study sets, so citing both double-counts one evidence base. The first pooled only univariate hazard ratios by explicit design, reported I² of 12% from seven retrospective studies with different definitions of oligometastasis, and never mentions immortal-time bias; the second found I² of 64.5% in the same literature. The second's meta-regression is the finding: the relative rate of chemotherapy between arms explained 87.1% of between-study heterogeneity, roughly half the non-surgical patients received gemcitabine monotherapy against multi-agent regimens in the surgical arm, and the adjusted effect reached HR 0.18 (0.08–0.40) only where both pre- and postoperative chemotherapy were given, with no difference in any other scenario — an estimate fitted to 7 comparisons with 11 candidate covariates that its own authors call mathematical rather than empirical. The first review's own data say the same thing: a 32.5-versus-9.2-month gap generated by a RECIST response criterion, and the best outcomes in the whole review coming from 52 patients whose liver metastases had completely regressed and who had only the primary resected. Nationally, 891 of 47,785 patients with liver-only stage IV disease (1.9%) had the primary resected, only 137 (0.29%) had a metastasectomy, only 13.5% had preoperative chemotherapy, 85% had the primary removed without touching the liver metastases, and the whole surgical cohort's median survival was 10.74 months — no better than chemotherapy alone in unselected metastatic disease.

honest.t: The comparator for the transplant question is 26 to 39 months, not 7 to 12 — and that makes the case harder, not easier.
honest.why: A protocol that requires a sustained response through at least 12 months selects precisely the patients whose expected survival on systemic therapy alone is long. In the registry cohort that quantifies this, median overall survival was 7 months (5–9) for all 241 stage IV patients with synchronous liver metastases and the same in the 144 with liver-only disease; 26 months (19–33) for the 54 who received chemotherapy and survived past 12 months; 26 months (17–39) for the 27 of those with liver-only disease; and 39 months (13–not reached) for the 9 who also had a resectable primary and resectable liver-only metastases. All of that was achieved with no operation. The 39-month figure rests on nine patients, five of them dead, and the 12-month landmark was imposed specifically to mitigate immortal-time bias. Two features make it conservative rather than flattering: CA 19-9 was deliberately excluded from the selection criteria, so the benchmark cohort's median CA 19-9 was 3,101 U/mL with 64% rising — patients no surgeon would operate on — and imaging was available for review in only 80 of 183 patients with liver metastases. It is still the right comparator, and the local protocol's own consent section concedes the point. There were no 5-year survivors in the benchmark cohort.

honest.t: Three of the references on this page are still cited from abstract only, and several more are carried only in the machine-extracted guideline text.
honest.why: No new papers were obtained for this depot in this pass. The ISGPS lymphadenectomy consensus (PMID 25061003), which supplies the nodal stations and the no-benefit claim for extended lymphadenectomy in the surgery gate, the IHPBA consensus on transplantation for non-resectable colorectal liver metastases (PMID 34506756), and TransMet (PMID 39306468) were not retrieved and are cited from their abstracts; their figures have not been checked against their published reports and their limitations have not been read. Separately, PAXG, RTOG 0848, the ESPAC-3 completion analysis, CONKO-004, maintenance rucaparib, the EUS staging figures, the 56% re-imaging figure and the margin-clearance survival figures in the pathology discussion are carried only in the NCCN discussion text supplied to the programme, with no primary report retrieved. Every one of those is graded D or flagged on the page, and every one should be read before it is leaned on.

honest.t: Industry sponsors chose the comparator in four of the trials this page cites, and in each case the choice was the one most favourable to the sponsor.
honest.why: APACT tested the sponsor's proprietary nab-paclitaxel added to a generic backbone against that backbone alone, in a trial the sponsor designed, monitored and analysed with a sponsor-employed statistician, after ESPAC-4 and PRODIGE-24 had already superseded gemcitabine monotherapy. MPACT did the same, continuing against gemcitabine alone for 11 months after FOLFIRINOX was published, with the sponsor designing the protocol, supplying the drug, monitoring the study and employing the statistician who vouched for the data. NAPOLI 3 tested a proprietary liposomal irinotecan against nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine rather than against generic FOLFIRINOX, with the sponsor participating in design, collection, analysis, interpretation and manuscript approval, and reported neither cost nor quality of life. RASolute 302 used unconstrained investigator's-choice chemotherapy as its comparator, with the sponsor performing and validating the analyses. None of this makes the results wrong; it does mean the comparator in each case is the weakest defensible one, which is exactly what inflates a hazard ratio.

honest.t: The tumour board operating model below is reproduced from the programme's other disease roadmaps so that there is one operating standard rather than seven. It is evidence grade D by construction.
honest.why: These are stakeholder-derived operating requirements, labelled Standard because the programme has chosen them, not because trials support them. Audit them for adherence, not for effectiveness. What is specific to this disease is the pace — a staging scan expires in 4 weeks, so a case that waits two board cycles needs re-imaging — and, after the full-text read, the need for someone to adjudicate the resectability category, because roughly a third of patients called resectable by their own centres are not.

board: Submission — an Epic form captures the clinical question, the resectability category with arterial and venous contact in degrees, the date and protocol of the staging CT, bilirubin and drainage status, CA 19-9 with the bilirubin it was drawn against, performance status with nutritional intake, germline and genomic profiling status, prior treatment, referring clinician and urgency. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage — a coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check completeness, imaging quality and protocol, duplicate cases, the urgent lane, and whether the question is actually a decision question. A non-pancreas-protocol CT is returned for re-imaging rather than discussed, and the degrees of arterial and venous contact are checked against the images by a named reader before the case is listed — in SWOG S1505, 29% of patients called resectable by their own centres did not meet the criteria on central review. Owners: coordinator and chair.

Imaging currency — the staging scan's date is read out with the case. High-quality CT older than 4 weeks is re-acquired before an operative decision is taken, and a case that waits two board cycles is re-imaged. This is the one operating rule specific to this disease. Owner: coordinator.
Agenda — stable at least 24 hours ahead, approximately 10–12 decision cases per session, each carrying one focused question. Owner: coordinator.

Urgent lane — a same-week slot with chair approval, used routinely here: cholangitis, a rising bilirubin and gastric outlet obstruction are time-critical, and so is a borderline resectable patient whose scan is about to expire. Owner: chair.

Attendance — surgical oncology or hepatopancreatobiliary surgery, medical oncology, radiation oncology, diagnostic radiology, advanced endoscopy, pathology, genetics or a genetic counsellor, nutrition, palliative care and coordination are all required. Transplant surgery attends only for cases routed to the liver-only metastasis gate, and attends with research governance. Owners: specialty leads.

Resectability call — the category is assigned in the meeting, by consensus, and recorded with the degrees of contact, the date and the names of those who agreed it. A single-reader determination is not accepted as the category, and the category is recorded as what it is: a consensus threshold nobody derived, applied to a measurement with no published inter-reader reproducibility. Owner: chair.

Pathology — pre-alerted for every resection specimen, with the agreed inking and slicing protocol and millimetre reporting of every margin within 1.0 cm of tumour; peritoneal washing results are reported to the board, not only to the chart. Owner: pathology.

Margin reporting agreement — the inking, slicing and millimetre-reporting format is agreed with pathology in writing once, and the local R1 rate is tracked, because applying the 1 mm rule moved the R1 rate at the centre that derived it from 44% to 79% and R0 rates are therefore not comparable between units or trials. Owner: pathology and chair.

Molecular — germline testing offered to every patient at the first board appearance regardless of family history, and comprehensive genomic profiling plus HER2 immunohistochemistry ordered for every patient with metastatic disease, with a named person responsible for chasing the report. Owner: medical oncology.

Output — one recommendation, one owner, one due date, one reassessment date, one documented alternative considered. For every resectable and borderline resectable patient the output also names who delivers chemotherapy and when, before the operation. Owner: chair.
Documentation — an Epic note within one business day, in the agreed structured format, recording the resectability category, the sequence chosen and the reason. Owner: named owner.

Registry — the case closed in the registry with the category, the decision, the modality delivered, the resection and margin outcome, and the outcome at reassessment. Any case discussed under the liver-only metastasis gate is entered in the research registry whether or not it proceeds. Owner: coordinator.

Referring relationships — the referring clinician is informed of the recommendation and of who owns the next step. Community-referring relationships are protected explicitly: the pathway returns patients with a plan, it does not capture them. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: Resectability category at diagnosis, sequence chosen (upfront resection or neoadjuvant), resection rate, R0 rate and time from diagnosis to first treatment — the audit that tests ratification item 1.

Proportion of staging scans that are pancreas-protocol, proportion re-imaged after referral, proportion of operations performed on a scan more than 4 weeks old, and the proportion of cases in which the board's resectability category differed from the referring report — the local equivalent of the 29% misclassification rate found on central review in SWOG S1505 (ratification item 12).
Proportion of staging reports stating arterial and venous contact in degrees against the SAR/APA template.
Proportion of jaundiced patients whose EUS biopsy and ERCP were done in one anaesthetic, and proportion of patients going to upfront surgery who were stented without an indication.

Jaundiced patients going on to neoadjuvant therapy: stent type, time to start of chemotherapy, cholangitis and re-intervention episodes, and treatment delays attributable to persistent jaundice — the population the one randomised drainage trial excluded (ratification item 13).
Stent type by diagnostic certainty, occlusion and re-intervention rate, and cholangitis episodes.
R0 rate with margin clearance reported in millimetres, by procedure and by vascular resection type; nodal yield and station compliance; 90-day mortality; annual volume (ratification items 2 and 3).

Adjuvant regimen, cycles completed, dose intensity, and time from surgery to first cycle — including the proportion of resected patients who never start adjuvant therapy, which is the number both sides of the sequencing argument rely on (ratification items 4 and 5).
In locally advanced disease: induction regimen, proportion reaching exploration, resection rate, R0 rate, local progression, and overall survival from the start of induction (ratification item 6).
In locally advanced disease, separately: 30- and 90-day mortality after conversion surgery, against the 8% 30-day figure in the only randomised trial that reports it (ratification item 14).
First-line metastatic regimen, performance status at start, and reason for discontinuation (ratification item 7).

Proportion of metastatic patients with a completed germline result and completed genomic profile before second line, time from biopsy to report, and proportion of actionable results acted on (ratification item 8).

Every case discussed under the liver-only metastasis gate: whether a protocol was open, whether the patient met criteria, the decision taken, and the outcome — recorded whether or not any operation was performed (ratification items 9 and 10).

Registry closure rate, and reassessment adherence: restaging before adjuvant therapy, restaging 4–8 weeks after neoadjuvant therapy, every 8 weeks on neoadjuvant or induction therapy, and per protocol on the research pathway.

Source currency: for every numeric criterion on the page, the edition and date of the source it was verified against, which references remain cited from abstract only, and which figures are carried solely in the machine-extracted guideline text (ratification items 11, 15 and 16).

approvals.q: For an anatomically resectable tumour with no high-risk features, is the local default upfront resection with adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX, or a neoadjuvant route — and if neoadjuvant, which regimen?
approvals.why: The trials disagree and the page does not resolve them, and the full-text read made the disagreement worse rather than better. No neoadjuvant trial gave its control arm modern adjuvant therapy except NORPACT-1, and there only 19 of 44 resected control patients (43%) received adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX; PREOPANC's control arm received adjuvant gemcitabine and only 51% of it received any chemotherapy; PREOPANC-2 has no upfront-surgery arm; S1505 and A021501 had no randomised control at all. Pooled across nine randomised trials the resectable subgroup shows no benefit (HR 0.90, 0.63–1.28) and the borderline resectable subgroup does (HR 0.60, 0.38–0.96), but the between-subgroup test is not significant (p=0.081) and the pooled estimate depends on post hoc removal of NORPACT-1. NORPACT-1's primary endpoint favoured upfront surgery at a two-sided alpha of 0.15, was non-significant per protocol, and had 21% of its neoadjuvant arm go straight to resection without the drug. ESMO recommends against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease at [II, E]. The pooled data also show no gain in adjuvant initiation (57.7% versus 55.6%, p=0.353), which removes the main mechanistic argument. A021806 has not reported. This has to be a local decision because there is no guideline answer to copy and no trial of the comparison that matters.
approvals.audit: Registry: resectability category, sequence chosen, resection rate, R0 rate, time from diagnosis to first treatment, and proportion of resected patients who never start adjuvant therapy.

approvals.q: Does this programme offer arterial resection, or arterial divestment, for PDAC — and if so at what minimum volume, by which surgeons, and under what consent document?
approvals.why: NCCN restricts it to centres with proven experience in pancreatectomy with vascular resection and reconstruction, in highly selected patients after extensive neoadjuvant therapy with objective response, and requires patients to be told that the long-term benefit is currently unknown. It names no threshold. This is a governance decision taken once, not a decision taken in the room.
approvals.audit: Audit: volume, 90-day mortality and R0 rate by vascular resection type; consent document on file.

approvals.q: What counts locally as a significant response after neoadjuvant therapy, and who decides?
approvals.why: NCCN hands the definition to the local treatment team and offers only examples — CA 19-9 normalisation, near-normalisation or at least a 50% decrease, and a complete or near-complete metabolic response on PET. Since the response category determines whether a vascular resection is offered, an unwritten definition is applied inconsistently.
approvals.audit: Audit: response category recorded for every neoadjuvant patient, resection attempted, R0 rate.

approvals.q: Is mFOLFIRINOX the adjuvant default for every recovered good-performance-status patient, and what threshold moves a patient to gemcitabine with capecitabine?
approvals.why: On mature 5-year data PRODIGE 24 gives median overall survival 53.5 versus 35.5 months and 5-year survival 43.2% versus 31.4%, at the cost of grade 3–4 adverse events in 75.9% versus 52.9%, in a trial restricted to age under 80, no coronary disease, WHO performance status 0–1, full surgical recovery and postoperative CA 19-9 below 180 U/mL. The effect attenuated from the 3-year report (DFS HR 0.58 to 0.66, OS 0.64 to 0.68), 5-year disease-free survival differs by only 7.1 points, only 33.6% of patients achieved a relative dose intensity of 0.80 or more, post-relapse survival was numerically worse in the mFOLFIRINOX arm (13.1 versus 15.0 months) with fewer of its relapsing patients receiving any chemotherapy (66.9% versus 83.0%), and in the 101 patients aged 70 or older the benefit did not reach significance (HR 0.86, 0.53–1.39). Nothing in it describes the patient who has not recovered from a pancreatoduodenectomy, which is a substantial fraction of the real population, and quality of life was never collected.
approvals.audit: Registry: adjuvant regimen, cycles completed, dose intensity, grade 3–4 toxicity, time from surgery to first cycle.

approvals.q: What is the local rule for adjuvant therapy after neoadjuvant therapy — total duration, same regimen or switch, and what to do after a complete pathologic response?
approvals.why: NCCN says only that the options depend on response and other clinical factors, and no trial defines any of it. PREOPANC-2's FOLFIRINOX arm gave no adjuvant treatment at all while its chemoradiotherapy arm gave four cycles of gemcitabine, so even the trials do not agree on the shape of the sequence.
approvals.audit: Registry: total perioperative cycles delivered, regimen before and after surgery, pathologic response, recurrence.

approvals.q: Is consolidative chemoradiotherapy after induction therapy in locally advanced disease offered routinely, only where conversion to resection is the stated objective, or not at all?
approvals.why: LAP07 (HR 1.03, P=.83, stopped at interim for futility with that analysis declared final, 18% major radiotherapy protocol deviations, survival measured from the first of two randomisations) and CONKO-007 (HR 0.937, P=.57, primary endpoint not met at 25% versus 18% R0) are both null for overall survival. CONKO-007's primary endpoint was changed mid-trial from overall survival to R0 rate with the new effect size calculated from its own unblinded interim data on 180 already-enrolled patients, its radiotherapy was never centrally reviewed for stated financial reasons, and its significant R0 advantage (69.4% versus 50.0%) is confined to patients who reached theatre, which was not randomised. What both trials do show is better local control (CONKO-007 locoregional recurrence HR 0.33, 0.206–0.530, P<.001; LAP07 32% versus 46%, P=.03). Neither tested radiotherapy after a FOLFIRINOX backbone followed by modern surgery and modern adjuvant therapy, so the local position has to be a judgement about objectives rather than a reading of evidence.
approvals.audit: Registry: induction regimen, radiation given or not, proportion reaching exploration, R0 rate, local progression, overall survival from the start of induction.

approvals.q: Which triplet is the local first-line standard in metastatic disease — (m)FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX — and what counts locally as good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake?
approvals.why: The two triplets sit at the same median overall survival (11.1 months) against different comparators in different eras, there is no randomised comparison between them, and NCCN states NALIRIFOX does not appear to have clear advantages over FOLFIRINOX or mFOLFIRINOX. The second half matters as much: NCCN's eligibility definition for intensive therapy is ECOG 0–1 with good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake, and the latter two are not currently recorded in a way that can be audited. [PAYER]
approvals.audit: Registry: first-line regimen, performance status, drainage and nutritional status at start, dose intensity, reason for discontinuation.

approvals.q: Who owns chasing the molecular report, and where does daraxonrasib sit in the local second-line sequence?
approvals.why: The commonest failure in metastatic PDAC is a genomic report that arrives after the patient is too unwell to act on it, which is an operational problem with a named-owner solution. The sequencing question is separate: RASolute 302 is a phase 3 result with dual primary endpoints met in the RAS G12 population (median overall survival 13.2 versus 6.6 months, HR 0.40; progression-free survival 7.3 versus 3.5 months, HR 0.45), but the benefit is not established outside G12 (non-G12 HR 1.38, 0.60–3.17), 38 of 252 patients (15.1%) allocated to the comparator never received it against 7 of 248 (2.8%) on daraxonrasib, and the comparator was unconstrained investigator's choice with a 6.6-month median at the low end of published second-line outcomes. The local position depends on availability, regulatory status and cost, and should state which RAS alterations it covers. [PAYER]
approvals.audit: Registry: proportion with completed germline and genomic results before second line, time from biopsy to report, proportion of actionable results acted on, second-line agent.

approvals.q: Does this programme open either liver-only metastasis transplant cohort at all, and under whose governance?
approvals.why: PDAC with liver metastases is not a standardized OPTN exception diagnosis and is not among the recommended diagnoses in the December 2025 transplant-oncology guidance; no MELD exception is recommended or guaranteed. There is no outcome data for either cohort anywhere. This is a graft-stewardship and research-ethics decision before it is a clinical one, and it requires prospective IRB approval, DSMB oversight, institutional transplant-selection and allocation-ethics approval, and independent living-donor advocacy where applicable.
approvals.audit: Research registry required if either cohort opens, with the protocol's own stopping rules as standing triggers. Until then, record every case discussed under this gate and the decision taken.

approvals.q: If a cohort opens, what is the consent standard — given that the honest comparator is 26 to 39 months of expected survival on systemic therapy in exactly the responders the protocol selects?
approvals.why: Patients must understand that transplantation for PDAC liver metastases is investigational with no established precedent, and that the incremental benefit of the operation over continued chemotherapy is unknown. The honest comparator is 26 to 39 months: in the registry cohort that quantifies it, patients who received chemotherapy and survived to a 12-month landmark reached a median of 26 months, and the 9 who also had a resectable primary and resectable liver-only disease reached 39 months (13–not reached) with no operation and with 5-year survival of 0%. The local protocol concedes the point. Consent must also state that the protocol's own ctDNA criteria rest on a figure (47% complete ctDNA clearance) that could not be found in the published phase 1–2 report, and that the daraxonrasib overall survival figure the protocol quotes (14.5 months) is 13.1 months in that report.
approvals.audit: Consent document on file and approved; every enrolled patient in the prospective registry; DSMB minutes recorded against the protocol's stopping rules.

approvals.q: What is the surveillance schedule after resection, and who owns the NCCN and OPTN update check?
approvals.why: The guideline footnote defining the surveillance interval did not survive the machine extraction supplied to this page, so no interval is quoted here. What is known is that regular surveillance CT showed no significant survival benefit in a SEER-Medicare analysis, CA 19-9 is category 2B, and serial ctDNA monitoring has no evidence of benefit — so the interval is a local choice about what surveillance is for. Separately, every numeric criterion on this page needs an owner for re-verification against the next guideline edition and the current OPTN policy text.
approvals.audit: Named owner plus edition and date, with an agreed update cycle; surveillance interval recorded and adherence audited once set.

approvals.q: Who adjudicates the resectability category before it is used to route a patient, given that roughly a third of patients called resectable by their own centres do not meet the criteria?
approvals.why: In SWOG S1505, at experienced US trial centres with a mandatory pancreas-protocol scan within 28 days and formal surgical consultation within 21 days, central radiology review found 43 of 146 patients (29%) did not meet the resectability criteria — 51% with arterial interface, 35% with venous interface of 180 degrees or more, 65% with suspicion of distant disease — and all had already started protocol therapy. A site radiologist checklist moved the rate only from 33% to 26%. The category decides which gate on this page a patient enters, so the group must decide whether a second independent read, a radiology lead sign-off or an external review is required, and for which categories.
approvals.audit: Registry: proportion of cases where the board's category differed from the referring report, by referring source; proportion of operations abandoned at exploration for disease more advanced than imaging suggested.

approvals.q: What is the local rule for biliary drainage in a patient going on to neoadjuvant therapy — stent type, expected duration, who re-images and who owns the jaundice if it does not settle?
approvals.why: The only randomised trial of preoperative drainage used plastic stents for 4 to 6 weeks, capped bilirubin at 250 micromol/L, excluded neoadjuvant chemotherapy by protocol, and required an operation within one week in its control arm, guaranteed by dedicated theatre capacity at all 13 hospitals. It showed that the drainage strategy caused more complications overall (74% versus 39%) while surgical complications did not differ (37% versus 47%, RR 0.79, 0.57–1.11), so it says nothing about bridging a patient through months of preoperative treatment. That situation is where drainage is now most often needed and where it most often derails treatment: NORPACT-1 stented 57% of its neoadjuvant arm against 16% of the surgery arm, and two of the 16 patients who never received neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX were lost to persistent jaundice after stenting and two to biliary infection; PREOPANC had 10 patients whose treatment was delayed by persistent jaundice.
approvals.audit: Registry: stent type by diagnostic certainty, time from stent to first cycle, cholangitis and re-intervention rate, and treatment delays or non-receipt attributable to jaundice.

approvals.q: Does this programme offer conversion surgery after induction therapy in locally advanced disease, and what operative mortality is quoted in the consent conversation?
approvals.why: CONKO-007 is the only randomised trial that reports it: of 336 patients randomised after three months of induction without progression, 122 (36% to 37%) reached theatre, 73 of 336 (22%) achieved R0, and 30-day postoperative mortality was 8% in both arms (5 of 60 and 5 of 62). The survival advantage of surgery within that trial (HR 0.525, 0.408–0.676) is a non-randomised comparison of operated with non-operated patients. LAP07, from gemcitabine-based induction, reached resection in 18 of 442 patients (4%). The 159 of 495 patients (32.1%) who progressed during induction had a median survival of 9 months with no 5-year survivors. The group must decide whether it offers this at all, to whom, and with what number on the consent form.
approvals.audit: Registry: proportion reaching exploration and resection, R0 rate with millimetre clearance, 30- and 90-day mortality, and overall survival from the start of induction including patients who progressed before any surgical assessment.

approvals.q: Who re-sources the daraxonrasib figures in the local transplant protocol, and does either cohort open before that is done?
approvals.why: Two figures the protocol relies on do not match the published phase 1–2 report read for this depot: the median overall survival quoted as 14.5 months is 13.1 months (95% CI 10.9 to not evaluable) in that report, and the 47% complete ctDNA clearance figure does not appear in it as read. The second matters operationally, because a declining or undetectable RAS-mutant ctDNA is an entry criterion in Protocol A and a ctDNA fall of 50% or more is a conversion criterion in Protocol B, so the protocol's own gates are calibrated against a figure that has not been verified. V2 already corrected V1's conflation of phase 3 survival with phase 1–2 response and ctDNA data; this is the same class of error one layer down.
approvals.audit: Named owner, source document and date for every daraxonrasib figure in the protocol, recorded before activation; V3 revision note if any figure changes.

approvals.q: Who owns retrieving the three references still cited from abstract only, and the figures carried solely in the machine-extracted guideline text?
approvals.why: No new papers were obtained for this depot in this pass. The ISGPS lymphadenectomy consensus supplies the nodal stations and the no-benefit claim for extended lymphadenectomy in the surgery gate; the IHPBA consensus supplies the immunosuppression reasoning borrowed into the transplant gate; TransMet supplies the whole analogy the transplant gate rests on. None of the three was read in full, so none of their figures has been checked and none of their limitations has been read. Separately, PAXG, RTOG 0848, the ESPAC-3 completion analysis, CONKO-004, maintenance rucaparib, the EUS staging figures, the 56% re-imaging figure and the margin-clearance survival figures are carried only in the NCCN discussion text supplied to the programme, and the margin-clearance figures appear in a sentence that inverts them.
approvals.audit: Named owner per reference, with retrieval date and a note of any figure that changed on reading; the page's grades revisited where a D was assigned for provenance rather than for design.

nccn: National Comprehensive Cancer Network. Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma. NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology. Machine-converted guideline text supplied to the programme; the local transplant protocol dates the same source to 22 April 2026. The extraction carries no printed version number, and the version string must be confirmed and recorded before publication. Sections used: Clinical Presentation and Workup; Principles of Diagnosis, Imaging and Staging, including the MDCT and MRI protocols and the radiology reporting template; Criteria Defining Resectability Status at Diagnosis; Criteria for Resection Following Neoadjuvant Therapy and its Table 1; Biliary Drainage and Tissue Acquisition; Pathologic Analysis; Principles of Systemic Therapy; Principles of Radiation Therapy; Palliative and Supportive Care; and the Discussion sections on diagnosis and staging, management of resectable and borderline resectable disease, postoperative therapy, surveillance, recurrent disease, locally advanced disease, metastatic disease and systemic therapy approaches. The extraction is layout-mangled in places — the margin-clearance survival figures in the pathology discussion appear in an inverted sentence, and the footnote defining the post-resection surveillance interval is missing — so both were flagged on the page rather than quoted as read.
optn: Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network. Policy 9: Allocation of Livers and Liver-Intestines, including Policies 9.4 and 9.5 on MELD or PELD score exceptions. US Department of Health and Human Services, HRSA. Named in the local protocol as a controlling allocation source at its policy review date of 16 July 2026. PDAC with liver metastases is not a standardized exception diagnosis under Policy 9.5. The current posted text was not re-verified for this page and must be checked before any listing decision.
optnonc: Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, Liver and Intestinal Organ Transplantation Committee. Guidance to Liver Transplant Programs and the National Liver Review Board for Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology. December 2025. PDAC with liver metastases is not among the recommended diagnoses. This document is review-board guidance, not OPTN policy, and does not define a clinical standard of care.
uthv2: UTHealth PDAC liver-only LT protocol V2

UTHealth Houston Experimental Liver Transplantation Protocol for PDAC with Liver-Only Metastases, Version 2. Revision timestamp 23 July 2026; policy review date 16 July 2026. Labelled HIGH-RISK / INVESTIGATIONAL throughout. This is the controlling local document for the liver-only metastasis gate on this page, and the only document from which this page speaks in an institutional voice. Its V2 revision note records that V1 conflated phase 3 daraxonrasib survival results with phase 1–2 response and ctDNA findings, proposed unapproved post-transplant drug combinations without IND controls, omitted inequality operators from its stopping rules, and included a non-retrievable personal citation.
uthv1: UTHealth PDAC liver-only LT protocol V1

UTHealth Houston Liver Transplantation Protocol for Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma with Liver-Only Metastases, Version 1 (undated, superseded). Retained on this page only to document what V2 removed: a fixed daraxonrasib dose of 300 mg daily outside an IND-authorized safety lead-in, chemotherapy combinations at investigator discretion, routine post-transplant daraxonrasib maintenance for a minimum of 12 months, an optional daraxonrasib-plus-afatinib cohort, deceased-donor transplantation described as acceptable if living donation were unavailable, and stopping rules written without inequality operators. V1 must not be used.
a021806: Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology. A phase III trial of perioperative versus adjuvant chemotherapy for resectable pancreatic cancer (A021806). ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04340141. Phase 3, enrolment 358, primary endpoint overall survival from randomisation, start date 13 October 2020, status active and not recruiting, primary completion scheduled 31 December 2028, no results posted; record checked 6 October 2026. A trials-in-progress abstract exists (J Clin Oncol 2023;41(16 suppl):TPS4204) but no results publication. Cited on this page only as an open question.
cap: College of American Pathologists. Protocol for the examination of specimens from patients with carcinoma of the exocrine pancreas. Cited through NCCN for the rule that tumour at or within 1 mm of a resection margin constitutes a positive margin, and for the requirement to report clearance with millimetre accuracy for margins within 1.0 cm of tumour. The current protocol version was not retrieved for this page and should be confirmed with pathology.
rtog0848: Randomised trial of fluoropyrimidine-based chemoradiation after adjuvant gemcitabine-based chemotherapy in resected adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head. Reported on this page through the NCCN discussion text only: longer overall and disease-free survival with added chemoradiation in node-negative patients, no improvement in node-positive patients, in patients treated with single-agent gemcitabine. The primary publication was not retrieved and should be read before the result is relied on.
paxg: Randomised phase 3 trial across 17 Italian academic hospitals (n=260) of PAXG — cisplatin, nab-paclitaxel, capecitabine and gemcitabine — against mFOLFIRINOX in pathologically confirmed resectable or borderline resectable disease: median event-free survival 16.0 versus 10.2 months, hazard ratio 0.63 (0.47–0.84), P=.0018. Reported on this page through the NCCN discussion text only; the primary publication was not retrieved. NCCN lists PAXG as useful in certain circumstances because not all centres have experience with the regimen.
espac3: Retrospective analysis of the ESPAC-3 trial finding that completion of the six-course adjuvant chemotherapy, but not the time to initiate it, was an independent prognostic factor for survival. Reported on this page through the NCCN discussion text only; the primary publication was not retrieved and the analysis is vulnerable to the obvious confounder that patients who complete treatment are patients well enough to complete it.
conko004: Randomised trial of prophylactic enoxaparin in advanced pancreatic cancer (n=160 versus 152): cumulative incidence of symptomatic venous thromboembolism lower with enoxaparin, hazard ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.19–0.83), P=.01, with no difference in progression-free or overall survival. Reported on this page through the NCCN discussion text only. NCCN does not recommend prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin, citing the absence of a survival effect.
isgps: Tol JAMG, Gouma DJ, Bassi C, et al. Definition of a standard lymphadenectomy in surgery for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: a consensus statement by the International Study Group on Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS). Surgery. 2014;156(3):591-600. doi:10.1016/j.surg.2014.06.016. PMID:25061003. Listed here as well as in the reference library to record that no full text was obtained for this depot: the nodal station list, the claim that extended lymphadenectomy gives no survival benefit, and the absence of consensus on what to do when a frozen-section node outside the resection field is positive are all taken from the abstract and the consensus statement's own summary, not from the trials behind them. The item it supports in the surgery gate is graded C for that reason.

provenance: Revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of this pathway's entire reference depot — 36 papers, each read in full and abstracted with the authors' stated limitations and an independent critique. The first draft was built from the extracted NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma guideline text supplied to the programme (undated in the extraction; the local transplant protocol dates the same source to 22 April 2026) as the spine, together with the two local liver-only-metastasis transplant documents — the UTHealth Houston experimental protocol Version 2, revised 23 July 2026 with a policy review date of 16 July 2026, and its superseded Version 1 — and primary literature retrieved and verified through PubMed on 6 October 2026, with every PMID confirmed against its journal, year, volume, first page and first author. This revision replaces figures read from abstracts with figures read from the full reports, corrects the figures that were wrong, and downgrades the evidence grade on every item where the full text showed the design would not carry the claim. The grades moved on roughly thirty strings and almost all of them moved down. The single most consequential finding, which runs through the resectable, borderline resectable and adjuvant gates, is that almost no trial on this page compared its intervention with the therapy this page recommends: every adjuvant comparator is gemcitabine monotherapy or observation, and every neoadjuvant comparator is upfront surgery followed by adjuvant gemcitabine or S-1, except NORPACT-1, where only 19 of 44 resected control patients received adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX. No new papers were obtained for this depot in this pass. Three references remain cited from abstract only, and the items they support are graded and flagged accordingly: the ISGPS lymphadenectomy consensus (PMID 25061003), which supplies the nodal stations and the extended-lymphadenectomy claim in the surgery gate; the IHPBA consensus on transplantation for non-resectable colorectal liver metastases (PMID 34506756), from which the local protocol's immunosuppression regimen is adapted; and TransMet (PMID 39306468), the colorectal trial the transplant gate's analogy rests on. For none of the three have the figures been checked against the published report or the stated limitations been read. Two files in the depot are not pancreatic cancer papers at all — a meta-analysis of mTOR-inhibitor immunosuppression after liver transplantation for hepatocellular carcinoma (PMID 34919773) and the AASLD and American Society of Transplantation guideline on evaluating adult liver transplant candidates (PMID 41405234). Both are legitimately cited by the liver-only-metastasis transplant gate, for the borrowed antitumour rationale and for standard transplant candidacy respectively, and both are used only in that gate; neither can support any claim about pancreatic cancer and the page does not use them for one. The figures previously attributed to the hepatocellular meta-analysis were not in it and have been replaced with what it reports. Several figures are still carried only in the machine-extracted guideline text supplied to the programme, with no primary report retrieved, and every item resting on one is now graded D: PAXG, RTOG 0848, the ESPAC-3 completion analysis, CONKO-004, maintenance rucaparib, the pembrolizumab and dostarlimab listings, the NTRK, RET, BRAF and FGFR basket results, the EUS staging sensitivities and the 56% re-imaging figure. Where the extraction is mangled the page still says so: the margin-clearance survival figures in the pathology discussion appear in a sentence that inverts them, and the footnote defining the post-resection surveillance interval is missing, so no interval is stated here. Three figures the first draft carried could not be verified against the full text and have been corrected or flagged: POLO's placebo-arm median overall survival is 18.1 months and not 16.1; the phase 1–2 daraxonrasib median overall survival is 13.1 months and not 14.5; and the 47% complete ctDNA clearance figure quoted by the local protocol does not appear in the published phase 1–2 report as read, which matters because ctDNA decline is an entry and conversion criterion in both local cohorts. SWOG S1505's perioperative completion rate, previously given as 76%, is 49% and 40% by arm. Allocation statements for the transplant gate remain those of the local Version 2 document, which names OPTN Policies 9.4 and 9.5 as currently posted and the December 2025 National Liver Review Board transplant-oncology guidance as its controlling sources; neither was re-verified for this page and both must be checked before any listing decision. Alliance A021806 is cited only from its ClinicalTrials.gov record (NCT04340141, checked 6 October 2026) because it has reported nothing. This remains a draft and there is no ratified roadmap behind it. Unlike the programme's five existing disease roadmaps, this pathway transcribes no approved institutional document other than the investigational transplant protocol, and it takes no institutional position of its own: where the published guidelines and the randomised trials disagree — most sharply on whether an anatomically resectable patient goes to theatre first, where ESMO now recommends against neoadjuvant therapy at grade II, E and the pooled trial data neither confirm nor refute it against a modern comparator — the page shows the disagreement and refers the choice to the sixteen ratification items in the approvals section. It is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.
